THE MILKMAID. A NEW SONG TO AN OLD TUNE. Acrosa the grass I see her pass; She comes with tripping pace,— A maid I know,—and March winds blow Her hair across her face;— With a hey, Dolly! ho, Dolly! Dolly shall be mine; Before the spray is white with May, Or blooms the eglantine. The March winds blow. I watch her go: Her eye is brown and clear; Her cheek is brown, and soft as down (To those who see it near!) With a hey, as. What has she not that they have got,— The dames that walk- in silk! If she undo her 'kerchief blue, Her neck is white as milk. With a hey, &c. Let those who will be proud and chili! For me, from Juue to June, My Dolly's words are sweet as curds— Her laugh is like a tune. With a hey, &c. Break, break to heat, 0 crocus-spear! 0 tall Lent-lilies, flame! There'll be a bride at Easter-tide, And Dolly is her name. With a hey, Dolly! ho, Dolly! Dolly shall be mine,— .he spray is white with May, Or blooms the eglantine. —Harper's Christmas Number.

div.head: HIS COLD.
div.p: HIS COLD.

Is it not hard to live one day, When God His face has turned away, When prayer is wingless, or her wing Droops earthward like some weary thing? Yet did no bent and broken light Pierce the dark vault of utter night, Of hope or memory no ray, Who could abide His cold one day? Summer and winter, sun and rain, The soul needs for her golden grain— Warm sun, warm rain, the ear to fill, His cold, love's selfishness to kill. Come, winter, come, to kill dull pelf, Love of His sweetness not Himself; Till we can kiss His frowning face, Tinniest our soul for summer grace. But when the harvest-tide is nigh, God grant His summer fill the sky, God grant His harvest-rays be shed, God grant His harvest-moon rise red. Cold is the shore, and dark the tide, Through which to His warm arms we glide; But if He then His face withheld, Who can that day abide His cold? Not in the winter be our flight! Then need we most His summer light, His presence felt, His angels near, His bride to bless, His bread to cheer. From strength to strength, from Thee to Thee, Grant, Lord, our summer flight may be; From veiled form and mystic grace To splendours of Thine unveiled face. —F. S'. Pierpoint, in" Good Words."

"Hobson," said Muggins, "they tell me you've taken your boy away from the school. What's that for?" "'Cause," said Hobson, "the master ain't fit to teach 'in'." "Oh," said Muggins, "I've heard he's a very good master." "Well," replied Hobson, apologetically, "all I know is he wanted to teach my boy to spell 'taters with a ' p." Women admire strength without seeking to imitate it; men gentleness without bestowing it in return. Patience is strength; impatience is weakness. To sit quiet, even though woat is going on wearies you, is a gain. Bads do not come up in a day, and if you wait you may find flowers where only a little while ago you thought it was all barren waste. Strive against the disposition to fly from one place to another. Your strength, as was Israel's, is to sit still. AseecnorE or THlCHERAY.—Thackeran was always at one time a welcome visitor at the house of Lady Ashburton, who was somewhat free with her tongue and opinion of others. Something that the saucy hostess said offended her guest, and he not only declined her invitations, bat spoke of her with discourtesy. Some months after, when his angry feelings had died out, he received from Lady Ash- burton a card of invitation to dinner. Ile returned it with a pen-and-ink drawing on the back, representing himself kneeling at her feet, with his hair all aflame from the hot coals she was• pouring on his head out of an ornamental brazier. The humorous expression of contrition was followed by a complete reconciliation. The satirist and the lady continued a warm friendship. WHAT SHALL I TAKE ?—A young lady called on a physician to do something for a rush of blood to the head. "I have been doctoring myself," said the languid fair one, with a smile, to the bluff though kind M.D., while he was feeling her pulse. " Ah,how ?" "hy, I have taken Morison's Pills Cockle's Pills, Allen and Bell's Pills, Bell's Balsam of Liquorice, and Powell's Cough Electuary. I have used Henry's Calcined Magnesia, Fawcett's Anodyne Pills, and—" "Madam !" interrupted the astonished doctor, "did all these do your complaint no good ?" "No. Then what shall I take ?" pettishly inquired the patient. "Take !" ex- claimed the doctor, eyeing her from head to foot, "take !" echoed he, after a moment's reflection—" take! why, take off your stays!" A TRANSFORMATION.—That lad Bill met a youthful ac- quaintance in the street, and exclaimed: "Didn't I tell yoa, Jack Busby, that I was a-going to whip you when I caught you out?" 'Go away, Bill, I don't want to fight." ,"May be you don't think I Can whip you." "It don't make any difference whether you can whip me or not. I don't want to fight. My mother —" "Yes, your mother knows I can whale you." "My mother's dead. She died this morn - hag." In a moment the braggart boy was transformed into a gentle child. "I didn't know it, Jack," he said, "and you mustn't think hard of me. I ain't got nothin' agin you. I wouldn't hit you, and if another boy was ter come up and hit you now I'd knock him down. There, don't cry. What yer got in that bundle ?" "A black dress." "Come on, and let me carry it for you." THE SHADES or NIGHT.—" Keep your little girls out of the streets at night, and save both yourselves and them grief and trouble," says a contemporary. This is sage advice, and we endorse it heartily. At the same time, keep your boys as well as your girls at home at night. The morals of a soil should be as precious to a parent as those of his daughter, and they should be guarded with equal strictness and jealousy. In fact, they should be watched even more closely, as in many ways the boys are 'exposed to temptation to which girls are ordinarily exempt. Parents who allow their boys to run the streets indiscriminately at night may de- pend upon it that no good will come of such practices' but, on the contrary, that much evil may be apprehended. Most lads are easily led, and unfortunately easily influenced, by wicked counsels, and it is often at night, when the darkness seems to shield them even from themselves, that they are led astray by bad companions. Usually % parents confide implicitly in the honour and integrity of their children. It is well that this should be so, and no one coald wish to see their faith in their offspring weakened; but if some of them realised to what evil influences their boys are exposed when out of the range of their eyes and voices at night, and how they are familiarised with vice till it gradually loses its re- pulsiveness, most of them, we venture to say, would unques- tionably be horrorstricken. It is only when some unsus- pecting father Mceives a rude awakening that he realises to what extent he is primarily responsible for the fate that has overtaken his child. Make your home attractive. Let the cheerful light of the domestic circle mellow the character of your sons as well as refine the disposition of your daughters, that both may grow up together as the "polished corners of the temple ;" but if you value the spiritual or temporal welfare of your sons, don't let them run the streets at night. " Climes " AND " Coms."—What is a cold? It is a disturbance of the balance between the several parts of the nervous system, brought about by the shock of a sudden or prolonged exposure to the depressing effect of "chill," although the same physiological results may be produced in the organism by the operation of any agent which is capable of giving the nervous system a similar shock, and thus creat- ing the same kind of disturbance. Nature's provisions against the consequence of a" chill" and for the prevention of a "cold" are sneezing and shivering. A violent fit of sneezing often &wee a chilled body the consequences of the nerve depression, or e aboeisi" to which it has been sub- jected; and :this shock may in its first impression be very limited in its area ; for example, the small extent covered by a draught of cold air rushing through the crevice of a door or window. The nerve centres are aroused from their "collapse" by the commotion or explosive influence of the sneeze. If sneezing fails, nature will try a shiver, which acts mechanically in the same way. If this fails,the effects are likely to be very serious, and bad consequences may ensue. The popular notion reverses the order of events, and hence the saying, "If there is sneezing the cold will be slight, if there is shivering it will be grave ; " whereas it is slight when sneezing suffices to recover the nervous system quickly from its depression, and grave when even strong shivering fails to do so. In case of chill, with threatened cold, sneezing may be produced by a pinch of snuff of any kind. This is how some of the vaunted " cures "of cold by snuff are brought about. Or brisk exercise may ward off the attack. The popular idea is that the circulation is se- stored by these remedies, but the true explanation is that the nervous system and centres are aroused. The first step towards an intelligent treatment of chill and cold is a scientific recognition of their nature.—The Lancet.

div.head: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.
div.p: SCIENTIFIC NOTES.

Professor Edlaud has discovered that a perfect vacuum, so far from being an electrical insulation as generally sup- posed, is really a good conductor of electricity. From experiments recently made at Bochum. Germany, it appears that the use of wetted coal instead of dry entails a loss of 14 per cent. It is popularly supposed that wetting increases the heating effect of coal. A writer in the last number of the Nautical Magazine makes the startling assertion that twenty-seven per cent. of the wrecks of British steamers within the last two years have been due to the use of defective compasses. The blind adherence of the owners to the ordinary pole compass is blamed for many accidents. In 1788 the ships Astrolabe and Boussole, in which Ad- miral la Perouse, the famous French circumnavigator, was exploring the South Sea, disappeared, and no trace could be found of the fate of ships or crew, though every effort was made by the French Government. At last, after the lapse of nearly a century, the wrecks have been found near the coast of the New Hebrides, and numerous anchors, cannon, and other relics secured, some of them fantastically wreathed in coral. An unexpected difficulty has presented itself to the en- gineer of the Panama Canal in the different levels of the ocean at the two ends. At certain times the waters of the Pacific at Panama are seven or eight feet higher than those of the Atlantic at Colon, and Mr. Dingier estimates that the canal will consequently be traversed by a current flow- ing at a rate from five to six miles an hour. It is proposed to build locks at the:Panama end to prevent this current, as it would seriously interfere with navigation. DR. EMIL HOLIIR.—Dr. Holub leaves England to-day on his expedition to the interior of Africa. The intrepid tra- veller, writing yesterday from on board the Pretoria at Southampton, states that he leaves for this journey of a year accompanied by his wife and 11 good servants, includ- ing a carpenter, a wagonmaker, a blacksmith, a gnnmaker, a tailor, and a butcher, besides his black servant girl and a dog. In South Africa he will increase his staff by 19, and afterwards in Central Africa by 40 more black servants. Dr. Holub remarks that he has known the six Europeans he takes with hiin for some years, that they are soldiers, and have been permitted by the War Department to follow him. Mach interest is felt in this arduous undertaking of the tra- veller, and everyone will wish him a successful expedition and a safe and happy return. A WHIS'iLING Mousz.—Several years ago, whilst sitting quietly in my study in Holloway, my attention was attracted to a gentle continuous whistling sound at one side of the room. This occurred on some successive days. I was much puzzled to account for it, until one day our housemaid called me to an adjacent storeroom to witness the performance of a mouse by which she had been startled. Going very care- fully into the room, I saw, sitting on his haunches upon a tin case, a mouse busily engaged in nibbling a piece of bis- cuit, all the while chirming a subdued musical trill, not unlike the softest notes of a canary bird. I listened to the sound for some time, and upon a few subsequent occasions, but soon lost my little lout-footed songster, who I suspect fell a victim to our cat's preference for mouse-flesh ever ' music. I interpreted this musical performance as being the expression of intense gratification, comparable with the pleased purring of a oat.— W. B. Kesteven, M.D., in the Science Monthly. LIQTTID FOU DETERMINING THE SPECIFIC GRAVITY OF Mnenms.—Nearly all natural minerals are heavier than water, and therefore sink in it. Bat when they are placed in a heavy liquid which does not dissolve them, some sink and others float. If two minerals of unlike gravity occur in the same rock, they can be separated by pulverising the rock and putting them in a liquid intermediate in weight between both. A new liquid for this purpose has been de- vised by C. Rohrback, having a density of 357. It is an iodide of barium and mercury, and is prepared as follows :- 100 parts of iodide of barium and about 130 parts of red iodide of mercury are mixed with about 20ce. of distilled water, shaken, and heated on an oil-bath to 150 deg. or 200 deg. C, until dissolved, and then concentrated until it will float a crystal of topaz. After standing several days, the clear liquid is decanted and filtered. It has a yellow colour, boils at 145 deg. C., and refracts light strongly. It can be used for separating axinite, kyanite' in part, epidote, heavy mica, some garnets, and nearly all hornblendes ; also jade, olivine, orthite, nearly all members of the pyroxene group, saussurite, titanite, topaz, heavy tourmaline, vesuvianite, and basaltic rocks. In diluting it to obtain any special density, it is mixed with a dilute solution of the same, so as to avoid precipitation. After the separation, the powdered minerals are washed with a few drops of iodide of potassium. —Science Monthly. BRITISH MEDICAL TEMPERANCE ASSOCIATION.—A quar- terly general meeting of this association was held on Tues- day afternoon, at the rooms of the Medical Society of London, Chandos-street, Cavendish-square. Dr. B. W. Richardson, F.R.S., the president of the association, occu- pied the chair, and in the course of an introductory address said they did not oppose the physiological and scientific administration of alcohol in disease; they treated disease as other physicians did, and they differed from others only in that they used alcohol as a medicine instead of as a food. The relationship generally of the profession, however, to the temperance cause was not so satisfactory. The public was very critical at that moment, and the public mind very much disturbed on general temperance questions. Two able articles which had recently appeared in The Times were in- I tended to have a direct curbing influence on the progress of total abstinence in the United Kingdom. Those articles were pieces of the most perfect irony. When the writer, for instance, spoke of different alcohols, he knew as well as they did that there was only one alcohol in all kinds of alcoholic drink, and when he spoke of alcohol as a food he was quite aware that there was no structural building power in alco- hol, and that it was a hydro-carbon and nothing more. He was frequently told of partially reformed patients who had returned to drinking habits through carelessness on the part of doctors. A man who had once gone wrong and gained the craving for alcohol had no will at all; his will was en- tirely gone, and after that alcohol could not be prescribed for him without great danger.—Dr. C. R. Drysdale then read a paper on "The Comparative Death-rates of Assured Abstainers and Moderate Drinkers."
He rises the highest in the Christian life who bends the lowest. _ _

Sympathy comes near and speaks low. The simple flowers are sociable and benevolent. HE WANTED TO KNow.-1 well-known Detroiter now prowling—not to say growling—through turope writes to an American paper the following touching experience :—I had been for about half an hour, he says, sitting on the deck of one of the miserable little "packets" that ply be- tween Dover and Calais, and exasperating my fellow-pas- sengers by refusing to join in the carnival of sea sickness going on around me, when a ruddy-faced, white-whiskered, bluff-looking individual who had been eyeing me for some time stepped up and said: " Beg pardon, I'm sure; but are you really the American ?" "The American !" I replied; "there are several, I believe." " Oh, of coarse, to be sure. I mean the one on board. I saw George B. Blank, San Francisco, California, U.S.,' painted on some of the bag- gage, and I picked you out right away as the owner." And the stranger inspected me from head to foot with as vivid a curiosity as if I had been a wild man of the woods. "Well," I finally exclaimed, lam an American. What can Ido for you ?" " Why-er—nothing--that is—no offence' I hope, and you are a Californian, too ?" he said, rubbing his hands as though he had met a rara eels. "Ever scalped by the Indians, eh ?" "I think not," I replied. "You've scalped some of them, though, haven't you ?" persisted my inquisitor. Concluding that inasmuch as I was in for being made a sideshow of I might as well indulge in some of the circus poster sort of thing, I looked my qaestioner calmly in the eyes, and replied, "Some twenty-six or seven, I for- get which; I have the tally nicked in the handle of my other scalping knife; I carry only one bowie in this coun- try. So seldom one rains across any fun here, you know." "Killed many white men ?" asked the stranger, who ap- peared to be actually quivering with excitement and curiosity. " Only eight or ten," I replied, carelessly. "Yon see, in California there is a sort of close season now for shooting white men. 'Tain't like the good old man-for- breakfast times. A fellow is only allowed to gun around promiscuous like four months in the year. So it's hard work to keep one's hand in, don't you see ?" "Well, I de- clare !" said the apparently stupefied man with the chop whiskers; "how about Chinamen ?" "Oh! we kill China- men all the year round, when they're fat," I explained. "Bat, then, there is lately some sort of an ordinance mak- ing it a misdemeanour to shoot a pigtail unless he is on the shady side of the street, or gets in your way. Folks are getting to particular over that, for a fact." "Is it really true that all Americans wear chest protectors, and eat nothing but pie ?" "Well, you see, the fact is that Ameri- cans are, as you know, such a frightfully busy people that they haven't time to sit down and eat a square meal like you English. They must have something portable—something they can carry about with them and nibble on the sly. I tell you, sir, it looks like business when you see 40 or 50 men all hanging on to the straps of a street car with one hand, and eating with the other." "I should rather think so," murmured the stranger. "As for the chest protectors," I continued, "they are really nothing more than pockets suspended around the neck, and large enough to carry a whole pie, which it keeps warm at the same time. A good hot mince pie stowed away in this manner not only imparts a gentle and grateful warmth to the entire system, but keeps a whole day's rations always within reach of the wearer. Grand idea, isn't it? " Well, I'm blessed !" said my fairly paralysed interrogator, gazing at my childlikeand ingenuous face with profound awe. " Would—er—would you oblige me with one of your cards," he said, "I want to show it to my family, or they'll never believe 'a word of thie_neyer. Thanks—here's mine," and, as we had landed, he walked up the gang-plank and was swallowed up by the mob of insane French cabmen. As I stepped chuckling into my own compartment, I glanced at the card of the stranger. It read, "Julius K. Juakina, San Francisco, Cal." I have spent about eight hours a day looking for that man ever since. There will be bloodshed out of this yet—mark my words. IMMUNITY FROM LIVER-FLUKE.—The fact stated by Mr. Knight, that flocks on Exmoor, one of the wettest districts in England, enjoyed entire freedom from the ravages of Fasciola hepatica, is conclusive (if confirmation was needed) as to wet-lying having, in itself, nothing to do with the liability to liver-fluke. A similar immunity is enjoyed by a wide tract of marshes upon the Eastern Coast, which are inundated at intervals from the sea; and, beyond question, the two districts, unlike in most respects, owe their safety to the same cause—that is to the one point they have in coramon in their saline herbage or in the amount of salt present in the soil, arising from the sea spray continually blown over it. This saltness destroys the intermediate agent—the small snails, Lymnsens truncatulus—and so, the fluke—even if infected sheep be driven into the district— cannot increase, but dies out with the first lot of victims. Mr. Knight's evidence as to the non-appearance of fluke on Exmoor is very noteworthy.—G. Gilbert, in Agricultural Gazette THE SCOTTISH FARMERS' ALLIANCE.—THE NEW rno- GRAMMH.—At a meeting of the General Committee of the Scottish Farmers' Alliance, held at Perth, for the purpose of considering a draft programme of objects of the Alliance prepared and revised by the Executive Committee, the fol- lowing were adopted :-1. To use every legitimate effort to have the law so altered as that tenants shall have a legal right to compensation for all improvements done by 'them that add to the value of their holdings. 2. To obtain the amelioration of the condition of farm workmen, more espe- cially with a view of securing them improved 'cottage accommodation and small holdings. 3. To promote the farther reform of the Game Laws, and in particular to obtain for the tenant farmer unrestricted and inalienable right to protect his belongings from damage from all kinds of game, and to urge on Government the necessity of re- stricting and keeping within reasonable bounds the growing tendency to turn so much of the area of the country into deer forests, grouse moors, ix.—To have all nnlet shootings, and fishings, and growing woods rated at their letting value, and woods at the income derived from theta over and above the expense of planting and maintenance.-4. To obtain the , abolition of the Laws of lintail and Primogeniture, and all the presumptions of the law in favour of the landlord and against the tenant. 5. To promote a law simplifying and cheapening the transfer of land; to enforce compulsory education. That is to say, to make the sale and transfer of
land as free, easy, and inexpensive as ordinary property.

6. To secure to ratepayers their legitimate shaie- in local government. 7. To ensure the better representation of tenant farmers in Scotland.- 8. To watch over and protect the interests of agriculture generally. 9. To obtain a Scotch Department, with a Minister responsible for the management of Scotch affairs.—That, as the whole of the above objects are conceived as much in the interests of the general public as of the agricultural community, the co- operation of all classes is invited. TEE MILE Tuarm—Prof. Sheldon, speaking at Downton, last week, to the students, said :—The consumption of milk as milk goes on increasing in the country, and the yield of cheese and butter is of coarse coincidently diminishing. Vast quantities of milk are daily sent along the railways to all large centres of population, and this new departure is altering the conditions of dairy farming very considerably. The bare fact that the supply of milk must be kept up in winter and ,eummer alike has caused a great .change in
various ways. A large number of cows are required to come into the dairy in the autumn and early winter ; and . _ _

so the period of gefitation has to be taken int-o consideration to-meet the demand for such cows. It is probable that autumn calvers have been dearer this year than they ever were before—a sequel of the milk trade. Then, again, the production of milk in winter necessitates the employment of a large ?volume of purchased feeding stuffs, and these greatly increase farmers' expenses, though they tend to im- prove the land. The great bugbear of the milk trade is the risk of bad debts with the dealers; yet the milk trade will sustain more bad debts than either cheese or butter-making will. Farmers' companies for the distribution of milk have frequently been advocated, and no doubt such commercial bodies are at all events in theory, the best that can be thought of. In practice, however, they do not act well. In any case, in the dairy farming of the future the milk trade is destined to become the most important feature ; in which event all the operations of the farm, the raising of stock, the gestation of cows, the employment of feeding staffs, as well as the wits of the farmer, will have to accom- modate themselves to the altered conditions of the future, whatever they may be. The future of dairy farming in this country will be a future of high pressure, in which catering for the milk trade will be the salient principle. Cheese and butter-making will diminish in volume as the milk trade expands. More earnestness and skill and enter- prise will be employed in the work, more capital will be required, and a more elaborate education and training on the part of the rising generation of farmers. LORD TOLLEMACHE'S EXPERIMENTS.—On Tuesday the first of four capacious silos constructed on the Horsley-lane Home Farm of the Peckforton estate, Cheshire, by Lord Tollemache was opened in the presence of a large number of agriculturists, dairy farmers and others. Lord Tolle- mache, who has taken a deep interest in the subject of en- silage, in June last filled four silos, two of them with grass cut in very wet weather, the third with dry grass, and the fourth with a mixture of vetches and grass. A pressure

of 56Ibs. to the square foot was placed npiin them. In July each had sunk about 2 feet 1 inch and they were refilled, about seven tons more grass being placed in them, making in all about 24 tons in each. No. 2 silo that had been stacked with very wet grass was opened on Tuesday. when about three inches from the top the ensilage was:found to be mouldy, but the rest was in excellent condition. A por- tion was given to horses, and they consumed it eagerly. Cattle and sheep also ate it with avidity, but pigs did not care much for it. It was estimated that the 24 tons of grass placed in the silo would yield about 21 tons of good ensilage. No. 3 silo was also tested. This was stacked in a drier condition, and proved to be of better quality. For convenience a pathway was cut abouti three feet wide rightl through the silo. The appearance of the:ensilage was that of a dark brown compact moss, with a sweet and pleasant aroma. It was explained by Lord Tollemache that the contents of the opened silo had been cut after a shower of rain, and that, therefore, in addition to the inherent moisture contained in the grass, the rain had made the ensilage moister than it would otherwise have been. A young mare that had been driven over from Peckforton Castle ate the ensilage eagerly, as also did cattle in the yard. The con- tents of the silos were critically examined by the agricul- turists present, and pronounced everything that could be desired. The entire experiment was regarded by practical men as a complete success. His lordship said he believed that ensilage' would prove to be of great value in farming operations in the future. He fully believed in it, having no doubt that it would be successful. Experience showed that dairy cows fed on ensilage gave a better yield of milk, and that was a point of great importance to them in that butter an cheese-making county. Sheep also would thrive well on it. Several farmers present spoke highly of the results of Lord Tollemache's experiments, and were allowed to take away samples with which to test their own cattle. NEW SPECIES OF POTATO.—The discovery of a new escu- lent having so much affinity to the "nobler tuber" as to merit the name of potato is a fact which will have much interest for many. The native place of this tuberous-rooted solanum, named after its discoverer, S. Ohroudi, is the little uninhabited island of Goritti, situated at the mouth of the Iriver La Plata. The most diligent search failed to discover more than one root of this solanum; but the tubers were brought safely to Brest, and delivered into the care of M. Blanchard, gardener, at the Seaman's Hospital of that town. This is what M. Blanchard has to say on the matter in the Revue Horticole :—"From the time it came into my hands I have cultivated, or rather left this plant in the same place, and for the simple reason that it was impossible to destroy it. Every year, at the end of June or beginning of July, I took up the produce. Notwithstanding all the pains taken in lifting, there remained enough in the soil to ensure a crop the following year." This new solanum has three sets of creeping stems, one of which runs near the surface and throws up at intervals young growths, which flower almost as soon as they appear. Another strikes deeply into the soil and produces tubers, whilst others take a path midway between these two, and content themselves with producing an enormous quantity of almost microscopical bulblets, which when detached effectually guarantee the plant against extermination. M. Blanchard adds :—" I believe it would be easy, simply by means of good culture, to improve this plant. Already there is a great improvement in the size of the tubers compared with those received from M. Ohroud. The latter were no larger than a nut, whilst some of those grown by me are as large as a small hen's egg and good in flavour, having a chestnutty taste accompanied by a slight amount of bitterness. We have used them both boiled and baked, but they are best baked. The tubers are perfectly hardy, having passed the winter of 1881 in the open ground, and I may add to that the present time the haulm has shown no thee of disease." M. Blanchard, having placed the original tubers under glass, and finding that they did not thrive, planted them out. The crop consisted of six tubers, which were lifted and stored for the winter. In the spring the space occupied by them was dotted with young plants. The six tubers were planted amongst them, and nothing more was done until July, when half a gallon of tubers were lifted. In September the ground was again swarming with young plants, covering about two square yards. They planted nothing and lifted the following year It gallons of tubers. That year they tried to root it out, but next Sep- tember there was again a crop of young plants, covering 61 square yards of soil, and we lifted a crop consisting of about 211bs. weight. If not suitable for table use, the plant may possibly prove useful for cattle, and the crossing of this new potato with our own might result in the production of a new race of a hardier and altogether more enduring char- acter than that which we now possess. At any rate it might be well to try the experiment. The habit of this potato is very dwarf. It is said not to exceed one foot in height, but it is very vigorous and excessively bushy, and the general appearance of the plant is that of the common potato. A TENANT'S TEEATMENT.—I beg to give you some par- ticulars as to the experience I have had as a tenant farmer in Devon and Cornwall. First, with Sir Massey Lopes, M.P. for South Devon. My father held a fourteen years' lease of Hill Barton (340 acres), Sir Massey's largest farm. This lease was transferred to me for its last six years. The great trouble was rabbits and, of course, other game; but about and after Sir Massey's election for South Devon, in which my father worked mast successfully as the chairman of his home committee (though I always believed my father outraged his opinions and feelings, for he was in heart a Liberal), during this contest rabbits were thrown at him, imuch in consequence of which Sir Massey allowed his

tenantry tacitly many facilities for killing them; but after- wards he withdrew them, whether because he felt safe in his seat Ido not pretend to say. The tenants, with myself as spokesman, protested against the withdrawal of these facili- ties. I was therefore spotted as a rebel. At another time we came into opposition over a school matter, when Sir Mas- sey exercised territorial despotism, backed up by the cleri- cal interest. The great objection he had to me was, how- ever, that I held religious services in my house—Evange- listic services, because our clergyman was extreme Ritualist —in which I was helped by all the other churches in the district, from Church of England to Plymouth Brethren. These are known facts. Sir Massey then refused to renew the lease, telling me I had not served the farm fairly; yet having taken away 53 acres, still asked £27 rent per year more than I had paid for it, and this, too, in 1879, an in- increase in rent of about £lOO per year. This increase was entirely upon my improvement, for which he paid me nothing, but charged as much as he could for deterioration. Lots of other cases of similar generosity (?) I know on his estate, but his tenants dare not oppose him. I had the highest testimonials on entering on Trewint, Menheniot, Cornwall. My lease was for fourteen years, terminable at seven years. I shortly found that my Blue Ribbon princi- I pies were not in accordance wiih the ideas of the son of the landlady, Mrs. Seccombe. But when a deputation came into Cornwall to propagate Farmers' Alliance principles at Cal- lington I joined the Alliance, which was supported by Mr. , Borlase as well as Lord Robartes, and I was made secretary ' to the Cornwall Branch in 1882. As secretary, I organised four meetings, to be addressed by Mr. J. Howard, M.P., Mr. Leadam, and local gentlemen, in the beginning of February, 1883. These meetings were held in one week, and on the following Monday Mrs. Seccombe gave her lawyer instruc- tions to terminate my lease at the end of its seven years, then seven months off, six months being necessary. She assigned to me personally and definitely that it was because I took "so much interest in the Farmers' Alliance, which was no other than an Irish Land League." This was itsserted to be the reason, too, by the solicitor to the estate, in reply to the inquiry of a steward of Lord Robartes. I leave my farm worth £3O per year more than I took it (present rent £345), by cleaning, manuring, dsc , and I only get a modi- cum of compensation. If the eviction had been the result of breach of promise or understanding it wco,uld be somewhat excusable; but no remark was made when I entered as to political or religious opinions, and I never expected any interference until it was rumoured that my connection with thh Farmer's Alliance would turn me out. That the Alliance is doing the right thing is my settled opinion; but I am sorry to have been a sufferer, as I cannot afford it, having a wife and five children. Nevertheless, I hold principles of justice and independence more dearly than immediate pecu- niary interest, and look upon the plea of expediency versus principle as being despicable. I can see no other chance for me than to go into a foreign country, driven from home by landlords.-11. TROUNCE, Heath Cottage, Horrabriclge, in The Mark-Lane Express.

THE MARQUIS OF ITARTINGTON AT ACCRINGTON. The Marquis of Hartington and Mr. F. W. Grafton, the members of Parliament for North-East Lancashire, addres- sed a crowded meeting of their constituents at Accrington on Saturday. T:2O Mayor of Accrington (Mr. Alderman Smith) presided. Lord Hartington began his address by making a brief reference to the late colliery disaster, and expressing his sympathy with the bereaved. He afterwards remarked that he was rather fond when he was addressing his constituents of making a text of the speeches of Sir Richard Cross, because that gentleman, with an enga- ging frankness, stated in very direct terms, what some of his colleagues insinuated in a less direct manner. Sir Richard Cross the other day said the blun- ders of the present Administration had been unparal- lelled. If that were the case surely such unparalleled blunders might have been exposed in debates of less dura- tion than those which took place during last session. And if the blunders of the present Administration were such as had been described, where were the unfortunate results of them to be seen? The noble Lord proceeded to contend that the foreign relations of this country were of an amic- able and satisfactory nature, and, alluding to an attack made on the Government by the Marquis of Salisbury in regard to our relations with France, said it was a most re- markable thing, considering the partnership into which, by the action of the late Government we had been led with the French Government in • Egypt, that we should have been able, as we were last year, to intervene solely in the affairs of Egypt and greatly to strengthen our influence in that country almost to the exclusion of French interests, without causing any estrangement be- tween the two Governments. He also stated that our relations with Germany are perfectly cordial and friendly, as was proved by the fact that within the past few days an intimation had been received to the effect that the German Government are willing to co-operate with us for the protection of the interests of English and German sub- jects in China in the event of those interests being brought into peril by the state of the relations between France and China. With regard to India, the present Government had remitted a portion of the salt duty and the whole of the duty on cotton goods imported into that great dependency. By taking that course the Government had relieved the people of India from taxation, and had done that which Lancashire asked them to do with some advantage to the interests of this country, but with far more advantage to the interests of India. The Indian revenues which were by the late Administration spent upon an unprofitable war had, under the administration of Lord Ripon, been diverted to the improvement of the Government of India, the development of its re- sources, and to the prosecution of those numerous public works which were during the tenure of office of the late Government suspended in order that funds might be ob- tained for the prosecution of the war with Afghanistan. In alluding to Ireland Lord Hartington said it appeared to him that the policy of the Opposition was to indulge in the most violent denunciations of the Irish legislation of the Govern- ment for home consunaption in England. The Land Act and the Arrears Act were denounced in England for party purposes as unworthy bids for the political support of a certain section of the Irish representatives, but Sir Stafferd Northeote in his progress through the North of Ireland had not a word to say of the Land. Act as an unworthy conces- sion. It was a misfortune that it was impossible for the Liberal party to act in harmony or co-operation with the representative's of a great portion of the Irish people; so long, however, as Mr. Parnell and his friends were not seeking to gain censtitutional ends by constitutional agita- tion, but were seeking to inflame the hatred of the Irish people against their English fellow subjects and against every institution by which property and order are secured, so long as they did not scruple to use violence and force to gain their ends, so long would it be impossible for any Eng- lish party to have any common action or any poli4ical al- liance with that party. The Irish legislation of the present Government was not intended to purchass Irish political support or conciliate Irish disaffection, but was intended to conciliate a sense of justice of the British people and of that portion of the Irish people who had not suffered themselves to be led away by appeals to a blind and national animosity, or by the temptations and seductions of an unlawful greed. In con- cludine Lord Hartington referred to the measures passed during the past session, and, referring to the obstruction which the Government had had to meet with in endeavour- ing to carry out their programme of business, he said he thosght the Government had a right to call upon the Op- position and its leaders in the same way that they appealed to their own supporters, to assist them to deal not only with the wilful disturber of the order of Parliament, but also with those who from inadvertence and want of thought were 'equally guilty of wasting the time of Parliament. Sir John ' Lubbock, M.P., aud Mr. Mundella, M.P., also addressed the meeting, which carried a resolution expressing confidence ' in the Government and in the members for the divison.

div.head: WATER QUESTION.
div.p: THE WATER QUESTION.

In the House of Lords, yesterday week, before the Lord Chancellor, and Lords Bramwell, Blackburn, and Watson, judgment was given in the appeal of Dobbs v. the Grand Junction Warterworks Co. It involved an important ques- tion as to the mode of computing the water-rate in the metropolis. The appellant Dobbs was the lessee for a term, of which about 70 years were unexpired, at a ground rent of £l5 year, of a house in Westbourne Park, Paddington, which he occupied as a residence. A rate was made upon him by the respondent company in respect of the water supply to the house for domestic purposes, and the amount of the rate was arrived at by a calculation of £4 per cent. upon the sum of £l4O, such sum being the gross annual value of the premises, as appeared in the valuation list for the time being in force under the Valuation (Metropolis) Act, 1869. The appellant claimed that the rate ought to be based upon the "rateable value" of the premises, which appeared in the same list as £llB. The cempeny were by their special Acts compelled to supply water to the occu- piers of dwelling-houses for domestic purposes at the follow- ing rates—viz., "where the annual value of the dwelling house should • not exceed £2OO at a rate per cent. per annum on such value not exceeding £4, and where such annual value should exceed £2OO at a rate per cent. per ' annum on such value not exoeeding X 3." It was also pro- vided by their special Act (7 George IV. c 140, s. 27) gilt the water rate was te be payable "according to the actual amount of the rent of the premises where the same could be ascertained, and where the same could not be ascertained ac- cording to the actual amount or annual value upon which the assessment to the poor rate was computed." It should be observed that in the present case there was no actual rent paid within the meaning of the Act, the occupier being the lessee of the house for a long term at a ground rent. In the first instance the case went before Mr. Major Cook, one of the Metropolitan police magistrates, who decided that the rate was chargeable upon the "gross value," as defined by the Valuation (Metropolis) Act, 1869, and therefore decided in favour of the company; but a Court of the Queen's Bench Division, consisting of Mr. Justice Field and Mr. Justice Bowen, reversed his decision, and held that the water rate must be computed on the "rateable I value " of the premises supplied with water, as appears from the poor-rate assessment, not upon the "gross value." The " rateable value," it should be stated, for poor-rate purposes, is arrived at after deducting from the "gross estimated rental" or "gross value," which corresponds with the ac- tual rent, certain expenses such as repairs and insurance. On the conclusion of the arguments before the House rose for the Long Vacation, their lordships intimated that they would give judgment in favour of the appellant Dobbs, but would state their reasons on a future occasion —Lord Bram- well, in now giving judgment, said: I think this case may be dealt with as governed by the 15 and 16 Vide c. 157, sec. 46. For either that is tile same in effect as the 7 Geo. IV., c. 140, sec 27 (which I do not think), or it is different. If the former, the meaning of the two being the same, either may be considered; if the latter, then the provisions of the later Act put an end to the operation of those of the former. In either case it may be disregarded. An Act which says the law in future shall be different from what it was may not, strictly speaking, be said to repeal it, but it abro- gates it for the future. The question then is, what is the meaning of "annual value" in sec. 46 of 15 and 16 Vic., cap. 140? Now, without undertaking an all-sufficient de- finition, it seems to me that we may safely adopt that in 6 and 7 Will. 4, c. 96, viz., "the rent at which they would Jet free of all usual tenants' rates and taxes, and deducting therefrom the probable average annual cost of the repairs, insurance, and other expenses, if any, necessary to main- tain them in a state to command such rent." This is their value. If a rent exceeding this cost could not be got they would be valueless. It is as impossible to say that the an- nual rent without such deduction is the annual value as it is to say that the daily hire of a horse is its daily value, without deduction for its keep, &c. This is the value, the net, the only value. The Solicitor-General said that this was to interpolate the word "net." That is not so. Value means net value, net value means value. He did propose to interpolate a word "gross," Now,gross value is different from value. It is, though a convenient, an inccurate expression, like "gross profits." The difference between what a thing costs and the larger sum it sells for is not profit if the buy- ing and selling are attended with expense to the trader. Value is net value, and involves those deductions from rent which the appellant claims. I am confirmed in this by the provision in 15 and 16 Vic., which makes the owner liable for the water rate of small tenements. What is the value of them to him ? What he gets minus what it costs him to get it. But the value cannot be greater in the hands of the tenant. " Hamilton v. Bass," 12 C., B. 631, is really in point. Property was let at a gross yearly rent of £75 155., with an agreement that the landlord should pay all rates and taxes. Deducting them, and £1 6s. for expenses of collection, and £4 for repairs, the net rent was reduced below £6O, and it was held that this did not qualify 303. or 40s. freeholders. The setute Henry VI., cap. 7, giving the right of votes to those "who have free land" or tene- ment, to the value of 40s by the year "at the leak above all charges," Mauls, J., saying, "If a man has a piece of land by means of which he can enable himself to expend 40s a year by laying out 5s upon it, can that be said to be of the value of 40s a year ? " Judgment was given against the vote on this reasoning. In Colvill v. Wood, 2 C.B , it was indeed held that the fair annual rent of premises is the pro- per criterion of their clear yearly value within Statute 2 Will. IV., c. 45, sec. 26, without making any reduction for the landlcrd's repairs. But that case was expressly decided on the ground that the vote was given to the occupier, and that it was obvious the Legislature could never have in- tended that the right of a tenant to vote should depend on calculations so nice, ar':';eial, and difficult of application as "on the use to which he puts i'," and other matters.—

The Lord Chancellor said he agreed in the result, and generally in the reaeons and opinions expressed by the noble and learned lord. He thought the words "annual value" in the latter Act had the same meaning as in the earlier Act, and it seemed to him to be perfectly clear that the mode of valuing for the purpose of computing the assess- ment for the poor-rate was first to ascertain what was called the "gross value," and then to make the necessary deduc- tions in order to arrive at the true value, and the value hav- ing been so ascertained, the computation for the -assessment of the poor-rate was to be made upon it.—Lords Blackburn and Watson concurred.—Lord Bramwell intimated that Lord Fitzgerald was unakle to attend, but he concurred in the judgment he had delivered.—The order appealed from was then reversed, and the judgment of the Queen's Bench Division restored, and the respondents ordered to pay the costs in the Court of Appeal and also in the House of Lords. MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

Another important stage in the second —application to Par- liament for powers to construct the Manchester Ship Canal was passed on Friday, when the plans for the work speci- fied. in the Parliamentary notice with the necessary books of reference, were deposited with the clerks of the peace at Preston and Chester, at the Private Bill Office of the House of Commons, and with the various authorities in the district along the line of the proposed canal, as required by the standing orders of the Houses of Parliament. The plans this year include the whole of the works proposed to be carried out in the estuary of the river Mersey, as well as those relating to the =al proper, and are consequently much more extensive than those deposited last year. Pro- vision is also made for the construction of extensive wharves on the Manchester side of the Irwell, for the purchase of Pomona Gardens and other important properties between Throstle Nest and Hunt's Bank, with the object of develop- ing the upper reach of the Irwell, and of affording increased facilities for Manchester traffic. The bill itself will have to be deposited on or before the 15th inst., and the estimates must be lodged on or before the 31st instant. A number of gentlemen repressnting the Provisional Committee have.in- ' spected the river Irwell between Throstle Nest and Hunt's Bank with a view to ascertaining how far that portion of the river can be improved to meet the requirements of the Cor- poration of Manchester!
A RUNAWAY LOVER HORSE- WHIPPED.

An extraordinary scene was enacted on Saturday in Dale- street, Liverpool. On the Yorkshire wolds, not far from Goole, a gentleman agriculturist farms his own estate. His family consists of an only son and a daughter. They are people of good position, and mix among the best society in the East Riding. The daughter of the gentleman yeoman is a young lady of nineteen, highly accomplished, and of great personal attractions. She was the belle of every party and dance she attended. As might be supposed, she had many admirers—gentlemen of wealth and position. But she turned away indifferently from all their advances. This conduct to her relatives and friends seemed inexplicable. The cause they have just discovered. Among the servants attached to the farm of the lady's father was a young Irishman named Tim M'Guinness. Tim is a somewhat rough, lumpy-looking fellow of a little more than twenty years; but while this Kerry boy, uncouth in manner and not prepossessing in appearance, was "whistl- ing at the plough," he seemed to have attracted the notice of his master's pretty daughter. An affection sprung up be- tween them, and she showed a preference to the Irish ploughman over all the well-to-do yeomen who sought her hand. Her friends did not suspect the attachment, and they received a rude shock on Friday. The young lady did not appear at her usual place at the breakfast table, and on in- quiries be* made it was found that she and the Irish farm labourer hid gone off together, and taken railway tickets for Liverpool. To this city they were promptly followed by the lady's father and brother. The matter was placed in the hands of detectives, who traced the runaways to a hotel in Dale-street, where their relations had been perfectly decorous. Here the father and brother went. A terrible scene followed. The lady became hysterical. The Irish- man was defiant. The enraged brother, brought a horsewhip with him, and was commencing to belabour the fellow who had run off with his sister, when the detectives interposed. It seemed that the runaways were to have been married by special licence on Sunday had not the father and brother so unexpectedly appeared upon the scene. The upshot of the affair at present is that the lady has been taken back to her home by her father and brother. The Irishman was left behind. But he need not despair. The last words of his lidy-love, as she was being taken away from him, were "Keep your spirits up, Tim; I'll have you yet. I could not live without you."

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

PRUNING FRUIT TRRES.—SIP far as the apple and the pear are concerned their pruning is frequently a controver- sial topic. The disputants are not so much at variance as to how they shall prune, but whether they shall prune or not prune. We consider one as much in the right as the other, and those who first introduced the restrictive system never intended it to supplant the natural one, and this is the point that is frequently overlooked by the contending parties. The restrictive system is suited for small gardens, and the trees for the purpose are worked or grafted on the paradise stock, and the pruning is chiefly done by the finger and thumb in summer. The advaatages are that the trees have not each a tendency to grow as those worked on the crab, and with the aid of pinching they are kept in a small compass for years; more trees can be thus grown, giving the advantage of variety, and the trees do not in- terfere with the vegetable crops. Those who have had ex- perience in growing vegetables on ground reach shaded by trees must have noticed the difference between them and those grown in the open. It is the pruning of large trees that we really have to deal with at present, for the sake of the tree as well as the crops surrounding them. We would advise all branches that in any way cross each other to be sawn off. All cuts should be made in a slanting direction and in such a way that water cannot possibly rest on them, and any dark paint pat on the cut will further protect it. Iflithe trees are very badly crowded we would prefer moving the worst this year and the others the next. It will be found that some trees, from their habit of growth, never require this pruning; while others soon become crowded, and there is nothing for it bat praning as above. There are other trees that make weakly growth, and when they have fruit on them they are swayed to and fro, and one lot of fruit comes in contact with the other. A strong sharp knife or branch-pruning shears should rectify that. We have the greatest objection to prune large trees except in -these special cases, believing there is nothing like extension for producing fruit in quan- tity; and now that we can have pyramids on the paradise, the place for the others is in the orchard or the field, or, as we read recently of a gentleman, who took advantage of a wood and planted an outer belt of fruit trees on the south side. We have been informed that the largest illustration of field-planting is to be seen near Leighton Buzzard, in Bucks., and carried out by the late Baron Rothschild on his Mentmore estate. Hundreds of acres may be seen from the railway, and the trees hitherto have not interfered with the grass crops, as they are no doubt planted far enough apart to avoid that at any. time. TER FRONT GARDEN.—" What am I to do with my roses to make them grow well?" was the question addressed to us a few days ago. Everybody loves a rose, and we are not surprised that our interrogator should be anxious about his. We stated early in this month that the season for planting roses had arrived, but did not particularise as to how it should be done; and as the planting season will be from now to March, a few plain directions may be of service. The rose will grow after a fashion in most soils, but to make them produce growth 3ft. or 4ft. long in a season, the ground must have some preparation. Turfy loam should be procured, if possible, and be buried a foot below the sur- face; failing this, road-parings, or sufficient of either so as to have a few spadefuls to place under and over the roots of each plant so as to give them a start. For only two or three plants, we should dig holes 2f I. square, and down 2ft. or as far as the good soil extends, stir the bottom up and leave it, placing 41n. of manure on it, and mix manure with the soil as it is thrown in, reserving the worst for the top, for its nature can be improved any time. If it is intended to form a row to any extent, we would begin at one end and throw out a trench 2ft. wide, regula- ting the depth according to the nature of the soil; move the bottom and add manure as directed for holes also mix manure with the soil as it is replaced. We would allow the ground to settle before planting, and any plants that have been taken up to allow the ground to be prepared will be quite safe if placed close together with plenty of soil on their roots; we do not mean just enough to hide them, but a depth of Gin, or Bin., and if the plants are laid in obliquely a portion of the stems can be covered. Press the soil with the foot against the roots. In planting them in their proper quarters 4in. to Gin, of soil will be sufficient over the roots, always bearing in mind to tread over each plant after three parts of the soil is in, and the remainder left loose on the top. The following varieties have proved themselves suitable for towns and smoky districts :—Anne Alexieffe, Baronne Prevost, Comtesse de Chabrillan, Lordy Clyde, Jules Margottin, Victor Verdier, Princess Louise, as well as the tea-scented Gloir de Dijon, with others we might name. THE WlNDOW.—Drauena Australis, a native of New Zealand, is a handsome window plant in a small state, and when they are too large for the window it is easy to dispose of them by exchange or selling. It is a plant that seldom gets infested with insects, and all that is required to keep it in health is to attend to watering and sponging, or brush- ing the leaves occasionally with a soft brush. All plants in the window should have the dust removed from their foliage in this way, for so long as it is allowed to remain on they cannot thrive. The leaves are the lungs of the plants, and they are covered withpores, and if these become clogged with dirt the process of respiration is impeded, the plant assumes a sickly appearances, and finally dies.

Distribute cheerfully in the time of health, for distribu- tion on a deathbed seems rather a cheat than a charity, in- asmuch as it is rather a distribution of another man's goods than of thy own. An aged Hebrew went to the opera, the other evening, to witness "Leo Huguenots." Suddonly ho burst intu Ip:draw, as if an idea had struck him. "Why do you laugh ?" inquired his Gentile companion. " Laagh ! the beth game I ever thaw. A, bloomin' lot o' Protethtanth an' Catholicth a-killin' of each other to music written by a Jew. Ha! ha !" A TRUE STORY OF THH GRHAT EXHIBITION OF 'sl. A venerable archdeacon, now deceased, thinking he recog- nised the back of a friend in a crowd, for a joke, picked his pocket of a handkerchief. Promptly was the clergyman seized upon by a detective. "Nonsense, my good man," said the reverend joker; "that's a friend of mine." But when the owner of the hankerchief turned round he re- vealed the face of an utter stranger. In vain did the arch- deacon protest at the station and declare his exalted rank. "That won't wash. "We've 'ad a bishop or two 'ere before now," was all the satisfaction he got; and things looked un- deniably serious until the arrival of those who could vouch for the identity of the reverend divine. . A few years since the priest of Fredericktown, having raised sufficient funds to erect a new church in place of an old wooden chapel that had been long the resort of the faithful, set a corps of masons at work on the edifice. As an appropriate inscription to be placed over the main entrance, and to be there engraved in stone, he selected Ifrom the Gospel of St. Matthew xxi., 13, these words- -1" My house shall be called the house of prayer." That the 'words might be copied literally he left his Bible with the master mason, and having pointed out the words distinctly, thought no more of the subject till the day of consecration, , when he was horrified, as were all his brethren, by reading ' in deep letters over the door, "My house shall be called the house of prayer, but ye have made it a den of thieves." As it was impossible to remove the inscription, the surplus letters were filled up with putty, as may be *seen by the traveller to the lead mines of Missouri.

div.p: THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND
COAL
TRADES.

Business in the iron trade continues very quiet, and buyers show little or no disposition to give out orders ex- cept at very low prices. The unsettled state of the labour market has of course had a tendency to induce a certain amount of caution on the part of makers with regard to for- ward contracts, and there has been no great pressnre to sell, but with the probable collapse of the wages agitation in the coal industry it remains to be seen whether trade itself will maintain a firm tone in the iron market. Lancashire makers of pig iron, although they are doing extremely little so far as new business is concerned, are not disposed to come below 455, less 2A-, for forge and foundry qualitie- delivered equal to Manchester. In district brands the leads ing district makers still quote 44s 10d to 453 10d, less 21, for forge and foundry Lincolnshire delivered here, but iron is to be bought at 13 per ton under these figures, and in Derbyshire foundry brands about 463 61, less 2-1, delivered equal to Manchester is being taken. In the finished iron trade business is very flat, and both local and North Staf- fordshire bars are to be bought at about £6 2s 6d per ton delivered here, with hoops offered at £6 7s Gd and sheets at about 1..z7 15s to £7 17s Gd per ton.— With the collapse of the threatened strike in the coal trade the pressure for supplies has disappeared from the market, but the brisk demand during the last two or three weeks has had the effect of bringing about an upward movement in prices. With the commencement of the month delivered rates for house fire coal have in the Manchester district been put up 101 per ton; where engine fuel was not put up list month there has been an advance of 5d per ton in burgy and slack, and in the wharf prices there have been advances varying from 5,1 to 101 per ton on different classes of fuel, but as a rule pit prices are untouched. In the West L Incashire districts there has been a pretty general advance in the pit prices of about is per ton on round coals, and 6d on other classes of fuel. Prices now average about as under :—Mancbester delivered rates: Best coal, 133 4d up to 15s; seconds, lie Bcl to 123 Gd ; furnace coal, 83 7d to 93 2d; burgy, 7s 7d; and slack, Gs 9d per ton. Pit prices in the West Lancashire districts :—Best coal, lie ; seconds, 8s 6d to 93; common, 7s al to 83; burgy, 5s to 55 Gd; good slack, 4s to 4s Gd; and common sorts, about 33 61 per ton. Following the result of the Sheffield con- ference there has been only a small business doing at the advanced rates, and as the bulk of the coal recently bought has gone into stock, a dull market may be looked for until after the turn of the year. A spell of severe weather would, of course, tend to brisken up the demand, but otherwise it would seem doubtful how fir colliery proprietors will be able to maintain the advanced rates so far as fuel prices are concerned.

An old Highland clergyman, who had received several calls to parishes, asked his servant where he should go. His servant said, "Go where there is most sin, sir." The preacher concluded that good advice, and went where there was most money. "DOWN IN FRONT."—An old contributor writes that there is among his acquaintances one at least who enjoys a high reputation, for he stands over seven feet in his stock- ings. Going to the theatre, one evening, he took a promi- nent seat in the stalls. When the curtain rose, a cry of '"Down in front !" became general throughout the back seats. The tall B—, finding the eyes of the entire audience fixed upon him, felt obliged to do something, and so, looking as though he would like to sink through the floor, he proceeded to raise himself to a standing position, in such a manner, however, as to convey an impression that there was no end to him. When at last he did get unfolded and straightened out to his full length, slowly glancing around at the astonished audience, he very deliberately re- marked, "Gentlemen, to satisfy you that I was sitting down, ' I now stand up !" A burst of laughter and applause suc- ceeded; audience and actors became convulsed ; the curtain descended rapidly; the manager with beaming face came forward, and, amidst the wildest applause, conducted the gentleman to a private box.—Harper's Christmas Number. A STORY OF THE COMIIIINE.—During the siege of the Commune, there was a regiment of defenders which con- tained three mechanics: one, the grandfather, sixty-seven years of age ; another, the father, forty years old; the third, the son, who was scarcely sixteen. The three were evidently of the same brood, they all had the eagle look, the tprond aquiline profile of the born warrior; all had the same blue eye, dreamy, unfathomable. Silent, sober, impassive, they had won an authority of which they had no idea. Their battalion remained three weeks outside Paris during weather in which the thermometer showed twenty degrees of frost. In the end the father fell, during a barricade fight, into the hands of the soldiers. To cover the fire of the insurgents, the Versailles troops took the prisoner, bound his wrists, and placed him in the middle of the street. The defenders of the barricade stopped firing though the soldiersbent in their shot like hail. The old man turned to his grandson and said, "Thy father will be shot anyhow, for they kill all the prisoners. Better for him to die at once. Fire straight." The boy trembled and turned pale. "Listen," said the grandfather : "this is the end for all who fight to the end. All is over now. Draw and die here. I swear to thee they shall never take us alive." Then turning to the insurgents he cried, "Fire, no agony for him!" They drew and the prisoner fell. For an hour, more the struggle continued, but at last the barricade was taken, and there was nothing for it but precipitate flight. Only two remained, the grand- father and the boy. Taking a revolver from the waist of one of the dead,. he Wrung his grandson's hand and then blew out his brains; themoment after he had killed himself. It is a terrible story, but one has an inward consciousness of its truth. It is the spirit of the Revolution, especially in France, intense, uncompromising, never to cease except in victory or death.—R. THE COUNTY FRANCHISE AND THE HOUSE OF PEERS. SPEECH BY MR. RYLANDS, M.P. Mr. P. Rylands, M.P., the member for Burnley, spoke at a meeting in connection with the Leigh Liberal Club on Tuesday, and touched upon the county franchise question and the House of Peers. Mr. Rylands said that Lord Har- tingtop, at Manchester, put before the country certain queo, tions on which he was desirous of ascertaining the view of the public mind. He asked whether it was thought that the borough and county franchise shoald be absolutely as- similated. Now, he (Mr. Rylands) was entirely of opinion that whatever the qualifications might be within the borough, they should be the same in the county. He con- sidered the question of the forty shilling freeholders was of very little consequence. It would be desirable to maintain them, with the condition that they should be residential. As to the Irish franchise, he had not the slightest hesitation in saying that they ought to give to Ireland exactly the same franchise as we possessed in England. And when men sail this would increase the power of Mr. Parnell and ethers, all he.said was that the best way to increase the mischievous power of Mr. Parnell was to cause grievances and give no remedies. Therefore, while he supported the Government in putting down violence and criminality he said "Give to the Irish people every possible justice, so that there might be no reasonable ground of complaint." As to whether the county franchise should be distinct from the redistribution of seats, he was altogether in favour of making it a distinct measure. Let them, carry the county franchise first. (Cheers.) The great point was to see that no man should be exoluded from political rights just because he lived out- side the boundary, but that every man should have a voice in the election of members. In that they had a principle on which there could be no mistake. They had a large minority againstthem in the House of Commons, and a great majority in the House of Lords, and it was quite possible—he believed it extremely probable—that the House of Commons would compel the Government to dissolve Parliament before they would allow any interference with what they called the "Constitution "—(laughter)—and which we were told was the priceless heritage of the English people. (Renewed laughter.) He believed they would have a dissolution be- fore this matter was settled, and then they would have before the public not only the question of the franchise, but there would he another question—Row far Can it ha right in this nineteenth century, when it was supposed the people of this country were working men, not idiots and children, that we maintain a House of Lords, composed of men having the power and authority of• controlling the legislative decisions of our country—men,, who were in the Chamber of Peers, not because they hail any special qualifications, but because they happened to be the eldest sons of men who may have been equally incompetent, and in fact may be the incompetent successors of an equally in- competent line of peers. (Laughter and cheers.) We had had dissolutions and defeats before, but in the end victory had always followed the Lioeral party. They might rely upon it that this struggle, which he believed would be a severe struggle, would end only in one way—we would take another great step in the progress of national rights, and in the interest of public reform. (Loud cheers.)

THE SOUDAN DISASTER. A telegram has been received by the Khedive from the Acting-General of the Soudan which confirms to some ex- tent the information previously to hand regarding the disaster to Hicks Pasha's army. Two men, he reports have arrived at Khartoum, who left El Obeid on the 16111 and 19th October respectively. One reports that the Mabdi left Et Obeid for the purpose of marching against the Egyptian troops, and that afterwards he returned "with guns, rifles, large stores of ammunition, and a train of camels belonging to the Egyptian army. No prisoners were brought in." The second confirms the entry of the Mabdi into El Obeid. A telegram from Cairo, on Thursday, states that no con- firmation has been received of the news telegraphed kr the Austrian Consul at Khartoum announcing the receipt of letters from Kordofan stating that only one-third of the Egyptian army, inclusive of the English officers, were killed, and that the remainder were encamped at Rahad. The latest intelligence from Khartoum reports that the panic is subsiding at that place. It is not believed that the False Prophet contemplates a forward movement at present.

Another conspiracy has been discovered, or reported, in the garrison of Barcelona. Five officers have been arrested and sent to Madrid for trial on the charge of treason. A portion of the Farwell Block, Chicago, was burnt on Saturday. Seventy-five girls who were in upper workshops, sewing furs, had a narrow escape. Two were killed. The lose amounts to 200,000 dole

A violent gale has visited the north-east coast of the United States and the coast of Nova Scotia. Several wrecks are reported, including the loss on the Nova Scotian coast of the steamer Princess Alice and eight of her crew. The New York Herald publishes a telegram from Ottawa stating that according to advicas from British Columria there is a probability of Indian disturbances shortly breaking out there, owing to some difficulty concerning a missionary. A deplorable calamity occurred on Thursday at /russels. Fire broke out in the Palace of the Legislative Bodies, and the building in which the Chamber of Deputies met was de- stroyed. Great damage was also done to other Government offices.

News has been received of the safety of an exploring party led by Mr. W. J. O'Donnell, which for six months has been lost to view in the interior of South Australia. All the members of the party are alive, but greatly weakened by the hardships incurred.

- The election- of Mr. Carlisle as Speaker of the United States House of Represmtatives is considered to have put the Democratic party "frankly on the Free-trade platform;" but the World thinks there is small probability of a tariff bill being passPd during the present session. There is no trustworthy confirmation of the report that the English Government had concluded a preliminary com- mercial convention with Spain. The Times correspondent states that the impending exit of the Liberal Ministry would render it very difficult to pass a commercial treaty through the Cortes.

The mail from the South-west African coast brings in- telligence of an outrage upon a British subject at Gaboon. On a charge of illegal importation of rifled guns, the Eng- lishman has been ordered by the French Governor of Gaboon to quit the territory, although French merchants are said to import and sell such weapons without restric- tion.

• THE MALAGASY ENVOYS ALIVE AND FETED.—A Times Durban telegram says the latest news from Madagascar practically contradicts the rumour of the strangling of the ambassadors who visited Europe. On the 17th October they were being, feted at Antananarivo. The French admiral ex- pects to more inland in MaJagasc ir about February or March. Much sickness exists among the French troops. ENCOUNTER WITH BANK ROBBER.—Four burglars robbed the Bank of New Washington, Ohio, last week. They escaped on a hand car along the railway to Vernon, and then went to Shelby. Here telegrams aroused the offi- cials, who intercepted them, and a pistol encounter followed. Several officers were wounded, and one burglar was killed. The others fled though the woods pursued by the citizens. After a pursuit of two miles the burglars turned and killed one of the pursuers. A second burglar was captured, and after a hot pursuit another was killed. The fourth burglar escaped.

MUSSULMIN FANATICS TN PERSIA.—A letter from Meshed, dated the 23rd ult., states that the Mussulman fanatic Khaf Seyd, who arrived at Mery at the end of October, subse- quently left that place, p.rid, travelling by the Mery road entered Persian territory at the head of a rabble of 2,000 Turcomans. Another small body of Turcomans had entered Persian territory by way of Zuraba, and a third is in the neighbourhood of Kelat. The three bands are reported to be slowly advancing towards Me shed, where perfect order prevails, although considerable anxiety is felt, giving rise to exaggerated reports. The Tkircomans are stated to be badly armed, the muskets they have being of a converted pattern. Persian troops have been sent to stop their progress. THE AMERICAN PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE —The President's Message was sent to Congress on Tuesday. It deals, as usual, with a vast number of subjects. With reference to the rejection by the United States of British "paupers," the President suggests the advisableness of further legislation. In regard to the finances, Mr. Arthur states that there will probably be a surplus in 1885 of sixty million dollars. There will be large funds in the Treasury, but while he considers further reductions of taxation and in the tariff wise, he does not advise the adoption this session of a measure largely reducing revenue. The President suggests that a portion of the surplus should be employed in strengthening the navy and coast aefences. The United States, whilst they will make,no attempt to compete with European navies, must have a navy capable of defending their harbours and protecting their commerce. The Mormon question gives the President occasion to recommend the abrogation of the Territorial Legislature and the assumption by Congress of the entire political control in Utah. ENGLAND AND THE ZULUS: AN EXTRAORDINARY R 17.• MOUR.—A report is current at Durban that Cetewayo will be reinstated at Ulundi with a resident British Commission, and that a small bo iy of British troops will remain at Ulundi until the permanent tranquility of the country is assured. An important meeting has been held at Ekowe, at which many natives of the reserve territory were present, together with Mr. Osborn, the British resident, John Dunn, and a large number of native chiefs. The latter complained strongly of the present state of the country, which they ascribed to the action of the British Government and white agitators, and requested, the immediate removal of Cetewayo. and a statement as to the Government's intentions. John Dunn predicted bloodshed in the reserve unless some settle- ment were quickly arrived at, and warned the Commissioner of the danger in this respect. Mr. Osborn replied that he daily expected to receive orders from the British Govern.e ment, and promised to forwarcl the requests of the chiefs to the proper quarter, assuring them at the same time that the settlement of the country was seriously occupying the at- tention of th% Government. The meeting then dispetsed quietly.

It is much easier to think right without doing right thaia to do right without thinking right. Just thoughts may, and woefully often do, fail of producing just deeds, but just deeds are sure to beget just thoughts. For when the heart is pure and straight there is hardly anything which can mislead the understanding in matters of immediate personal concernment. But the clearest understanding can do little In purifying an impure heart, the strongest little in straightening a crooked one.
