THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECF/MBER 8, 1883:

_ WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. ' The monthly meeting of the Council was held in the Council Chamber, at the Town Hall, on Tues lay evening. Present :—The Mayor (Alderman J. Harrison), Aldermen Webster, Kean, Chandley, Pickmere, Holmes, and Burgess; and Councillors Dakin, Sutton, Marsh, E. Wright, Bolton, Dixon, Caldwell, Whittle, W. Pierpoint, Monks, Greening, Wallington, Broadbent, Platt, Woolfall, W. J. Burgess, Tay- lor, Brown, Mackie, and Litton ; W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), C. Chorley (borough treasurer), and T. Longdin (borough surveyor). WATCH COMMITTEB : A QUESTION OF POLICE PROMOTION. The MAYOR moved, and Councillor BROADBENT seconded, the adoption of the minutes of the Watch Committee. Alderman HoLuss asked what was the meaning of the recommendation that Sergeant James be promoted to the

rank of inspector of the force. The MAYOR said that the only answer was that the Chief Constable recommended the Watch Committee to take that coarse because in his absence Sergeant James was the most competent official to represent him. Councillor BROADBENT explained that the argument brought before the committee by the Chief Constable was that Sergeant James would not be an inspector in the ordinary sense of the word, that was, he would have nothing to do with inspecting the outdoor police, bat that it would be convenient that Sergeant James occupying the poeition he did as clerk, that at all times and especially during Mr. Hunt's absence he should be able in his correspondence to write as inspector rather than as sergeant. The arrangement would be advantageous to the force, convenient to Mr. Hunt,

and involve no additional expense. This explanation being accepted as satisfactory the minutes were thereupon confirmed. FINANCE COMIIITTE2. The minutes of this committee, which evoked no discus- sion, were adopted on the motion of Alderman HOLMES seconded by Councillor GREENING. THE LIGHTING or. THE BOROUGH. The minutes of the Street Improvement and Lighting Committee were adopted °a the motion of Councillor BROADBENT seconded by Councillor PLAIT. Alderman WEBSTER drew attention to the want of better lighting in certain parts of Church-street and Dolman's-

lane. - PAVING AND SEWERAGE COIISIITTER : OUTCAST WARRINGTON." Alderman KEas, in moving the adoption of the minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Committee, said that a sub-com- mittee had been appointed to examine the backyards, alleys, and courts of the town, and as they had the assistance of Dr. Gornall, the medical oflizer of health, they hoped to
put those places in a better state. Councillor WOOLFALL seconded the adoption of the
minutes. Councillor PLLTT asked whether it was the intention of the committee to improve 114ydock-street, as that was pro-

mised some years since. Alderman BURGESS asked & similar quest;en with regard to Sankey-street. Ten years ago, and even longer, it was determined that Sankey-street should be dealt with, but Sankey-street remained to-day in the same condition, and even worse. Councillor BROADBENT was glad to bear that it was the intention of the committee to pay attention to the condi- tion of the courts and alleys of their town, as that formed the subject of the great consideration of the present day. The improvement of such places was the most important question that could be dealt with just now, and he was pleased to know that Warrington would be beforehand, and that they would not have the "bitter cry of outcast War- rington" to deal with. Alderman BURGESS: That has been done already. Councillor BROADBENT: But there is something left. Alderman KEAN observed that with regard to klaydock- street they had the mind but not the means to effect an improvement there. As to Sankey-street, a resolution had been brought forward that they should have wood paving in Sankey-street, and they were making great preparation for that, and were getting all th 3 information they could. The matter was net being lost sight of.

The minutes were then adopted. THE MUSEUM AND ITS PATRONS. FIRE ENGINE COMMITTER.

On the motion of Alderman PicEMERE, seconded by Councillor BURGESS, the minutes of this committee were confirmed. WILDERSPOOL CROSSING AND THE SHIP CANAL. The MAYOR moved, and Alderman Hourns seconded the confirmation of these minutes. Councillor Dr. Macnin drew attention to the changes pro- posed by the Ship Canal Company, and asked if it was not possible for the Council to take advantage of the proposal to carry the line from Latchford station on to Warring- ton or close to Warrington on arches, to have that height continued by arrangement with the Londm and North-Western Railway Co., even if at the Council's expense so as to get rid once for all of that dangerous Wilderspool Crossing. If the viaduct were continued over the Wilderspool Crossing and over the river on to Arpley Station, the dangerous level crossing might at once and for ever be got rid of. The railway company would be bound to do it at their own expense some day, and perhaps they would willingly assist in doing it at present if the Corpora- tion were to bear part of the expense. Alderman PICEHERE was rather afraid if the arches were made the gradient would be too heavy, but, of course, that was a subject for the engineers to consider. The MAYOR thought Councillor Dr. Mackie might rest assured that when the matter came before the General Pur- poses Committee for consideration they would not be slow to take advantage of everything they could. The plans were only deposited on the 30th November, and the Bill was not out yet. The remarks of Councillor Dr. Mackie would not be forgotten when the committee had to deal with the scheme, which had not as yet been reported upon. The minutes were passed. do—unCilloVScerriarr proceeded to move "That the follow- ing resolution of the Council of the 4th September last be rescinded, and that a further extension of the time be ' allowed to Mr. Martin Brown :—That the Town Clerk give the necessary notice to Mr. Martin Brown to remove the wood building known as the Theatre of Varieties in Sankey- street." CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT WARRINGTON- SPEECH BY MR. ASHMEAD-BARTLETT, M.P. A meeting largely attended, and under the auspices of the Warrington Conservative Association, was held at the Public Hall on Wednesday evening. It was announced that the principal speakers would be Mr. Aehmead-Bartlett, M.P., for Eye, and Colonel Burnaby, and some disappoint- ment was evinced when it became known that the gallant colonel was unable to attend. Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart, presided, and he was supported by Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett, M.P., Mr. F. T. Atkins (secretary to the United Railway and Government Servants Association), the Mayor (Alder- man J. Harrison), the Revs. S. Wilkinson, E. C. E. Carleton, and F. G. Richards, Aldermen Kean, Webster, Pickmere, and Councillors Mackie, Sutton, Marsh, Burgess, Whittle, Fran- comb, Taylor, Ashton, J. Pierpoint, and Litton.; Mr. W. Beamont, Mr. J. R. Buckton, Mr. R. Pierpoint, Mr. J. Carson, Mr. E. Nicholson, Jac. The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings, said that the meeting was the first of a series which they intended to hold during the season, and that in organising these meet- ings they meant business. (Cheers.) After announcing apologies for non-attendance from Lord Winmarleigh, Colonel J. Ireland-Blackburne, M.P., and others, the bon. baronet expressed his regret that Colonel Burnaby had found it impossible to be present amongst them. Mr. JAMES CARSON then moved—" That this meeting con- demns the policy of the present Government both at home and abroad." The terms of the resolution, he said, were warranted by the events which had taken place since the advent of the present Government. Mr. R. PIERPOINT seconded the resolution. and in doing so said that the Government had allowed riot and murder to ran through Ireland in order that remedial legislation might be made possible. (Hear, hear.) But were they as Subjects of the Queen going to allow the Irish to continually occupy the time of Parliament ? (Cries of "No, no.") It was all very well to talk about "Ireland for the Irish," but they wanted a little bit of England for the English. They were thoroughly determined that the union between Ireland and England should never die. In Egypt they had been obliged to engage in a war which was not a war—(laughter) —and which might have been avoided if they had adopted the same policy as that pursued by Lord Beaconsfield— (cheers)—when he sent the fleet of England up the Dar- danelles with a much greater enemy in his face than the Egyptians, and secured a peace without shedding a single drop of blood, and at a price of only a threat of war. (Cheers.) Again, did they ever see any set of business men make such a bungle of any matter as the present Government had done with reference to the second Suez Canal? Turn- ing to India, they had the unjust Ilbert Bill, but he hepel that Lord Ripon might yet be made to understand that he was the servant of the Queen and the people of England, and that they had been born and were the governors of the people of India and intended to maintain their rule. (Cheers.) Mr. ASHMEAD-BARTLETT, M.P., who, on rising, was re- ceived with cheers, said that the difficulty he had in dealing with that resolution, so comprehensive and yet so true, was not want ef subject-matter, but to know where to begin and where to end the long category of blunders of the present Ministers of the Crown. He desired first to direct their at- tention to the pernicious measure which was now being forced by the crotcheteer Viceroy on the people of India against the wishes and feelings of the great majority of them. The Ilbert Bill proposed to give jurisdiction over Europeans to native magistrates, and thus to put English- men, Scotchmen, and Irishmen in India under the jurisdic- tion of men who were of a different race, men who were idolators, and many of them were sensualists, men who worshipped a cow and despised a woman. How could such a measure elevate the Hindoes? (Hear, hear.) If this measure was persisted in and British supremacy in India interfered with—if they allowed Mr. Gladstone to aim the blows of his axe at another Upas tree as he had done in Ireland, they would have results more disastrous and diffi- cult to deal with India than they had in Ireland. Mr. Pierpoint had well said that, whether the Bill be small or great, the result of it was too fatally apparent. It had stirred up from end to end of India antagonism between the whites and the native subjects of the Queen; it had caused British-born men to feel hatred towards the natives, and caused natives to detest the whites. This condition of things wise statesmen in the past had always striven to avoid. It had been the object of British statesmanship to maintain good and peaceful relations between the Europeans and t-e natives, and they had succeeded in doing so till this fatal measure was introduced. He repeated that this fatal measure had stirred up turmoil and discontent from one end of India to the other. Was not that a contrast, and a great one, too, between Lord Beaconsfield's Administration and

Mr. Glad.tone's? (Applause.) He add that at the risk of I being stiginatised as a Russophite, and at the risk of incur- ring the displeasure of a local newspaper of this town, a copy of which someone had favoured hirn with daring the past week, and which announced that he had discovered something about the Russian advanc,3 that no one else had discovered. That great statesman—(cheers)—w hose memory he saw from their cheers was still green _

_ amongst them and. revered, left India not only tranquil and contented in itself, but strong and secure with regard to its external enemies. lie gained for them a splendid and an invincible frontier. (Loud laughter at one corner of the room.) That, continued Mr. Bartlett, is the practised laugh—the mechanical jeer. (Cheers.) I have no doubt that under the inspiration of some local print they have been arrauging that laugh for some period. (Renewed cheers.) I doubt if half the men who raised the laugh could even mention the name of a single place on the frontier to which I have just alluded. But we will pass over the frontier, and let those men laugh, if they can, at the name of Candahar. That is the greatest position for commerce in the whole of Central Asia, and it is the key to India and Afghanistan. And that position was won for England by the genius of Lord Beaconsfield— (cheers)—and by the courage of your soldiers. A rail way was being made to that position, which would have enabled you to have conveyed there the manufactures of England, and the soldiers of India within four or five weeks of leaving _ _ _ .

your shores. Then, if Candahar had been held, those fool- ish persons at the back of the room might indeed have raised that senseless jeer if I had then talked about the dangers of a Russian advance, for with Candahar in your hands you would Irive been secure. But you gave up the position, you retreated while your foes were advancing; and within the last two years the arms of the Czar have spread over a distance of 500 or 600 miles. We know not exactly where the soldiers are, as our inforination is so bad, owing to the reckLissness of the Government. (Laughter and

cheers.) The speaker then went on to say that I Egypt gave an example of a policy rashly adopted and I precipitately reversed. The menacing state of affairs in the Soudan was perfetly well known two months ago, when Hicks Pasha started on his ill-starred expedition. The False Prophet had collected a vast following among the wild Arab tribes, and had defeated all attempts to subdue him. Twelve months ago he cut to pieces an Egyptian force of over 2,000 men. The dangerous ferment among the Arab race throughout Upper Egypt, Tripoli, Tunis, and Arabia itself was notorious. Yet poor General Hicks was allowed to start on his difficult task with nothing but wretched Egyptian conscripts at his back. A single British or Indian battalion would have ensured his success. But our Ministry _ _

-slut their eyes to the danger. And worse than this, they announced the evacuation of Cairo before anything was known of the result of General Hicks' efforts. Mr. Glad- stone knew, Sir Evelyn Baring well knew, that a deadly struggle was in progress in the Soudan between the forces of order and civilisation and those of fanatical barbarism. Common decency should have made them wait at least till the fate of General Hicks and his army was de- , termined. Within a fortnight of that reckless ' announcement comes, as usual, its ccantermand. The same persons who devised and who directed the evacuation were now compelled to reverse their policy. Let there be no illusion as to the danger. Unless the progress of the Mandi be resolutely checked Northern Africa and Syria might soon be destroyed by an irruption more fierce and savage than the Mussulmaa conquests of the seventh cen- tury. British or Indian troops should be sent at once to resist his advance. If those were not forthcoming, the Sultan should be invited to send some of his brave Ottoman _ _ _ _

-soldiers to repel the False Prophet. Though he blamed the Ministry for their neglect and shortsightedness. he would promise them his loyal support in a firm and effective policy. (Hear, hear.) As for Madagascar, we just learned that five British subj9cts had been cannoned to death by the French admiral. It was a nice rule of three sum. If it took Mr. Gladstone four months to coax and wheedle for the

imprisonment of one missionary an apology so stiff and formal that he dared not publish it, how long would it take him to extract reparation for the murder of five British sub- jects? With reference to the Suez Canal, the agreement

t-- just concluded between English shipowners and M. de Les- seps brought out in stronger light than ever the astonishing want of business capacity, as well as the political inaptitude shown by the Ministry in their abortive convention of last July. The shipowners were terribly hampered in their negotiations by the fact that Mr. Gladstone and his col- leagues had yielded to the French company without a struggle, the whole basis on which rested the British position to a control over the canal and to a reduction of dues. British trade had already keenly felt the injury done to its interest by the reckless and unpatriotic concession, on the part of our Ministry, of the Suez monopoly to M. de Lesseps. (Hear, hear.) British political interests were certain to suf- fer even more grievously and for many a day from the same blunder. The Radical newspapers which defended Mr. Gladstone's scheme four months ago were now railing at the shipowners for making what they called an unsatisfac- tory agreement. Yet the shipowners had succeeded in get- ting the three English directors on the Suez board increased to ten. (Cheers.) Our Ministry failed to increase their number even by one. The shipowners had obtained the im- mediate remission of the pilotage dues, amounting to 7p. per ton. The Ministry only got a promise of their remission when the shareholders should have received 25 per cent. in- terest gp their capital. But it was in the reduction of the tonnag'Pdues that the superiority of the shipowners' agree- ment viras most conspicuous. Under Mr. Gladstone's scheme the shareholders were to receive 25 per cent. interest before British clmmerce, which furnished five-sixths of the revenue of the canal, was to obtain even the paltry remission of sd. off the present monstrous charge of Bs. per ton. The share- holders were also to have 30 per cent. on their capital before British shipping obtained a reduction of is. 3d. per ton. Under the shipowners' agreement all receipts above 18 per cent. were to go equally towards the shareholders' interest and the reduction of dues, and all receipts above 25 per cent. were to go absolutely to the reduction of dues. So that, the last dividend having been 18 per cent., a very handsome reduction of tonnage dues, as well as a complete remission of the pilotage charges, would be effected at once. Had British interest been properly supported by the Mini- stry very much better terms might readily have been ob- taintd.. Under the threat—a perfectly legitimate one—of a rival canal, M. de Lessepa would either have sold his whole interest to us at a fair valuation, or he would have fixed his minimum interest at a much lower rate than 18 per cent.

(Hear, hear.) A British Ministry was bound to safeguard great imperial interests as well as British trade. In their Suez scheme, Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues protected neither. They sacrificed the political control over the Suez Canal and the avenue to India; and they sacrificed in the most incredible way the claims of British commerce to an adequate reduction of the transit dues. Lord Hartingten had lately affirmed that we were on good terms with Germany, and in proof he stated that Germany wished to co-operate with England for the mutual pretec- tion of English and German iaterests in China. We were very glad to hear this and hoped that Her Majesty's present Ministers who have been wandering for the past three years in the wilderness of subserviency to the French Republic and the Russian despotism, had at last returned to tie() wise policy of Lord Beaconstield—(cheers) and accepted a German alliance. Lord Hartington was a simple-minded statesman, who did not give too close attention to the per- formances of his colleagues. So perhaps he was unaware that the whole policy of the Ministry of which he was a member had been for the last three years leased on subser- viency to the French Republic, and that every sacrifice of British honour and British interest had been made ia the vain attempt to keep on good terms with that fretful and wholly unreliab.e Government. It was the Radical section of the Cabinet, and especially Sir C. One, who were mainly tesponsible for the hankering after the French Alliance. Perhaps Lord Hartington has never heard of the protest of the four Powers, headed by Germany, against that fatal j)int note—parent of evils for England and Edypt. Yet, after all, the commercial treaty, which had been used as a bait to lure our credulous statesmen to acquiesce in the Tunisian and Egyptian imbroglios, was contemptuously re- fused Sir C. Mike by his French friends. The annexation of Tunis, the Egyptian muddle, the refusal of the com- mercial treaty, the buccaneering expeditions against Mada- gascar and Tonking had, it might be hoped, opened the eyes even of Mr. Chamberlain and Sir Charles Dilke to the im- possibility of an alliance between England and the French Republic. Of course, Sir Charles Dilke puts this all on one aide as "ancient history." Ancient history was a convenient term invented to describe any phase or event in the conduct of the present Government during the past three years which was toe foolish or discreditable to bear examination. The Irish terror, the Transvaal shame, the abandonment of Kandahar, the Kilmainham compact, the blundering in Egypt, the abortive Suez scheme, and the Guildhall evacua- tion of Cairo, were excellent instances of "Ancient history." (Cheers.) It was all very well for Lord Hartington to talk about a cordial understanding with Germany. When we had heard one-tenth of the fine phrases, the admiration, the coaxing, and the flattering which have keen addressed during the past three years by Mr. Gladstone, Sir Chatles Dilke, and Mr. Chamberlain to the demoralised and unstable French Republic, offered to the splendid Germany monarchy. He should believe that the impotent and factious European policy of the present Ministry had indeed been reversed. But he expected that we should in a few days hear Mr. Gladstone apologising to France for Lord Hartington's sug- gestion of an Anglo-German understanding in China, as he apologised for having wheedled out of the French govern- mont the explanation for the Madagascar insults so stiff and formal that he dare not publish it. (Cheers.) The resolution was put and carried. The CHAIRMAN then called upon Mr. Atkins to address the meeting on the subject of the Ilbert Bill, observing that Mr. Atkins had been very much associated with the working men of India. Mr. ATKINS, in the course of his remarks, said he had been in India for nearly 23 years, and all during that time he had been a workingman and working with his fellow- country throughout the length and breadth of that great country. Those men were now threatened with a great and terrrible danger in the Ebert Bill. Ile fancied many people in England did not understand the terms of that Bill—at least such was the opinion of their countrymen in India, for they could not believe that the working men in England were so little wanting in sympathy to those who had exiled themselves in that foreign land. They had had many pri- viliges taken away from them from time to time. The chil- dren of their countrymen in India were not allowed the pri- vilege of competing on equal terms with the natives for ap- pointments in the Public Service. Those present might think that unfair and unjust, but it was true, and Lord Kimberley told him that it was the policy of the present Government to carry it out. Their countrymen had suffered that; they had appealed and petitioned from time to time, but they had had no response—in fact

they had been ignored. Now at last a great trial was coming, and the Governmerat wished to deprive them of the great right which they held in common with the people of England—that of being tried by their equals. (Hear, hear.) They petitioned against this, and appealed against it, and because they did so a telegram was sent to India to the effect that Mr. Gladstone had said in the House of Parliament that their ascendency must be checked. When that telegram arrived in India their fellow country- men and workingmen said, "What have we done that this message should be sent to us—this reply to our petitions, our appeals?" At once meetings were held all over the country from east to west, north to south, and resolutions were passed that it was expedient that someone should be sent to England to tell the people here cf the great dangers their countrymen were likely to saffer. Much of that representation fell upon himself, and so that no one should be able to dispute the position he occupied he would hand to the chairman of that meeting a copy of those resolutions, so that he might be able to satisfactorily answer any ques- tions that might be put to him regarding himself. The Itbert Bill was a bill introduced by Mr. Ilbert, and some said he was responsible for it, but it must be a difficult matter to the minds of many to say to whom it owed its paternity. Mr. Mart first refused it, then Lord Ripon did the same, and it was referred to the former Lieu- tenant Governor of Bengal, but he would not have anything to do with it. When, however, Lord Kimberley answered a communication in the Times on the subject, he did not deny that he was responsible for it, but he admitted he (Mr. Atkins) had to .reply to that communication in the same journal, and then Lord Kimberley said he made no such statement. What were they to think of a man who ad- mitted one moment having made a certain statement, and then with the next breath denied that he did anything of the kind? But Lord Hartington had nobly come to the front and taken the blame on his own shoulders. Mr. Atkins then referred in detail to the Bill, and concluded by moving a resolution condemning it. Mr. E. NrcaoLsos seconded. He observed that many came there acquainted but little with that insidious measure known as the Ilbert sill. They only knew that it was a statute endeavoured to be imposed on the English com- munity in India against the feeling of every man woman, and child in that community. Until they heard the elcquent speech of Mr. Atkins's they were not aware of the absolute iniquity of any such measure. (Hear, hear.) He did not believe any of those scoffing gentlemen in the back ground—(laughter) upon whom Mr. Ashmead Bartlett had let his hammer fall with such sledge-hammer force—(renewed laughter)—he sincerely hoped they enjoyed the castigation_ they received—he doubted whether those persons could go away and say that they approved of such a measure as the Ilbert Bill. It was one step towards the disintegration of the Indian Empire. (Hear, hear.)

At this juncture Mr. H. WHITHAM, who was sitting in one of the side galleries, rose and intimated that he wished to ask a question of the last speaker, but he was greeted with loud cries of "Sit down," " Bradlanzh," " Atheist," " Order," and "Chair." This uproar was continued for several seconds, when The CHAIRMAN said he was always most anxious himself to show fair play, but he thought it was very inconvenient to put a number of 'questions just then. If, however, Mr. Whitham had only one quastion to ask, and only expected one answer, he could be heard. Mr. Whitham then endeavoured to gain a hearing, but without success, his voice being drowned with groans and repeated cries of 46 Sit down," "Turn him out," and "Throw him over." A number of men stationed themselves below the gallery, we suppose, for the purpose of " receiving " Mr. Whitham in the event of his opponents precipitating him over the balustrade. Order being partially restored, the CHAIRMAN (who could scarcely be heard beyond the reporters' table) observed that he should like to say with as mach courtesy as he could, that he perceived Mr. Whitham could not ask the question, but the gentlemen would sleep at Walton Hall that night, . and the question could be sent by post. Dr. MACKIE then proposed a vote of thanks to Sir Gilbert Greenhall for presiding. Referring to the presence of Mr. Ashatead-Bartlett among them that evening, the doctor ob- served that the hon. gentleman had been spoken of in the public press in kindly and gentlemanly enough terms, but as a gentleman who only represented a very small constituency indeed, and he (Dr. IClackie) wanted to tell his hearers that that was not Mr. Bartlett's fault; it was not unwillingness that prevented him representing either Liverpool, Manchester, or Middlesex, because he was prepared to go in for the biggest constituency there was in the three king- doms. (Hear, hear.) He would ask whose fault it was that the town their friend represented was so wretchedly small. It was not the fault of the Conservatives. At the passing of the Reform Bill of 1832, when an enormous change was made in the constituencies of the country, the town which Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett represented, a place with 330 householders paying £lO rental, was found worthy of retaining a member still, al- though other places were abolished. Thetford, an adjoin- ing town with 203 houses and a rental of £lO had no less than two Liberal members—(laughter)—but when their great and glorious friend, Lord Beaconsfield—(cheers)—brought in his Reform Bill in 1867 .there were thirty towns exceedingly smaller than Eye and Thetford having thirty members, and he knocked fifteen of them off. Mr. Ashmead-Bartlett re- presented a town manufactured originally by the Liberals,' and by them allowed to pass muster at the great change made in 1867. He coupled with the resolution the names of those gentlemen who had come such a long distance to give them all that valuable information with which they bad been furnished that evening. Captain LirroN seconded the proposition, and tha CHAIRMAN having briefly replied to the compliment, the meeting dispersed.

LYMAI LOCAL BOA,RD. On Thursday evening a meeting of the above Board was held at the Board-room, when there were present Messrs. Cameron (chairman), Callender, Dewhurst, Rogers, Wool- ley, Fester, Appleton, Gibbon, Thomason, Ridgway (clerk), and Mußard (assistant clerk). MR. RIDGWAY'S APPOINTMENT UNDER THE NEW BANKRUPTCY ACT.

The CHAIRMAN said that before the business was pro- ceeded with he would like to propose a resolution so that all the members of the Board could join with him in con- gratulating their clerk, Mr. Ridgway, on the appointment which had been given to him by the Government. Of course they were all aware that Mr. Ridgway had been ap- pointed official receiver under the new Bankruptcy Act. He thought the Government bad done a wise thing, and Lymm especially would think so, in selecting Mr. Ridgway. They all knew that Mr. Ridgway had conducted the business of the Board with tact and energy, and he was sure Mr. Ridgway would devote the same tact and energy to his new office. While saying this he could not but express regret for Mr. Milliard, their assistant clerk, for whom they all entertained the greatest respect, and who had lost his chance, be believed, simply from a technical point. But he hoped Mr. Ridgway's appointment would act as a little solace to Mr. Mullard. He trusted that none of them would have the misfortune to fall into Mr. Ridgway's hands. (Laughter.)—Mr. DEWHIIRST seconded the chair- man's resolution, which was carried unanimously. Mr. RinGwAY said he was much obliged to the chairman for mo- ving the resolution, and to the other members for the way in which they had received it. He hoped that he might be able to do his duty in his new office, especially so far as the creditors were concerned, for he thought that they ought to ibe looked after. (Hear, hear.)

• COMPLETION OF THE SEWERAGE WORKS. The Board's engineers (Messrs. Wilson and Mu'liner) submitted their monthly report respecting the progress of the sewerage works. It showed that the works are now practically complete.—Mr. WILSON said that the original estimate for the work was £3,362 2s sd, the contract was £3,353 13s, and the cost of the work which had been actually executed under the contract was £3,347 17s 3J, so that they had a small margin to the good of some £5 odd. This was work actually executed under the contract. Then as to the authorized extras which had been found necessary. These extras amounted to over £9OO, which was made up of the following items. On the outfall works the extras were £4l odd. The extras for the junction of Lymin branch and the junction of Rush Green were £330 2s 4d. This amount was made up of extra for earthwork which was found necessary by the moving of the line of sewer further from the railway, £192; the passing of the sewer underneath the railway, when it was found necessary to have a culvert which was not contemplated, £56, the cost of the flushing apparatus which was removed from the junction of the two sewers up to Rush Green, £36; the original estimate being £66, and which had cost £lO3 ; the small wrolight-iron bridge to carry the pipes over the stream, which was not contemplated, £32. The extras for the bridge approaches were a odd only. Then the extras for the Lymna branch amounted to £412. The first of these was the alteration at Lymm Bridge, between the Bridge and the canal, which the Board would remember was done to avoid a compensation of £5OO, and which cost £241. As regarded the syphon, they had got that about £ll under the estimate. In connection with the culvert required by the railway company there was an extra of £166. The Statham branch bad cost an extra £139, which was ex- clusively for the culvert under the railway, not contem- plated, and forced on them in addition to the other.—The CHAIRMLN said that the Board entered into a contract with the railway company, or the railway company would not have allowed them to go under the railway. Prior to this the company's engineer and the Board's engineer had ar- ranged as to what the company would want, and after the contract was signed the company's engineer altered his mind, and wanted things quite differently, hence the extra expense.—Mr. DENVIIIIRST: They have treated us rather hardly in the matter, but it was a matter we could not get out of.—Mr. ROGERS : But we had signed the COntratt to do the work to the satisfaction of the corn- company's engineer.—Mr. DEWHIIRSP : Exactly.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board in answer to one from the Board, with reference to the borrowing of £1,200 for the completion of the sewerage works, asking for a statement showing the items of the original estimate, the actual or probable expenditure, and an explanation, of the cause of excess, where there was an excess, on each item.— A resolution was passed, on the motion of Mr. DE7HURST, seconded by Mr. ROGERS, that the statement be furnished.— There was no other business of public interest.

A "No RENT" RESOLUTION.—It is stated that the crc.fters of the district of Glendale, Skye, held a meeting last week in the church, summoned by the sounding of the horns throughout the glen, at which they adopted a resolu- tion to pay no rent until they see what is the outcome of the inquiry by the Royal Commission.

The nomination for Ipswich is fixed for to-day, (Satur- day), and the polling for Wednesday. Thomas Bowring, who esc.iped from Shrewsbury prison a fortnight ago, was recaptured on Soudan night at Newport, Salop. Cressingham House, near Reading, the handsome country residence of Mr. Lonegan, was destroyed by fire on Saturday morning. Mrs. Patrick Staunton, the widow of one of the convicts in the Staunton murder case has just been released from prison by an order from the dome Secretary. In the Queen's Bench on Saturday, Mr. Justice Field held that a marriage with a deceased wife's niece came within the prohibited degrees, and that the offspring of such mar- riage were illegitimate. EXTRAORDINARY SUICIDE.-At Cullingworth, in York- shire, a cottager named Thomas Lund, having fallen into arrears of rent was threatened with the sale of his furniture. To avoid this result, he saturated the furniture with petro- eum and set it on fire. Immediately afterwards he went to a neighbouring reservoir and drowned himself, having first tied round his neck a favourite cat and a clock weight. Meanwhile the furniture and the cottage were destroyed by the fire. .

DESTRUCTIVE FIRES.—On Monday morning, about five eyclock, two large cloth drying stores belonging to Messrs. John Orr-Ewing and Co., Croftengea Works, Alexandria, Dumbartonshire, were burned down. The damage, which is estimated at about £B,OOO, is covered by insurance.—A fire which broke out on Sunday evening in a range of ware- houses in Robert-street, Liverpool, was not extinguished until ten o'clock on Monday morning, despite the utmost exertions of the fire brigade. The amount of damage is roughly estimated at £60,000. THE EXTRAORDINARY WILL CASE.—After a trial lasting fourteen days, the extraordinary will case of " Priestman v. Thomas and others" was concluded in the Queen's Bench Division on Tuesday. The plaintiff, illegitimate son of James Whalley, who died worth sixty thousand pounds, brought the action to set aside a compromise made respect- ing his father's will, whereby the defendant Thomas got seventeen thousand pounds, en the ground that it was ob- tained by fraud, and that the will set up by Thomas was forged. The jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff.—Mr. Justice Manisty said the finding was entirely according to his own feeling, and he ordered the documents to be im- pounded. EXTRAORDINARY DEMONSTRATION OT ANTI-VACCINA- TORS.—On Tuesday morning, at Leicester, several thousand persons attended a sale of the goods of ten persons, includ- ing a guardian of the ppor, seized for non-payment of fines for refusing to vaccinate their children. The approaches to the saleyard were packed with dense masses of people, and in the yard the chief-constable, 30 policemen, and many de- tectives present to preserve order. The auctioneer was re- ceived with groans, and on Mr. Amos Booth, the secretary of the National Anti-Vaccination Society, protesting against the proceedings, the auctioneer called upon the police to re- move him. The crowd yelled and rushed on the policemen, driving the men back, but at length Mr. Booth was removed. The furniture was sold amid the wildest disorder, and the police were quite exhausted by their efforts. At a Maki meeting, attended by many thousands of persons, in the Market-place, resolutions were passed condemning the pro ceedings. DEATH OF LORD HOWARD OF GLOSSOP.—Lord Howard of Glossop died at his London residence, Rutland Gate, at half-past nine o'clock on Saturday night. The deceased nobleman was the second son of the thirteenth Duke of Norfolk, by Lady Charlotte Sophia Leveson-Gower, eldest ' daughter of the first Duke of Sutherland. He was born on the 20th January, 1818, and educated at Trinity College, Cambridge. Lord Edward Howard, as he was then called, was Vice-Chamberlain of Her Majesty's Household from 1846 to 1852, and Deputy Earl-Marshall of England from 1861 to 1863. He unsuccessfully contested Shoreham in 1847, and Horsham in 1848, but on petition was seated the same year for the latter borough. He continued to represent it in the Liberal interest till 1852, when he was returned for Arundel, which constituency he represented till 1868, at the general election of which he unsuccessfully contested Pres- ton. During the 20 years in which he sat in the House of Commons, Lord Howard was regarded as the mouthpiece of the English Roman Catholics, whose claims, especially in the matter of education for the poor, be unflinchly sup- ported, as he afterwards did in the House of Peers, to which assembly be was summoned in November, 1869, by the title of Baron Howard of Glossop, in the county of Derby. In 1870 Lord Howard unsuccessfully contested Westminster for the London School Board. MINERS' WAGES: GENERAL STRIKE ABANDONED.—The proposed general strike of miners, which, whatever its result, must have had many disastrous consequences, was on Tuesday abandoned. A conference of miners' delegates, representing 40,000 miners and nine counties, met at Shef- field, on Monday, and reassembled on Tuesday, when, after a long and somewhat personal discussion, they decided to recommend the men to withdraw their notices, and to ad- journ the conference to the 27th inst., when future action will be decided upon. A conference of Yorkshire delegates only was afterwards held, and they also decided to continue at work. Many of the delegates regard the agitation as practically at an end, and think there will be no further attempt at present to obtain more wages. The whole of the Claycross (North Derbyshire) colliers who had given notice to quit work on Tuesday in the event of the employers refusing 15 per cent. advance have unconditionally with- drawn their notices. A. general strike in Derbyshire is thereby averted. On Tuesday, a large number of the 2,000 miners on strike at Oldhill, Netherton, Dudley, and other places in South Staffordshire visited West Bromwich, with the object of persuading the local men to join them. Their efforts were unsuccessful, the West Bromwich men treating their brethren on strike with marked contempt and indiffer- ence. Later in the day the strikers resolved to resume work at the old rate of wages. THE TRIAL OF O'DONNELL : SCENE IN COURT. Pat- rick O'Donnell, charged with the murder of James Carey, the Irish informer, was found guilty at the Central Criminal Court on Saturday, and sentenced to be hanged. The Observer, describing the closing scenes of the trial, states that while the judge was passing sentence, O'Donnell stood at the front of the dock, entirely self-possessed, and occa- sionally turning his bead to look up into the gallery, as if in quest of a friend, or expecting some demonstration. Sen..- tepee over, the warders, who had closed around him, Are about to remove him, when he waved tkem back with his right band. "Wait a minute," said he, "my lord, may I speak ?" "Not now," was the answer, and already he was being taken away, when he broke loose for a socond to wave his arms above his head. "Three cheers for old Ireland !" he cried; " Down with Queen Victoria!" By this time six or seven powerful men had seized him, and he was strug- gling violently. "Three cheers for America," he went on to cry out. "Curse the Saxons; down with the judge ;" and as he was carried out of court by force, and before the door was shut upon him, he could be heard pouring forth blasphemies and execrations, of which it was difficult to catch the exact words, and the sound of which was instantly lost as the door was shut to. If any of the jury bad re- mained in doubt to the last moment, they must at once have realised how utterly untruthful had been the instructions upon which Mr. Russell's defence had been grounded. THE MURDER OF AN OLD WOMAN: BUNGLING EXECE- TIoN.—The man Henry Dutton, sentenced to death at Liver- pool Assizes for the murder of his wife's grandmother, attended what is known as the "condemned sermon " at Kirkdale Gaol on Sunday. The chaplain, at the culprit's request, drew the attention of the prisoners to the dangers of drink, ungovernable temper, and hasty marriage, to which three things the wretched man no doubt attributed his position. At Kirkdale prison, on Monday, Dutton was hanged. Binns, the newly appointed executioner, per- formed the talk of pinioning the criminal in a " bungling " manner, and on the scaffold conducted himself in such a way as to induce a juror to question his sobriety. The sobriety of the executioner, however, was certified, The gaol surgeon, at the inquest, strongly condemned Binns's method of procedure, which he said was "clumsy and in- efficient." Death had resulted from slow strangulation, as the executioner had used too thick a rope and Riven too short a drop to dislocate the vertebrie The jury found their verdict in accordance with the surgeon's evidence.—Binns, the hangman, has given to the world an explanation of the delay which took place at the execution. He alleges that the convict was " ready " no less than four minutes before eight o'clock, and was kept waiting until he was seen to be fainting. Then, without waiting longer for the Governor's signal—for which he had asked three times—the hangman finished 14 task. He denies that he was in the least affected byliquor. A correspondent of the Times indig- nantly calls attention to the " exhibition " of Binns in a public-house on Sunday night in Liverpool, and says there "is no disgrace bigger than this in our national life." BRITISH SHIPOWNERS AND THE SUEZ CANAL COMPANY. —A convention was agreed upon on Friday night, aft!r a lengthened discussion between the committee of British Shipowners and M. Charles de Lessens on behalf of the Suez Canal Company, of which the following are the leading parts :—The company shall either sufficiently. enlarge the present Canal or construct a second; a commisser of en- gineers and shipowners, not fewer than one-half inn En- glish , to decide upon this question; seven new British direc- tors to be added to the Board; a consultative e!iintnttee, to be formed in London, consisting of the English directors; arrangement to be made for payment of dues in London; the number of English speaking officials to be largely in- creased; the damage from accidents en the Callal to be borne by the company, with certain reservations; pilotage dues to be extinguished from July Ist; the transit dues to be dimi- nished from Ist January, 1881, by 50 centimes, thus reducing the charge of nine francs 50 centimes, and should dividend for 1883 amount to more than 18 per cent., a further reduc- tion to be made from the same date on the Uasis of half socb dividend; the company further to divide with the ship- owners on every succeeding Ist of January to the extent of one-half the profits that excess over the amount previously divided, such moiety to be applied in reduction of dues, the division to continue until a profit of 25 per cent, is reached, above which all the net profits to be applied to reduction of dues until such dues are reduced to five francs. The com- mittee express an opinion that the shares htlmt by the British Government should carry adequate voting powers, but M. de Lesseps demurs.—At a meeting of the Peninsula.! and Oriental Company, at London, on Tuesday, the Chairman referred to the arrangement made between.M. de Less.eps and the Shipowners' Association as File securing many i!n- -p ,rtant advantages to shipowniug interests—At a meeting of the Sunderland shipowners, on Tuos,l iy, it wis stated t,. tt the shipowners who negotiated Ow Suez Canal Con- s-, ntion with M. :Merles de Lesseps (.1;(1 not acknowledge nor did they waive the right to make the Lesseps' inonopoly, a second canal.

div.p: POLITICAL.

M. CILMBERLA.IN ON THE CHURCH QUESTION.-.-31X. Chamberlain writes to Mr. Thomas Edwards, Mountain Ash: —" I find it difficult to believe Welsh Nonconformists need advice from me on the Church question. Mv opinions are well known. I think the Establishment injurious to reli- gion, and unjust to all outside its pale. The property of the State Church is the property of the nation, and should be applied, after paying all personal rights, for the benefit of the whole people, and not for the advantage of a single sect."
MR. TRETELYAN AND COUNTY FRANCHISE.-Mr. Tre- _ -

yelyan addressed a Liberal demonstration at Kelso, on Tuesday night, on the county franchise. Speaking unolli- *jelly as a member of the Liberal party, he did not hesitate to say tkat the party were agreed that people living outside a county ought not to have votes for the county, and that those living within the county should have votes for the county. It was said that the Franchise Bill must have a Redistribution Bill tacked on to it, but he thought the people of Scotland would accept whatever Government gave them. Until the county householder was enfranchised, the redistribution of seats could not be eff cted without inflict- ing grievous hardships upon individuals. Teen SPEALERSHIP.—The Times, in one of its leading articles, stated that Mr. Goschen has declined the invitation to be put in nomination for the Speakership of the House of Commons. The Times says :—His reason for declining the high honour placed at his disposal is so well known that there can be no indiscretion in naming it. Among the many intellectual and physical qualities which go to make a good speaker must be reckoned the power of seeing clearly everything that goes on in the House, and this power, en- joyed in perfection by so many less gifted men, Mr- Goschen unfortunately does not po=sess. He has, we believe, cen- suited an eminent specialist with a view to discovering whether science can do anything to render hie defective eye- sight equal to the tasks that the Speakership would impose The answer, we regret to say, is unfavourable. SIR EDWARD WATRIN, M.P., AND NATIONAL Frelawen.— Under the heading "If I were Chancellor of the Ex- chequer," Sir Edwerd Watkin, M.P., contributes an article on the subject of national finance to the Pall Hall Gazette. Sir Edward says that the suggestion for an amended Budget which he has to make is the result of 40 years' ex- perience of finance, and is very simple. Its basis is to deal with the liquidation of the debt on principles of ordinary common sense, and instead of paying off the £700,000,000 of perpetual three per cents by taking ;e7,000,000 a year bodily out of the taxes as a standing charge, the object be- ing apparently to pay the debt of in 100 years—that is. by 100 annual payments out of current taxation of £7,000,000
. , each—to get rid of the debt by the ordinary principle of terminable annuity, supplemented (to stop the old-fashioned traditions of the Treasury), if need be, by a sinking fund.

In the one case £7,000,060 Per annum has to be annually; taken bodily out of the taxes: in the other, only £1,162,000 has so to be taken, leaving £5,838,000 per annum available for remission of taxation and other good objects. LORD SAusßunY AND THE CABINET.—Lord Salisbury was present on Thirsday evening at a Conservative banquet at Watford. Responding? the toast of. "The House of . . _ _

Lords," he said' Lord—Hartington had designated for the Upper Chamber the • function of saying 'Amen" to the House of Commons; bat he (Lord Salisbury) did not think it required so numerous or able a body to perform this duty. The function of the House of Lords was to correct, if neces.

sary, the decisions of the other House. In reference to the question of Parliamentary reform, he contrasted the recent utterances of Mr. Chamberlain and Lord Hartington, and said if he were a betting man he should always bet on Mr. Chamberlain. Lord Hartington's functions appeared to te to mix water with Mr. Chamberlain's wine. The present

attitude of the Conservative party was that of spectator?. They could not tell what to do with a bill they had not seen, and which probably did not exist in any human mind at present; but if the coming measure at all resembled the picture marry of its friends had drawn of it, it was.likely to be strongly opposed. He commented on the variety of opinions represented in the Cabinet, but insisted that the utterances of any one of its members should he taken as representing the whole. MR. CHILDERS AND THE FRANCITISE.-Mr. Childers, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, addressed a large meeting of his constituents on Thursday night in Knottingley Town Hall. He cited symptoms indicating that the area of acri- monious discussion between the political parties was being narrowed. The extension of household fratchise to the counties was now almost generally admitted as desirable. Sir Stafford Northcote, in Ulster, had taken population as a criterion in advocating larger representation there. But the West Riding, on the basis of population and wealth, had much stronger claims. He hoped that the country would en- courage the present Parliament to deal with the reform of connty and London government by a representative system of popular election. He heartily congratulated the ship- owners on the result of their recent negotiations with M. de Lesseps. No feeling of personal pique or jealousy would weaken the desire of the Government to promote a settlement for the best interests of British commerce. 'With regard to the Australian Conference at Sydney, he admitted that the premature engagements of territory were mischievous, but Britain's colonial empire must expand, and one of the beet proofs of statesmanship was wise regulation and guidance of the expansion. MR. CHAMBERLAIN AT WOLVERHAMPTON.-Mr. Cham.

berlain attended the banquet of the Wolverhampton Liberal Club, on Tuesday night, and in replying to a complimentary toast denied that Liberals were "setting class against class." Liberalism, he said, was a bond of union between classes which was not to be obtained by charity, however well in- tentioned, or patronage, however beneficial. Speaking sub- sequently at a public meeting the right hon. gentleman said there were no 41v1sions in the Cabinet, as people were asked to suppose. Ministers were all working with the same general principles in view. Moping melancholy had marked the Tories for their own, and the country was not to notice the fretful irritation of politicians out of office. He re- gretted that the state of Ireland was not satisfactory, nor would it be until the franchise question was settled. This must be done throughout the three kingdoms; and that im- mediately. The country would net wait ,patientlY for it any longer, and it must be completa, or the agitation would be renewed. The extension of the franchise must not wait

for redistributtion, but that was necessary at the earliest pos- sible moment. Ile hoped the House of Lords would have the wisdom to appreciate the demand and the justice of the claim, and not provoke a conflict in which they could not possibly be victorious.

'IRE CHIEF SECRETARY ON IRISH AFFAIRS.—The Cnief Secretary for Ireland addressed a meeting of his constituent! on Thursday evening at Galashiels. .Mr. Travelyan's speech was devoted to the consideration of Irish affairs. He pointed with satisfaction to the great decrease in the number of agrarian crimes, there having been last month only 24 throughout Ireland, as compared with more than ten times that number in the corresponding month of 1881. If the noblemen aied gentlemen who blamed the Irish Executive for not suppressing public meetings univereally throughout Ireland had been in power, he doubted whether crime would have been any less, and he was sure that the future diffi- culties of governing the country constitutionally would by this time have been incomparably greater. Anyone who ex- pected success in Ireland to be rapid and striking must in- deed be sanguine. But he and his colleagues had faithfully endeavoured to follow tertain definite ends on a certain fixed line of principle, and the results had been such as to en- courage them in believing that that line was the right one. Their first business was to put an end to the reign of terror which made the lives of quiet people miserable throughout vast districts of the country, and to enforce the perform- ance of civil ana commercial obligations. A government might or might not be able to change men's hearts, but it was bound to regulete their conduct ; and the result of the endeavour to do so in Ireland eves not unpromising. 'MR. CHILDERS AT PONTEFRACT.—The Chancellor of the Exchequer addressed a crowded meeting of his constituents at Pontefract on Wednesday night. As the right hon. gentleman was war secretary when he addressed the electors last year, he devoted the first portion of his speech to a re- view of the military improvements recently effected. He asserted that it was quite a delusion to suppose that the short-service system had failed to give a sufficient number of recruits Referring to the legislation of the past session, he remarked that the Cheap Trains Act was not passed for the relief of railway shareholders, but rather for the benefit of workingmen and the operatives of large cities, to enable them the more easily to live in suburban districts where sites for dwellings were less expeosive. The measure to devise means towards the reduction of the National Debt was necessary because the machinery previously provided by Parliament for that purpose would have ceased to work in 1885, and signs of peril were apearent in the shape of amendments on the notice paper. Dealing with recent criticisms on the financial policy of the present Administra- tion, Mr. Childers compared the taxation per head of the population 14 years ago with that of the present time in order to show that there was a greatly improved appropria- tion of the public funds. Legislation for Ireland was also noticed, the right hon. gentleman contending that what that country wanted was not merely dry justice but sym- pethetic justice, which ought to be given in spite of the almost hopelessness which seemed to surround Irish ques- tions. The Acts passed recently.had brought us within measourable distance of the completion of what might be called a new settlement of the country, and this settlement, unless it WAS disturbed by wild schemes kr the relief of landlords by State purchase, would cement a new social order brought about in Ireland without revolution. He was of opinion that there would be a greater probability of co- , operation in practical measures for developing Irish resources if the spectre of Kparation was less often seen in the back- ground. As to the work remaining to be done by Parlia- ment, he urged them not to minimise or underrate the. changes which intact be made, which included the enfran- chisement of the peasantry and labourers, not onl7 in agricultural districts, but also in unrepresented towns, the transfer from magistrates to popularly elected councils of the Government of counties, and the grant of a municipal constitution to London. Personally he had no fear of the result, but to perfect it would reqeire all the wialeee end patriotism, not only of a party, bet of a people.

LOCAL GOVERNIENT INQUIRY AT FROSH THE WATER ANISEWERAGE SCHEMES.

A local inquiry was lid in the Town Hall, Frodsham,_ on Thursday, by Major ector Tulloch, Royal Engineers,. in reference to an appliction made to the Local Govern- ment Board by the Runcn Rural Sanitary Authority for sanction to borrow £4,77' for works of water supply, and £BOO for works of sewege and sewage disposal for the township of Frodsham. The following were present at the‘ inquiry :—Mr. Charles ltynolds, J.P., Mr. A. Thomas, J.P:, Mr. F. Rigby, J.P., Rev El. B Blogg ; Messrs. Jno. Ashton,. W. D. Jolliffe, Thomas Andrews, John Challoner, Robert Andrews, Thomas Dav 3, Joseph Cunnah, Thomas Riley, H. G. Linaker, Booth, Henry Tiley, H. E. Hey- wood, Henry Beswick also Mr. H. Linaker (clerk to the Authority), Mr. W. HLinaker (solicitor), Mr. H. Bancroft (engineer), Dr. Abs (deputy medical' officer of health), and Mr. Tames Farrington (inspector ef nuisances).—Mr. H. Ltaker read the notice of the inquiry, and stated that the qution of a water scheme for Frodsham was first started in the ear 1873, and during the, last ten years six schemes had eon considered, the present scheme being similar to the unprepared by Mr. B3ncro% in 1874, but extending over a lager area. The first scheme was not carried out in consequete of the large amounts claimed for land and water rights. The subj•?ct was agaia revived in December, 1882, and the pesent scheme was adopted, the total estimated cost, incltsive of land, wayleava., water rights, &c., being 4779 15.6 d. With reference to the loan of £BOO, required for the sewrage scheme, Mr. Linarer said that on the 10th July, 1883, he Authority had nrultr con- sideration a complaint by Meprs. Heywood and Massie of a nuisance caused by the sewag from houses in Water-sa and Newton flowing into a stream supplying Messrs. Heyvood and Massie's works at Frodslem Bridge with water. The nuisance was not a recent ore, but was considered in tae year 1874, and a portion of the sewage was afterwarua diverted from Water-street, Int still found Its way into Mu stream complained of at a lower point.—Mr. Bancroft, engineer, gave evidence as to the details of the schema, after which several que.ation3 were asked as to the mode of raising the annual amount required for principal and inter- est on loan on the water scheme, to which the Inspector replied that it was proposed to raise the amount by a rate on the water consumers, and it was calculatee4 that if the water was generally taken there would be more than suffi- cient to meet the annual charge. Any deficiency would, however, have to be met bv a rate levitd over the whole of the township of Frodsham, to which t!ete land, dm., would be rated at one-feurth of its rateable value. The Inspector then closed the inquiry, and proceWed to inspect the dis- trict.
