SATURDAY, DECEMBER 8, 1883.

THE visit of M. DE LESSEPS and his son, M. C. DE LESSEPS, to this country has been, we are gratified to find, attended with the most satisfactory resul.s to the commercial and shipping interests. It was at one time feared that our guests would depart without any agreement being arrived at as to the future working of the Suez Canal, and their hurried visits to Liverpool, to Manchester, and to Newcastle without any practical ad- vantage being derived, seemed to give colour to this fear; but happily their sojourn in London and their friendly intercourse with some of their best customers has been the means of awakening them to a sense of what is required from the Company which they represent. The statements of the famous Frenchman in the provinces were vague arid discouraging; what he is prepared to do has now been committed to paper, and the concessions he has promised are certainly much larger than was expected. Since the abandonment by the Government of the now celebrated Convention whieh they entered into with the Company—and the terms of which were, it must be admitted, as good as could then be obtained—we have had various schemes suggested for improving our com- munication with the East. One was the making of a separate and independent Suez Canal, supposing that we have the power to do so, which is questionable ; another the con- struction of a canal through the valley of the Jordan; and a third the making of a ship rail- way or a fresh water canal to Cairo, and thence across the Nile to Suez—these and other schemes were suggested, and they seemed remarkably feasible at first, but it is doubt- ful whether all or any of them were whothor thoy woro co or not the money was not forthcoming for their promotion. We need not, however, any longer trouble our minds with those schemes, for the agreement which has been drawn up between the leading ship owners of London and the head of the Suez Canal Company are such, we feel sure, to meet the demands of all the users of the Canal. The terms are very much more favourable than those which the Government obtained, and all parties are to be congratulated on the result. It is worth while, we think, to com- pare the terms now secured with those which the Government were prepared to accept. It was proposed by the Govern- ment to lend to the Company something like £8,000,000 at 31 per cent. for the purpose of widening the Canal or making a new one; the Company are- now to enlarge the present canal or construct a second channel without any advance of money from the British Exchequer. Under the new agreement the pilotage dues, which it is said amounts to from £l5O 000 to £170,000 a year, are to be extinguished from the Ist July next; -older the Convention of the Government those dues were to be returned to the ship owners—one-half when the Company paid a dividend of 21 per cent., and the other half when the dividend reached 23 per cent. It is fair to assume, considering the condition of trade that it would have been several years before either of these dividends could have been reached, so that the advantage to the ship owners under this head is very great. With respect to the transit dues, these, under the Government Convention, were to remain at To francs per ton until after the company had paid 25 per cent. profit, after which they were to be re- duced half-a•franc for each additional 21/e per cent. up to 30. When the shares paid 30 per cent. dividend, the reduction was to be so cents for every 3 per cent. additional dividend, till the dues became only 5 francs per ton. Under the Ship Owners Convention, the transit dues will be diminished from the ist January next by half-a-franc ; and should the dividend of 1883 amount to more than 18 per cent., a further reduction will be made on the basis of half such dividend above i 8 per cent. The Company is further to divide the ship owners on every succeeding ist January, to the extent of one-half, the profits (whatever the amount of such profits may be) in excess of the amount of profits last pre- viously divided, such moiety to be applied to the reduction of dues, and this division of the moieties is to continue until a profit of 25 per cent. is paid, above which all the net profits of the Company are to be applied to the reduction of the dues until the minimum of 5 francs shall have been reached. The financial result of this arrangement is, we believe, that by the time a dividend of 25 per cent. is paid the Company will have, by the abolition of the pilotage dues, the reduction of the transit dues. &c., returned £500,000 to the users of the Canal. It will be readily seen from the foregoing that the financial advan-

tages to the commercial commuuity are, under the Ship Owners Convention, very con- siderable and important, and so satisfactory that there is little, if any, cause for complaint. Other advantages of scarcely less importance have to be noted. The extension of the present Canal, or the making of another, is to be carried. out by a committee of engineers and ship owners appointed to study the ques- tion, half the members of the committee being English; and in addition to the three English directors who at present sit on the Company's Board, seven new English directors are to be nominated. A revision of the statutes of the Company is to be at once made in order to give these di- rectors voting power. It will not, therefore, be any longer a grievance that England has no voice in the management of this great waterway. A Consulting Committee consis- ting of English directors is to be formed in London, where an office will be opened and dues will be payable; and the Company undertake that in all future appointments to the transit service they will increase "to a large extent" the number of officials speak- ing English. The difficulties and incon- veniences arising from the fact of so few English speaking officials being in the service of the Company has long been acknowledged, and the provision to augment the number is a very judicious arrangement. One of the most satisfactory features about the terms is this, that they have been obtained without making any concessions to M. DE LESSEPS. He never asked the ship owners to recognise what he believes to be his exclusive right to make another canal—though we are inclined to think that has been more than once fully conceded by both the present and the late Administrations—and they never offered to do so. What the rights and privileges of the Canal Company are, therefore. still re- main to be decided by a court of law; and whatever they may be there is no extension of them now. The whole matter has been entered into in a purely commercial spirit from beginning to end, the ship owners have obtained the best terms they could, and those terms are very much better than the terms the Government proposed to accept for them. This only shows the wisdom of the course adopted some time ago by Earl Granville, who, when he was waited upon by a number of ship owners interested in the Suez Canal question, referred them to the Company. There was then a great outcry about Lord GRANVILLE'S discourtesy, but events have proved that the noble earl was only adopting a safe policy. Of course the Convention between the ship owners and M. DE LESSEPS leaves the political aspect of this question untouched; this may be safely left to the Government, who have already shown themselves ready to protect our political interests in the Canal at all costs.

div.head: BOUNDARIES OF RUNCORN AND HALTON.
div.p: THE BOUNDARIES OF RUNCORN AND HALTON.

It will be in the recollection of our readers that some time ago a Local Government inquiry was held for the pur- pose of more exactly defining the boundaries of those parishes in the Runcorn Union which had been in some un- accountable way in the dim past hopelessly mixed,ithe town- ships in question being, we believe, Runcorn, Halton, Frod- sham, Frodsham Lordship, Norley, and Ore wton. So strange was the mixing that a good portion of the business centre of Runcorn was in the township of Halton, though for sani- t iry purposes included in the Urban district under the control of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, the conse- quence re sulting that the district rates in the mixed area were paid to tha Co:nmissioners while the poor rates (in- cluding ia some small degree sanitary rates) were paid to the overseers of Halton. • So far as Runcorn and Halton are concerned this is inlpar t and from the 24th of March next, wilt be wholly a thing of the past, the township of Runcorn for all purposes, Poor Law, Burial Board, School Board, and S mitary government being co-terminous, and although the dividing line between the contiguous townships is yet any. thing but symetrical, the gain in administrative facilities cagnot fail to be very great. The Local Government order which has bean sent to the overseers, states that it is also issued with the consent of the Education Department, so far as the new arrangement may affect the constitution of the school district, which enlarges very considerably the re- spontibilities of the School Board with respect to school accommodation in the very near future.

THE B EGGING NUISANCE AT WIDNES.—On Thursday, at Widnes Police Court, Edward Barton was charged with begging, and he was sent to gaol for seven days with hard labour. Inspector Wood remarked that there was a great deal of begging in the town,—in fact, more than he had ever known in any other,—and it was time it was stopped. RUNCORN STARE-BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY.— An appropriation in connection with this society took place at Weston on Wednesday evening, under the presidency of Mr. F. J. Claudet. There was a fair audience. The first ballot resulted in the number 480 being drawn, to which no shares are attached. Number 179 was then drawn, and Mr. John W. Towers, chemist, of Widnes and Runcorn, is entitled to £2OO for 14 years, free of interest. ENTERTAINMENT AT WIDNES.—A. public entertainment was given on Monday evening, in Albert-road Wesleyan Chapel. by the members of the Band of Hope connected with that place. There was a good audience. Mr. J. P. Morewood presided, and delivered an appropriate address. During the evening Mr. R. Balmer, of Oswestry, delivered a lecture on temperance topics. An excellent programme of songs, recitations, &c., was gone through. THE ROUBERY BY A MARRIED WOMAN AT WIDNES.— At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Mary Maehr, a mar- ried woman, residing at Simms Cross, was brought up on remand charged with stealing 14 yards of shirting, valued at 19s 3d, the property of Messrs. Reid and Co., of Widnes. Lie fact,s of the case have been previously reported in th e Exanziner. The evidence having been repeated, the pri- soner, who protested her innocence, was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour. HALTON WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL BAND OF HOPE.— A meeting of the above society was held on Tuesday even- ing. The chair was taken by the Rev. S. Mees, the resident minister. Songs, dialogws, recitations, &c, were given by the children and other friends, and there was a large atten- dance. The meeting was brought to a close by a very hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman, and also to those 'wh ) took part in the programme. Eighteen pledges were afterwards taken, making a total of 120. CHRISTMAS PRESENTATIONS AT RUNCORN. MOWS. Unsworth Bros., the enterprising hatters and clothiers of Runcorn, are offering a novel inducement to their customers. They announce that instead of the usual pictorial almanack they will give two splendid pictures, one an oil painting of "Killarney by moonlight" and the other an historical engraving of "Nelson receiving the Sword on the San Joseph." Both pictures are charming productions of art, are handsomely framed, and the presentations will doubtless inspire great interest. , THE COOKERY LECTURES AT RUNCORN.—The course of !lectures on cookery by gas appliances by Mrs. Thwaites I have been an unqualified success. Each lecture has been w4ll attended, and the Gas Company are deserving of every praise for the enterprise which prompted them to bear the cost of such a course for the benefit, mainly, of the public. On Thursday Mrs. Thwaites provided a luncheon, to which about 80 persons sat down. Highly commendary remarks were made as to the excellent manner in which the victuals had been cooked.

YOUTHFUL THIEVES AT WlDNES.—Before Mr. Brock, at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, Patrick McKenna, 13 years of age, was charged with stealing a bag, value is, the property of Mr. James Fowler, Central Hotel, Widnes. On Wednesday, a cab driver in the employ of the prosecutor took five bags to the works of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co., to be filled with sawdust. When the bags were filled, the man left them standing in the works, and shortly after- wards P.C. Murray saw the prisoner, who was accompanied by another young boy, empty one of the bags, place it under his coat, and walk away. He followed him, and took him into custody. The prisoner pleaded guilty, and was sen- tenced to receive six strokes with the birch rod. As INHUMAN MOTHER AT WIDNES.—Yesterday, at Widnes Police Court, before Mr. F. H. Gossage, Catherine ' Dogherty was brought up under a warrant charged with neglecting her child. From the statement of Mr. Scannell, the relieving officer, it seemed that the prisoner went away from Widnes some time ago. leaving her child in the cars of an elderly woman. The mother made no inquiries about the child. nor forwarded any money towards its mainten- ance, and it was given over to the .parish authorities and taken to Prescot Workhouse. The prisoner was apprehended at Bolton, where she was maintaining herself as a domestic servant. The magistrate remanded the prisoner until Mon- day to give her an opportunity of paying the £2 141 ad due to the Gra,di,ins.

div.head: EXAMINER,. SATURDAY, DECEMBER. 8, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER,. SATURDAY, DECEMBER. 8, 1883.

IRUNCORN Y.M.C.A.---Professor Andre, of the Alpine Choir, has made a donation of £5 to the Young Men's Christian Association for services rendered the choir during their visit to Runcorn. LECTURE AT WIDNES.—A lecture OR the subject of "Love, conrtship, and marriage " was delivered in the Baptist Chapel, Widnes, on Monday evening, by Mr. John Passey, of that town. The Rev. J. Yeatman, the pastor, presided, i and there was a good audience. WIDNES CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY. —On Thursday evening, Mr. R W. Roulston, of Liverpool, delivered a lecture .en "The Safe Anchorage," under the . auspices of the above society. There was a good audience, and the Rev. J. Wright-Williams presided. ST. MARY'S SCHOOL, WIDNES.—III behalf of these 1 schools, the St. Patrick's amateurs gave a dramatic enter- tainment on Monday evening, the piece represented being "The Irish Emigrant." The concluding farce was "Day after the Fair." There was a crowded audience. Rureconer RATAPAvEns' ASSOCIATION.—The annual meet- ing of this association was held on Tuesday night in Bethesda class-room. Mr, H. Coleburn occupied the chair, land criticised the work of the Commissioners for the past ' year. Mr. J. N. Lello was appointed to succeed Mr. Cole. burn in the presidential chair. Mr. C. Cooke was re-ap- pointed hon. sec., and Mr. Mellor hon. treasurer. ...CONCERT AT ST. BEDES, APPLETON.—In connection with St. Bedes Young Men's Society an entertainment was given in the schoolroom on Monday evening. There was a crowded attendance. An excellent musical programme was gone through in unimpeachable style by the following ladies and gentlemen :—Miss Nono, Miss Brown, Miss Leatherbarrow, Miss Johnson, and Messrs Morrison, Lawton, and Heyes. The chair rendered several glees. A DROWSY TRAviera.ma.—A young man named Michael Furlong was, on Monday, charged at the St. Helens Police Court with having travelled on the railway from Wigan to St. Helens without a ticket.—Furlong, it seemed, belonged to St. Helens. On Sunday he paid a visit to Liverpool, and on returning instead of getting out at St. Helens he went ' right through to Wigan, where he was c'eerged 9d excess ' on his ticket. Later on in the evening he was noticed by a . rail way official to get into a St. Helens train, and being ' suspicious, this official came to St. Helens by the same train and caught Furlong as he was trying to evade the 1 ticket collector, and brought him to the police station.—A 1, fine ef 10s and costs was imposed. STORM AT WIDNES AND RIINCORN.—During Monday ! night and Tuesday a gale of considerable intensity blew ' over Runcorn and Widnes, and some damage to property resulted. A. large workshop belonging to Mr. Farrell, con- tractor, Runcorn. had a portion of its roof, made of corru- gated iron, removed. The premises are built beneath one of i the arches of Runcorn Bridge, and were totally demolished ' recen.ly. A basket roof in five sections which was being 1 I put upon the building in course of erection for Messrs. J. H. Denis and Co., Widnes, was greatly damaged. Eight principals were dislodged and dashed to the ground, one of the sections being destroyed. The damage, which is esti- mated at £IOO, will fall upon Mr. Latham, ef St. Helens, the contractor for the work. A shed in course of erection at the Widnes Alkali Works was overturned, but the damage was very slight. UNITED METHODIST FREE CHURCH, WIDNES. The members of the Band of Hope in connection with this , church gave an entertainment on Monday evening to a good audience. Mr. Joseph Betney presided, and delivered a short address. In the course of the evening Mrs. Yause, the wife of the pastor, delivered an eloquent speech en the temperance question, and woman's relation thereto, her remarks being frequently applauded An excellent pro- gramme, consisting of songs and recitations, was gone through in capital style by the following :—Misses Ethel Atherton, Bertha Lloyd, Willcock, Katie Craig, Furber, Price, E. Waight, Camay, Robinson, Pummerbell, A. Bet- ney, J. Betney, Worthington, and L. Waight ; Messrs. F. I Price, Bate, H. Wilcock, W. Price, J. Mellor, J. H. Bushell, I E. Evans, A. Perrin, Bushell, and W. Mellor. The chil- dren sang a number of melodies in tasteful style. The usual votes of thanks concluded the proceedings. ALLEGED BURGLARY AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Pe olice Court on Thursday, before Mr. John Brock, Alfred Knock, a labourer, was brought up on remand, charged with bur- glariously entering the Castle Hotel and stealing therefrom , 28s in copper money. From the statement of Inspector Wood it appeared that the Castle Hotel, which is occupied by Rachael Hunt, was entered between midnight on the 28th and six o'clock on the morning of the 29th November. The robber had effected an entrance by forcing the pantry win- dow, 28s was abstracted from a jar which was placed behind the bar. The landlady remembered that one of the pennies in the jar had a punctured hole in it. On Monday night the 3rd inst. the prisoner went into the bar, and in payment for some beer which he had tendered the identical penny. The landlady was looking intently at the money, when the prisoner said, "What are you looking at? Do you remember to have seen the penny before ?" She replied, yes and it had been stolen. Information was conveyed to the police and the prisoner was subsequently apprehended. He was remanded for a week on the application of Inspector Wood. MARRIAGE OF MR. S. K. MITSPRATT, J.P., TO MISS MOLESNYORTH.—The marriage of Mr. Sydney Knowles Mus- pratt, J.P., of Widnes, to Miss Constance F. E. Sackville Molesworth, was celebrated in St. Peter's Church, London, last week. The guests assembled at the noted Grand Hotel,' Trafalgar Square, and were driven from thence in about 20 ' carriages to St. Peter's Church, where the bride and bride- groom were united by the Rev. W. L. Nicholas, rector of the parish of Flint. The service was choral throughout, and the choir in attendance rendered appropriate selections in an impressive manner, and as the happy couple left the church Mendelssohn's "Wedding March ". was played by 1 the organist (Mr. Sergison). On the wedding party and guests arriving back at the Grand Hotel a sumptuous feast was pat taken of, and the happy pair subsequently left for Dover en route for Paris and Algeria, where they will spend the honeymoon. The presents were numerous and of a costly character. The people of Flint made the event the occasion for great public rejoicings, the day being observed as a general holiday. A public dinner in honour of the marriage was held in tho Town Hall, when the usual toasts were honoured, and the complimentary addresses given. The toast of the evening, "Long Life and Happiness to Mr. and Mrs. S. K. Muspratt," was received with the greatest enthu- siasm. On the following evening (Wednesday) the festivi- ties were brought to a close by a canoe in the Town Hall, many local laeties and gentlemen being present.
SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT A WIDNES
WORKS.

About two o'clock yesterday, John Walker, a laboUrer at Messrs. Hutchinson's chemical works, and living in Pitt- street, was seriously injured. He was engaged repairing a cistern in the works, when a portion of the stonework gave way and alighted upon him, fracturing his skull anl smashing his right ann. Dr. McDonnell and his assistant, Mr. Richards, quickly arrived on the spot, and ordered the unconscious man's instant removal to the hospital, where they attended upon him and performed all necessary opera- tions. But slender hopes are entertained of the injured man's recovery.
' BRITISH AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY. ANNUAL MEETING AT RUNCORN.

• Under the presidency of the Rev. E. Williams the annual meeting of the Runcorn auxiliary of the British and Foreign Bible Society was held in Bethesda Chapel. There was a moderate attendance, and oa the platform were the Revs. J. Lewis, M.A., of Shrewsbury (deputation), W. Preston (local secretary), J. D. Thomas, J. Pickwell, and Mr. J. Humphreys.—The Rev. W. PRESTON read the annual report, which stated that the subscriptions to the society had been as follows :—The dowager Marchioness of Cholmondeley £5, Parish Church Association (collected by Miss Edwards and Miss Samons) £6 16s—decrease on last year 15s, Trinity Church Association (collected by Miss Warner and Mrs. Hankinson) £2 17s—decrease 13s, Wesleyan Association (collected by Miss Harrison and Miss Speakman) £l4 8s 6d —decrease :£2 us 6d, Congregational Association (collected by Mrs. Thomas and Miss Williams) £4 7s—increase £1 7s 6d—(applause), Presbyterian Association (collected by Miss Pritchard) £4 13s—decrease 2s, Primitive Methodist Association (collected by Mrs. Pickwell) £1 3s—decrease lie, Welsh Association nil—decrease 9s, United Metho- dist Free Church (collected by Mrs. Vanse) Ss 6d—decrease 9s, Halton Church Association (collected by Mr. A. Povey) £1 ss—decrease ss, Halton Wesleyan Association (collected by Miss Cramon) 2s 6d—decrease Li. 6s, Weston Point K=sociation nil—decrease £1 is; total £4l Os 6d—decrease £7 15s. Mr. Preston ex- plained that the Welsh Association preferred to send what they collected direct to their own association at Liverpool, and he had ir) doubt that the ,falling off in the collections from Weston Point was owing to the death of Mf. Ford. The number of Bibles sold during the year was 281, Testaments 113, and portions 138. (Applause.)—The CHAIRMAN, who was received with applause, said he re- gretted the decrease in the contributions, but he hoped next year there would be an increase which would more than make up for the present decrease. There was no society to which they owed more, as Christians of every denomination, than the British and Foreign Bible Society. Much of their success at home in the Sunday school, in the various mis- sions, and in the foreign missionary field must be attributed Ito the aid that they received from the Bible Society. Its aim, which was to put a Bible in the hands of every man and woman upon the face of the earth, was one of the noblest. It enabled men to read for themselves the wonder- ful works of God and the gift of His love in the redemption that had been wrought through Christ. He hoped they would express their gratitude in such a way that it would enable the society to achieve this. The society had done much, and it was destined to do much more, but its-efforts must be supplemented by their own as well as the contribu- tions of other Christian folk. (Applause.)—The Rev. J. Lmwis. M.A., then addressed the meeting at length upon the labour and achievements of the society, and observed the society had now expended nine millions sterling since its establishment 80 years ago, in printing, translating, and circulating the Word of God. It had circulated 97 million copies of the Holy Scriptures in 255 different languages and dialects. Last year alone 2,964,636 copies of the Bible were circulated.—On the motion of the Rey. J. D. THOMAS, seconded by the Rev. J. PICKWELL, a vote of thanks was unanimously passed to the deputation for his able address, and a similar compliment was paid to the Rev. E. Williams for presiding, on the motion of Mr. HUMPHRETS, seconded by ihe Rev. W. PRESTON.—The thanks of the meeting were also accorded to the minister and deacons of Bethesda Chapel for the use of the edifice.—The Rev. E. J. Robinson having pronounced the benediction the meeting concluded.
Loseby, Miss Marion Hood, who is a very pretty singer, and
Miss Nene Verona, who is a very pretty girl.

At the Lyceum, Mary Anderson has turned oat a success. If she had not undoubted merit I would s,y that she had been written and photographed i'ato fav,ur. Great things ars expected from Mr. Galatea. both because it is a modern play and because she is sore to look well as a statue. No actress can make much of such parts as Parthenia and Pauline. Miss Anderson sees that she nide a blunder is commencing with them, but wall-deserved success has come at last, and, though she must surrender the Lyceum in the ' spring, she will pass from it to some other theatre, pro- bably the Globe,. Unfortunately for lessees, never was there a season with so many untenanted theatres.

A couple of months ago the photographs of a very pretty actress were at a premium. I don't mean that they were rare, but that they were dear. They were 20 per cent. dearer than the Premier. The reason was that the pretty actress was going to retire into private life. She was to make a great match, and to be seen no more as a love-bora 'esthetic maiden, or a palpitating fairy. Now the photo- graphs are again abundant at the normal price at which a loyal subject can purchase the likeness. of the Princess of Wales or her husband. I am told the reason is that the marriage of the pen i with the peer seems more distant now than it was last September. It may be that the stage will keep one of the prettiest girls fiat has ever trod it.

But the most important theatrical news of the week is that Salvini is about to retire from the stage, and will in- clude London in his farewell tour. We shall have him here in February, and he must expect a great success, as the house he has secured is the Coy/31A Garden Opera House. Of course he will open with Othello, but lam told he will add Hamlet and Lear to his repertoire, which will also include two modern Italian plays. No artiste has such an extraordinary opinion of the English public as Salvini ; because nene ever had so extraordinary an expe- rience. He came here almost unknown, and won rich ap- plause, as was only to be paralleled by the receptions of Jenny Lind or Sarah Bernhardt. He came the next year to a much smaller theatre ; and, after playing to empty benches, had to retire a heavy loser. lam told that to this day he cannot make it out.
RUNCORN FREE PUBLIC LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

The usual monthly meeting was held an Thursday, in the Town Hall. In the absence of the chairman, (the Rev. Canon Barclay), the vice-chairman (Dr. Steele), occupied the chair, and there were present :—Messrs. J. Simpson, J. Meadowcroft, W. Handley, F. A. Lake, and T. Riley. A letter was read from the secretary of the Runcorn branch of the St. John Ambulance Association asking for the use of the reading-room, for the purpose of lectures.—After con- sideration, the committee came to the conclusion that they had no power to let the reading-room without the consent of the Commissioners, to whom the communication was referred. The Librarian reported that 1,081 books had been borrowed from the lending library during the month of November. looks presented during the month: By the trustees of the British Museum, 145 vols., compris- ing catalogues, autotypes, and guides; by Messrs. Willimer Bros. and Co., the "Liverpool Review" weekly for the , reading-room, It was decided to close the library on Tues- day, 25th inst.—Christmas Day. Among the books pur- chased this month and added to the library are "Oliver Cromwell: The Man and His Mission," by J. A. Picton ; "Among the Mongols," by J. Gilmour; "Thirteen Years among the Wild Beasts in India," by Sanderson ; "Fire Fountains," by Miss Gordon Cumming ; "Our Home in Cyprus," by Mrs. Scott-Stevenson; "The Last Journals of Livingstone," and "Our Inheritance in the Great Pyramid," by P. Smyth. A well-selectel list of magazines and perio- dicals for the reading-room was ordered to be purchased.— On Thursday evening, at 7 o'clock, Mr. T. Riley, a member of the Committee, formally declared the reading room open for the use of the public in the presence of Messrs. J. R. Frith, W. Brookes, H. Sefton, J. D. Jones (the librarian), and a number of the members of the Library. The room is very comfortably fitted up, and he tables will be supplied with the best periodicals of the day, the readers having also the advaLtago of a reference library of 300 volumes. We may state that the ladies have equal privileges with the gentlemen in the reading room.

div.head: CONSECRATION OF ST. AMBROSE CHURCH, WIDNES.
div.p: CONSECRATION OF ST. AMBROSE CHURCH, WIDNES.

St. Anbrose Church, Halton View, which was erected at a cost of £5,000, and opened about three years ago for divine wcrship was only consecrated on Thursday afternoon. Although the edifice was duly licensed, the Bishop of Livea- pool declined to consecrate it until a substantial boundary wall had been erected.. Every effort was made to comply with his lordship's desire, and by a variety of methods £250 WAS raised. The erection of the wall was then c)m- menced, and has now been completed at a cost of £5OO. The usual order of service was observed on Thursday afternoon. The petition for the consecration of the church was pre- sented to the Bishop by the Rev. George Bond, M.A., vicar of Farnworth ; Mr. T Sutton Timmis, Mr J Brock, J.P.' and Mr E Carey. The document having been read, the Bishop, followed by the clergy present, proceeded through the aisles of the church chanting the twenty- first psalm. Tne clergy present were : His Lordship the Bishop of Liverpool; the Von. Archdeacon Bardsley, MA. ; the Rev George Bond, M.A., vicar of Farnworth ; Rw J Wright-Williams, M.A., vicar of Widnes; Rev S A Spooner, M.A. ; Rev J Holden; Rev S Wilkinson, vicar of St. Paul's, Warrington ; Rev F W Cory and Rev A M Mitchell, curates of Parish Church, Warrington ; Rev E S Jackson, M.A., vicar of Sankey ; Rev H Vernon, curate of Sankey; Rev J Barnacle, vicar of Rainford ; Rev T CharrAers, M.A., rector of Halewood ; Rev R 13 Stewart. M.A., vicar of Halo; Rev J Ward, Orford; Rev D Llewllyn, curate of Holy Trinity, Runcorn; Rev II A MacNaughten, vicar of Prescot ; and Rev F Lea, curate of Prescot. • Amongst the congregation were—The Right Hon. Sir R A Cross, NI P., Colonel J Ireland Blackburne, OLP., Mr T S Timmis' Mr J Brock, J.P., Mr 11W Deacon. Mr J Matthews, and Mr Doyle. The prayers were read by the Revs George Band and S A Spooner. Tee Rev H A MacNaughton read theifirst lesson, and the Yen. Archdeacon Bardsley the second.
The Bisnor preached a sermon from tha text, "Let all --- • ..- - -

things be done unto edifying," being part of the Nth verse of the 14th chapter of the first epistle to the Corinthians. He said they were gathered together that day upon a very solemn occasion, namely, the dedication and consecration of another church to the worship and honour of God. The church licensed now for a long time had at length been set apart as one of the regular places of worship in connection with the Church of England. He had thought it a wise and proper thing that this consecra- tion service should be made as solemn as possible to all that lived around the church. He heartily prayed that God's blessing might be upon the building, and that in days to come large congregations might assemble there for the glory of God, and their own benefit for ages yet to come. He prayed that the Church of England might be true to her- self and that the time would never come when she should no lolv;er be the established church in the land. So long as she was true to herself he believed God would never forsake her. So long as she was true to her first principles, true to her articles, true to her prayer book he believed God would not forsake her. Referring to the principles and uses of public worship, his Lordship said there had been a great improvementin Church worship since the days of their grandfathers, when the par- son and die clerk used to perforra a kind of duet before the congregation, but it was far lower than it ought to be. A hearty true and real service was that in which every person joined sincerely and earnestly. In making an appeal for pecuniary aid to the St. Ambrose Church, the Bishop remarked that they might have felt that he was too severe in requiring that the wall should be built before the conse- cration, but in his opinion the House of God should be free from intrusion and surrounded by its own wall before the ceremony took place. The collection made at the close of the service amounted to 148 is.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
THE O'DONNELL TRIAL-THE HANGMAN SCAN- DAL-LIGHTS OF LONDON-A PICTURE EX- HIBITION-" GUNG'L REDIVIVUS "-POET AND PEER-THE ALHAMBRA-MISS ANDERSON AT THE LYCEUM-PHOTOGRAPHY AND MARRIAGE
LONDON, THURSDAY.

I think the most remarkable thing connected with the O'Donnell trial has been the little amount of interest which it excited. The elaborate preparations of the police seemed to be quite uncalled for. No newsboys paraded the West End late on Saturday night announcing the verdict and the sentence. The Court certainly was full, and I was sorry to see that the fair sex was more largely represented than is usual even in sensational murder cases. I think it is net using too strong a term to speak ef this attendance as dis- graceful. It was the more so because there could be little doubt of the issue. These ladies came to see an illiterate rebel proved guilty of a murder and sentenced to be hanged by the neck for his crime. I suppose the only excuse for them was that Charles Russell was expected to make a very great speech. And this he certainly did. Already efforts are being made to have the sentence commuted. The jury are being asked to participate in the movement, but I do not think they will. It is of the worst precedent for juries to come forward with explanations of their verdicts. They alone have the privilege of stating their opinions. Perhaps in the recent Case of Miller v. Joy the Middlesex jury, who made such fools of themselves, were right to prove the method of their folly. I fear O'Donnell threw up his only chance of mercy by his rebellions ravings in the dock. The hangman scandal is sure not to end at the point to which it has now reached. Recent experience shows that post is not considered an unenviable one. There would be plenty of oat ndidates, and so there is no excuse if a fit per- son is not chosen. It remains to be seen whether the charges made against Ilium are well founded. But two things at leastare clear from the occurrence of the scandal. One is that the representatives of the Press should always be pre- sent. Their attendance has hitherto depended rather on the caprice of the sheriffs. The other point is that the execu- tioner should have an as.sistant ; this, indeed, for two reasons, either of which is more than adequate. The help is needed. It was a horrible thing to have that wretched :prisoner standing uasupported in an almost fainting c3ndition waiting till the governor should hear the clock strike eight, as if the murderer was to start on his journey to eternity with the punctuality ot an express train. It is. a disagreeable subject to write of, but Calcraft's method of drawing the bolt from below enabled him to shorten the period of torture for the .dying man if the drop he gave him proved insufficient. There was, of 1 course, the terrible interval between the adjustment of the noose and the descent of the executioner te draw back the bolt. But if the hangman has to wait till the governor hears the clock strike eight the sufferings of the patient are the same. But, above all, the advantage of an assistant hang- man would be that the apprentice would be learning his craft. Hanging in these days is an art, and it is necessary that the execution should have a competent, well-trained, and -tested expert to render a ~well paid, but detestable service.

It seems as if we were coming near the beginning of the end of the lighting of London. Certainly we have been a long time getting so far. Still it looks as if at least busi nets was meant. The city is to be portioned off into dis- tricts, and five different companies will be permitted each to take a district, put that little fifth of the city under its own electric blaze and then the authorities will be able to com- pare and to take their notes and to decide. It will be a question of the best light modi- fied and controlled by another question of the cheapest price. All this is most excellent, provided only it leads to anything definite. But we are quite tired of these experiments without results. Piccadilly, Regent- street, the Embankment, and Waterloo Bridge have all afforded trials to gas companies and electric companies, but nothing permanent or general has been done. The lighte of London are as patchy at ever. Vhat is wanted is, that the best illuminant should be carefully chosen, and Then univers- ally adopted. We passed through the disagreeable period of transition with our pavement, but at least it ended in a practical result,

A charming little exhibition of pictures was opened this week at Mr. Agnew's Gallery. It consists of the works of one painter, all of them landscapes, and all from the same locality. Mr. Keeley Halswell is the painter. Years ago, and not so many years ago, either Lis studio was at Rome, his models were the Italian peasant, and his subjects were genre. The results were excellent and uninteresting. Then he went to Venice, and its wonderful climate exercised its accustomed inflaence on the painter, making his . work mere poetical and less stagey. Then he came to England, aban- doned genre and took up landscape. Six years ago he had a great boat house built and launched on the Thames, a floating studio, where he lived during the summer months,' and worked with extraordinary industry. Hence these 60 canvases. All the favourite bits of Thames scenery are here given with the fidelity of open air work. In the painting of what David Cox called weather Mr. Halswell is peculiarly happy, sunset effects, the breeze in the trees, the rushes blown about by a passing wind—these have great charms for him. He is so faithful a painter that the grey- ness which characterizes nearly all these pictures is perhaps explained by the sunless summers of the last six years. It is annouuced on adequate authority that Gung'l the waltz writer and violinist is not dead. The authority is Gung'l himself, who is perhaps most interested in correcting the blunder, the more so because he is almost an annual visitor to London, and is both well known and well liked. Is he is notably one of the ugliest men in existence, no one who has ever seen him can forget him. For years he has been to Berlin and Frankfort what Strauss was to Vienna. He had a small orchestra admirably trained who performed his waltzes at open air evening concerts, the composer him- self takit,g first fiddle. They were always popular, and I think the ugliness of the first violin contributed in no small degree to his power of drawing.

Everyone is surprised, and many people are disappointed, at the news of the Laureate taking a peerage. At first, indeed, it was not believed, and even now it is thought that Mr. Tennyson will think twice, and that second thoughts will be best. Years ago be refused a baronetcy. Only a short time ago he was offered a fortune, if he would take the name of Turner, but he preferred to remain poor and Tennyson. When I say poor, the term of course is rela- tive. It is understood his works used to bring him between three and four thousand a year. If he were now producing " Maud " or "In Memoriam" he would get much more. His political views are certainly no secret. He has suffi- ciently expressed them in his works to indicate the party to which he belongs. Bat he is neither a statesman nor a wealthy man. I have never known an announcement take the public so completely by surprise, less that a peeerage should have been offered than that it should have been accepted.

In theatrical circles the. most important event this week has been the re-opening of the Alhanabra, and it has been in some sense a disappointment. The building is rather distressing, like what it used to be. It is vast, and even when full has an empty kind of look, the voices of the actors sounding spectral and thin. In the old building this was intelligible. It was designed as a kind of palace of art and science, and afterwards was converted into a circus. With such antecedents its conversion into a theatre could not be attended with any very remarkable success. But the new building has certain advantages. If there is no at- tempt to conciliate teathetes, the creature comforts at least are considered. The seats are roomy. You move in and. with ease. The theatre does not get too hot. And you can see the stage from every part of the house. The pro- gramme is practically the old programme. An opera will be put on the boards with some tuneful music and unintelli- gible plot, relieved by ballets of great brilliancy and beauty. The caste includes some old favourites like Taylor and Miss

OFFICER (Dr. Mouritz) presented his monthly report, which statecrthat the number of deaths re- gistered in Runcorn during the past month amounted to 13, representing a death rate of 14 per 1,000 per annum. This was the lowest death rate for the month of November since he became Medical Officer of Health in 1863. Of the above deaths boar were due to bronchitis, four to marasmus, three to senile decay, three to diseases of the nervous system ; croup, diarrhce?„, phthisis, and premature birth account for one each. Thirteen deaths occurred among children five years and under, and of these twelve were below one year.— in answer to Mr. Norman, Mr. BIRVIR said the deaths in the corresponding period last year numbered 36.

A letter was read from the Clerk of the Peace, asking the amount of money received by the Commissioners during the past year from the Government, in respect to the main- tenance of main roads.—On the motion of Mr. NORII&N, seconded by Mr. Dom," it was decided that a reply be sent to the communication to the effect that the Board had no main roads, and had not therefore roctived anything from Government.

div.head: MR. 3. R. FRITIE AND THE FREE LIBRARY.
div.p: MR. 3. R. FRITIE AND THE FREE LIBRARY.

The Cuarustax said he had received the following letter dated November 14, from Mr. J. R. Frith.:—" In reply to yours of yesterday, informing me of my appointment upon the Free Library Committee, I beg to say that whilst it will always be my endeavour to further the interests of the Library, I respectfully decline to accept the appointment."— Dr. STELE, amid expressions of disapproval, gave notice that he would move the appointment of Mr. Rhodes to the vacant seat.—Mr. SHAW thought this an appropriate time to reduce the Free Library Committee to a reasonable size. For the work it had to perform that oommittee was much too large. He gave notice to rescind the resolution appoint- ing the committee.—Dr. STEEL agreed with Mr. Shaw, whom he askod to defer action until the annual nae,eting for the appointment of committees, and in the meantime allow this vacancy to lapse.—Mr. Shaw was understood to agree to this course.

The Cmaramax read a communication he had received from Mr. John Buckley, one of the wardens at Holy Trinity Church, asking if the trustees would be liable to any charges for street making if they purchased and enclosed a piece of waste land on the south side of the church.—Mr. FISHER explained that Sir Gilbert Greenall had offered to sell this land, which was an eyesore to the pastor and congregation, on easy terms, but they desired to know whether they would be liable for any portion of street mak- ing. It was intended to be added to the burial ground.— The LAW CLERK said if the ground was to be used for church purposes pure and simple, the trustees would not be liable. He read a section from the Act of Parliament on the sub- ject.—Mr. LAKE did not think the Board ought to supply six and eight pennyworths to this or that church.—Sub- sequently the Law CLERK Said he would write a copy of the section and hand it to Mr. Fisher. THE OVERSEERS' OFFICES.

The Secretary to the Local Government Board wrote stating that the overseers had applied for their sanction to the hiring of offices from the Improvement Commissioners in Waterloo House. The Board wished to know if the Commissioners intend, d to apply for their sanction.—The Secretary was instructed to make formal application for the Local Government Board's sanction.

div.head: HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTER.
div.p: HIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTER.

The minutes of this committee contained a recommenda- tion that a letter be sent to the General Post Office suggest- ing that the best site for the intended branch post office is between the Derby Arms and the pillar-box at the foot of Waterloo Bridge. The committee had resolved " That the Commissioners in disposing of the late Public Offices to the County Authority did not contemplate that they were also selling the clock, and that it was the inten- tion of the Commissioners to remove it to the Market Hall, or to some other position, but that if the County Authority degired that the clock should remain in its present position, the Commissioners would consider any offer that might be made fol. it."—The Surveyor reported that Mr. Cliff was not performing the cleansing of the streets in a satisfactory manner owing to the want of a mud cart.—The Secretary was instructed to write to him with reference thereto.—The Secretary was instructed to write to the local medical prac- titioners to enquire whether in their opinion the emanations of vapours from the Glycerine Works in Widnes is injurious to the health of any portion of the inhabitants of Runcorn. —After some discossion, not of general interest, the minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. NottatlN, seconded by Mr. BRISCO2.

div.head: FINANCES.
div.p: FINANCES.

The Finlnce Committee reported that the receipts for the past month amounted to £414 155 101, and accounts amounting to £327 55 91 were recommended for payment. The committee recommended that £5O be transferred to the Free Public Library Committee, and that £5O be paid to Mr. Linaker on account of his charges in connection with the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, and that the bill of costs be submitted to the late Ship Canal Committee for examina- tion.—Mr. FISHER moved, and Mr. Noummi seconded the confirmation of the minutes.—Mr. LIGHTBEHN said he had objected to the indecent haste with which the Ship Canal Committee were disposed of before their work was finished, and he individually declined to have anything to do with the bill of costs. It was very much like treating the com- mittee as an old fiddle picked up and played upon at will. It was impossible to refer a recommendation to a non-existent committee, and he objected to do the work.—Mr. LAKE ob- seryed that the cornmitee was non-existent, and they might as well refer the recommendation to a dead man. (Laughter.) —Dr. STEELE said the bill was simply referred to the com- mittee so that they might see to what an enormous expense the town bad been put, and congratulate themselves upon having had the permanent enjoyment of going to London at the ratepayers' expense.—Mr. LIGHTBURti : For which we gave our time and money.—Mr. LAKE moved that that part of the recommendation referring to the Ship Canal Com- mittee be omitted.—The motion was seconded and carried, and the minutes tus passed.

THE CONDUCT or BUSINTSS. The Parliamentary and Legal Committee made the fol- lowing recommendations :—That every committee of the Board shall refer all business involving legal proceedings to this committee ; that the instructions to the LAW Clerk and Inspector of market and lodging houses as to legal pro- ceedinge be rescinded ; that in cases of infringements of the market and lodging house bye-laws, this committee be empowered leith the advice of the Law Clerk to take pro- ceedinge in urgent c ises ; that the Law Clerk be supplied with a copying letter book in which he shall copy all the correspondence conducted by him on behalf of the Board, and deliver a press copy thereof, together with all letters received to the secretary ; and that all books, papers, and documents when finished with, be deposited for safe cus- tody in the Commissioners' offices ; that all bills of costs and charges be referred to this committee; and that the resolution of the Board dated July 11th, 1551, " That all letters addressed 'Clerk ' be forwarded to the Law Clerk " be rescinded.— Mr. Siraw, in moving the adoption of the first three re- commendations, s sill that after-the recent lawsuit in which the Board had been involved, it was felt by the members, as well as the public outside, that there was a want of con- trol over certain business for which the Board was respon- sible. Tie members would remember that during the whole time of that litigation the Board knew nothing of how the case was proceeding from the beginning to the end, except on one or two occasions when they were asked to vote. From the last election it would appear that the ratepayers were dissatisfied with the manner in which the Commis- sioners bad managed their business They might fairly come to the conclusion that they ought to have a committee that should be respensible for the Board's law preceedings, that should confer with the law clerk in every possible way during the progress of any particular business, and that shoukl acquaint the Board from time to time with what was being done. If this cemmittee recommended the Board to go into any useless litigation, they had then some persons that they could charge with having advised the Boaid. He did not believe that a question of litigation, similar to the Beasley case, where so much money was in- volved, ought to be in the hands of any one person. He did not care who he was. He did not think that things of this kind should be commenced and carried out from the beginning to the end without the control of the Board. (Hear, hear.) In the Beasley litigation the Board had spent a considerable sum of money, and there was nothing to see for it. What they desired, he understood, was, as far as possible, to remedy that state of things. Sometimes the Board had disputes with buihders. in the town with reference to the paving and flag- ging with which they were charged, and the Parliamentary and Legal Committee would have control of this, and with the aid of the law clerk might be enabled to make arrange- ments which would prevent litigation or involve any ex- pense. It was to attain these ends that these recommenda- tions were made. Referring to the resolutions with regard to letters, LT., Mr. Shaw slid he did not think the office • the solicitor to the Board was the proper place in which to keep letters and documents referring to the business. There were many important communications passing to and fro with regard to the Comtni.sioners, and the Board had no re- cord of these transactions whatever in their office. This lied been the custom for a very long time before the present law clerk was appointed, so that this state of things did not reflect upon him. He had only been carrying out the cus- ' tam. All these matters of business should be brought to the proper place. The eopointment of this committee and therms recommendations were an endeavour to try to improve per- manently the working position of the Board. Dr. STIELN seconded the motion —Mr. ',Agri 1 linlight it objectionable . that any committee should send business to another com- mitt". He was of °Pinion, however, that the members agreed with the general intention of 'Mr. Shaw that the Board should have control ever legal proceeding:, but he did not see that any of the recommendations now brought for- ward by the Legal Committee would have prevented the re- cent litigation. He could not understand how the Legal Committee would have been better able to advise with ,the likes' clerk then the whole Board—The CLARK observed tnat i the Properties Commi'tee advised with Min, and that corn- ils.l tee's action was confirmed by the Board.—Mr. FISHINE ~ suggested that all the ~,,rt ees should be rolled into the Le-gal and Parliamentary Committee. (Hear, hear, and la.tighter.)—The CDAT EVIAN remarked that the law clerk saw no objection to the recommendations, and lie (the chairman)

did not see that they could do better than pAgg The three recommendations were then passed, Memo. Lake, Lightburn, Fisher, and Taylor voting against.— 1 -- Mr. SHAW then moved the recommendation with regard to documents.—Mr. bOBSON seconded.—The LAW-CIARIC said he objected to the words " t -Tether with all letters re- ceived." For two years he had kept a separate copy of all letters, but he could not be expected to part with the originals until the matter in question had been disposed of. If the Botird would supply him a book be would let them have a copy of all letters.—Mr. SMAW said if the Law. Clerk would suggest any means by which the committee could be kept posted on any matter that was proceeding step by step, then he was sure the committee would be glad to fall in with his suggestion. But if the committee should have a law suit, and 01117 get hold of the papers when they got the bill, then they might as well dispose of the com- mittee. The Board ought to be in the same position as a private individual who had litigation proceedings.—The re- commendation was then passed in the fc4lowing form : That the law-clerk be supplied with a coppying letter book, in which he shall copy all correspondence received or for- warded by him on behalf of the Board, and deliver a press copy thereof to the secretary, and that all books, in.— The other recommendations were then conllrmed without comment.

NOTICE OF MOTION. Dr. STELE gave notice that at the next meeting of the Board he woald move that inasmuch as the Board had de- cided to pave the footpath in Green way-road in front of Mr. Ditchfield's untenanted houses, that in common fairness to the inhabitants of the houses in Moughland's-lane, which were larger ra'epavers than Mr. Ditchfield's future tenants would be, that the Board pave the footpath in Mongbland's- lane as far as Mr. Preston's house."—Mr. P. SPHAIMAN gave notice, staid laughter, that be would move at the next meeting that Waterloo-road ba widened and the foot- path flagged. This concluded the business.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOoL BOARD'.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOoL BOARD'.
The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday. The Rey. Canon Barclay presided, an,t there were present : Messrs. John Simpson, P. Briscoe, T. Norman, J. Pritchard, R. Lea, and F. Rigby (clark).

div.head: ATTENDARCE OF CHILDREN.
div.p: THE ATTENDARCE OF CHILDREN.

The CLERK laid before the Board a quantity of corres- pondence that had passed between the National Union of elementary teachers and the Education D,partment with re- ference to overwork in schools and irregular attendance, The Education Department in their communication observed that irregular attendance could be checked by nothing so effectually as by the co-operation of managers and teachers with the local authorities in the exercise of their compul- sory powers. That co-operation, it added, WAS often wanted. The Clerk (Mr. Rigby) remarked that if the Runeorn School Board had that co-operation, the average attendance and the number on the rolls would be enormously increased. The teachers, he believed, did not visit the parents of absent scholars, and use their influence. 13 fore the new code was introdnced the number of irregulars reported averaged about 150 per month, but there were now reported 15,000 a month. With the help of a man five hours each day it was almost impossible for Bowyer to deal with them.—Mr. NORMAN asked if it would be wise to call the teachers' attention to the matter.—The CLERK said he thought it would be better to wait what the Department had to say further on tie 'lubject.—ln answer to Mn Simpson, the Visrrou said parents whose children made five or six attend- ances were not proceeded against.—Mr. SIMPSON thought the Board ought not to be satisfied with this.—The CLIIRK said if they were to proceed against parents whose children were making six-tenths of theie attendances, it would be a serious matter.—Mr. PEITCLIARD thought it would not be necessary. to prosecute the fifteen hundred. A few special examples would be sufficient.—The CLERK said the magis- trates would not convict the parents in such cases. He pointed out that the average attendance this mouth was 74 per cent.—Mr, SIMPSON: It ought to be more.—The CLERK observed that compared with other places the average attendance of Runcorn was very good.—Mr. SIMPSON said they must not lose sight of the fact that it was simply for the good of the rising generation that the Board compelled children to go to school to be educated. If the children only made five or six attendances in each week, they were not getting properly educated.—Widnes was pointed out as having a better average attendance than Runcorn.—The CLERIC replied that two generous gentlemen had given about £5OO in prizes to the children in that town, and a Council of Education had been formed to carry on the system, which would cost 400 annually. The Widnes School Board had found that neither punishments nor threatenings would get the children to school, and they had to bribe them with prizes. He thought it was an excellent thing indeed.—The discussion then ceased.
VISITOR'S REPORT.

M. BOWYER, the visitor, made the following report "sth December, 1883.—Returns from the Public Elementary Schools for November, 1883: Certified Government accom- modation 2,716, total number on the rolls 2,987, number on the rolls corresponding period of last year 2 898, increase in the number on the rolls 89; total average attendance 2,196.2, average attendance correspondin g period of last year 1,893.6, increase in average:attendance 297.6, per een- tages of attendances .73 5 ; average attendance for the year 1874, 1,252; increase in average attendance as compared with 1874, the year preceding the formation of the Board, 9442; accommodation in excess of average attendance 519 8, number on the rolls in excess of accommodation 271, number attending adventure schools nudbr 9d per week 53. Since the last meeting of the Beard 1 have taken proceed- ings against 10 parents in contravention of the bye-laws. ILI nine cases convictions were granted, and a fine of Sc in- flicted in each Case. Two parents were dealt with under the Canals Boat Act. and two cases where the fathers are seamen I took out a summons against the mother, convic- tions were granted in both cases and A fine of 6s imposed. One case was dismissed with a caution where the Guar- dians are paying the fees, the magistrates feeling disposed to give the parent another trial. At the Attendance Com- mittee meeting, held on the 14th November, 33 cases were summoned before the committee. Five applications were made for half-time and granted, one C 36,3 was adjourned for a fortnight, and in the remaining cases the parents were ordered to see that their children attended regularly in future, 'or proceelings would e tak n against them."
VICTIMISING A RUNCORN TRADESMAN.

At Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. A. Thomas, Michael George Turner was charged with obtain- ing from Arnold Unsworth, clothier and shoe dealer, 40, High-street, Runcorn, a coat, waistcoat, a pair of trousers, a cap, and other articles by false pretences.—On Monday night the prisoner, who was a " baud " on the schooner Philanthropist, went to Mr. Unsworth's shop in company with Captain Pottwood, who ordered a pair of boots for the prisoner, observing that he would be responsible for pay- ment. When the captain left the prisoner told Mr. Unsworth that he had £4 due to him from the vessel, and if he would let him have a few articles he would pay for them when he received the money. Mr. Unsworth permitted him to select different articles (produced), which he wanted to take away, but Mr. Unsworth refused to allow him. Next day Mr. Unsworth took them to the vessel, which WU lying in the Arnold Dock, and as the captain was not present the parcel was placed in the cabin in charge of a lad. On returning from Weston Point, Mr. Unswortb saw the prisoner leaviag the vessel and discovered that the parcel had been removed from the cabin. He went to the railway station where be found the prisoner, who had booked for Liverpool, on the platform. He was bringing him to the police station when the prisoner said " Here, stick to this coat; I just want to speak to that man across the street." Mr. Unsworth released him, and when he had reached the opposite side of the street he ran away in the direction of the cemetery. Information was then given to the police.—Captain Botwood deposed that the prisoner had due to him the sum of Bs. Ed. only, which was paid to him on Tuesday when he was discharged.—J. Craddock, pawn- broker, Church-street, said the prisoner pledged a coat which lie had obtained from Unsworth for five shillings.— Inspector Hollingsworth deposed to apprehending the pri- soner in a lodging house in pverpool.—The prisoner was committed to the Sessions for trial.

LECTURE BY MR. H W. DEACON AT WIDNES. In aid of the funds for the erection of St. Paul's Church, Mr. H. W. Deacon delivered a lecture in Widnes National Schools on Tuesday evening. There was a good audience,. The Rev. J. Wright Williams, the vicar, introduced the lecturer, whose subject was "The structure of insects." The lecture, which was illustiated by sketches thrown upon a screen by a lantern manipulated by Mr. Driffield, was of a very interesting ani instructive character. The sketche were drawn by Mr. Deacon. Amongst the many curious things which Mr. Deacon exhibited on the canvas and ex- plained was the month of the common tea. In a few humourous remarks he described its structure. Woman's tongue, he said, had been called her sword, and in the female flea it really was so, for it was that insects tongue which was the cause of so much discomfort to the rer- sons upon whose bodies the insect chanced to infest. The male insect was unable to inflict any injury.—At the close of the lecture Dr. McLennan proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Deacon for his lucid, instructive, and interesting lecture.--P*. .1. Wriirkt Williams seconded the motion in a few cordial remarks. fie heartily wished that they had in Widnes some plan or power of bringing before the public these wonders of nature, because they =et naturally in- crease their knowledge.-Ihe vote was enthusiastically carried.— reply Mr. Deacon said he should be glad if Inde- sired to deliver a continuation of the lecture in February. (Applause.) He also expressed his willingness to aid any- body who was interested in natural history and were in want of information. He did not profess to be a very learned scientific man, but he was greatly interested in scientific subjects, and it was very likely that he might be of somt2, assistance.

CATS, COLDS, SHIVERING, SNEEZING, AND SNUFF.

Sir,—l do not know whether-- -there is any truth in the Chinese saying that "sitting down in a chair still warm augurs that you will shortly fall out with the list sitter." I only knew that this forenoon I have had to "wake up" the young man who kept my seat " warm " while I was dressing, and also his brother, for interfering with our own cat because it sneezed in the sitting-room, and for rather roughly routing a stray cat from the wash-house. As I have as a penance made them hunt up and ponder over some facts and fancies in connection with cats and sneezing, it has occurred to me that if they wrote them down they might prove interesting to your readers, especially as the Lancet this week has some- thing to say in connection with sneezing, shivering, and colds. I condense their notes, and begin by remarking that though at the present day in some parts ot Bussex the most patted cat is turned at once out of doors, if it sneezes, en the belief that if it was allowed to remain and sneeze three times, every person in the house would have colds or coughs, it is remarkable that in the account of the raising of the Shunamite's son by Elijah, the lad is said to have given his first signs of renewed vitality by sneezing seven times. According to an old Jewish legend, the custom of saying "God bless you !" when a person sneezes, dates from Jacob. The Rabbis say that before Jacob's time, when men sneezed the shockhilled them. In the comedy called" Lingua, or the Combat of the Tongue and the Five Senses for Superiority" (1607), there is an allusion to sneezing as a fortunate portent. Tactus in a soliloquy observes :—" "Pectin, thy sneezing somewhat did portend

liVas evir Erie' n so fort-unate as I? This is considered interesting from a curious tradition respecting Oliver Cromwell, who is said to have played the character of Tactns in his youth, when the comedy was acted by the scholars of the school to which he at the time belonged. Nurses and mothers in Durham, in Germany, ti/c., invoke a blessing on children when they sneeze; while the folk-lores of all nations look upon the in- voluntary act or sensation in the main as a good omen, though some, like ourselves, hold that there are exceptions to the rule. For instance, in Devonshire the saying is "To sneeze on Monday, hastens anger; To sneeze on Friday, give a gift ; Sneeze on Sunday morning fasting, You'll enjoy your own true love to everlasting.' Some lines current in Buckinghamshire run thus :

Sneeee on Monday, sneeze for danger; Sneeze on Inesday, kiss a stranger; Sneeze on Wednesday, get a let'er ; Sneeze on Thursday, something better; Sneeze on Friday, sneeze for sorrow; Saturday, see your true love to-morrow." The Lancet gives some curious and valuable information on the physiological side of the question. In an article on " Colds and chills," after asking the question, "What, then is a cold ?" the writer goes on to remark : "Clearly it is a disturbance of the balance between the several parts of the nervous system, brought about by the shock of a sudden or prolonged exposure to the depressing effect of chill ; ' although the same physiological results may be produced in the organism by the operation of any agent which is capable of giving the nervous system a similar shock, and thus creating the same kind of disturbance. Nature's provisions against the consequence of a chill 'and for the prevention of a 'cold' are sneezing and shivering. A violent fit of sneezing often saves a chilled body the conse- quences of the nerve depression, or shock,' to which it has been subjected; and this shock may in its first impression be very limited in its area: for example, the small extent covered by a draught of cold air rushing through the crevice of a door or windoW• The nerve centres are aroused from their °Haim' by tht Commodori o eiplosive Influence of the I sueete. If sneezing fails, nature will try a shiver, which acts mechanically in the same way. If this fails, the effects are likely to be very serious, and bad consequences may en- sue. The popular notion reverses the order of events, and hence the saying, 'lf there is sneezing the cold will be slight, if there is shivering it will be grave;' whereas it is slight when sneezing suffices to recover the nervous system quickly from its depression, and grave when even strong shivering fails to do so. In case of chill, with threatened cold, sneezing may be produced by a pinch of snuff of any kind. This is how some of the vauated 'cures' of cold by snuff are brought about. Or brisk exercise may ward off the attack. The popular idea is that the circulation is restored by these remedies, but the true explanation is that the nervous system and centres are aroused. The first step towards an intelligent treatment of chill and cold is a scientific recognition of their nature." I hope the medical writer's remarks will not make snuff- takers saucy. lam in receipt of a Lancashire paper with an advertisement marked, and which runs as follows "Wanted, to bay a hurdy-gurdy and a bagpipe. More for ornament than use." If the " want "is felt or craved for by one of the " peculiars," Newtonian asstheticism has indeed reached a unique phase, if it can see anything ornamental in bagpipes or hurdy-gurdies. —I remain, sir, dze. AN G LO - SCOUTS.
