Sir,—My perusal of Mr. Caurenson's letter on the above important subject has done little towards making a pro- tectionist of me. I put before him a plain question, based upon the arguments he had himself previously used; this question ke has thought fit to term a "Corkscrew, or twisted one," for why? Simply because I used the word "foreign" instead of "home." Now, I put it to any sane man, Is not the foreign trade of vastly more importance than the home trade? Why Mr. Laurenson should object to my introducing local firms and individuals I cannot make out e - , am that wrie l pinches, there we are 'likely: A r-es ti.e shoe to be most in earnest to find a remedy. Mr. Lanrenson has a great desire to pose, as a national benefactor repudiates curiosity, but "respectfully declines te Inswer any letters that may be written for a private motive." Sir, if Mr. L. is in earnest he will answer my question in half a dozen lines. It is one of those answers, that if bright and telling may work a revolution in the country, there is no necessity to wriggle through it, corkscrew fashion or otherwise. Mr. L. knows as well as myself, that every social question of the day is so inter- woven with party polities tnat it is mere folly to attempt to deal with them outside the political arena. This is why I state that as a Radical politician I wish to get at the truth. "Fair Trade" had its birth in the tail end of a political party, it was adopted by them as a war cry, and had it been taken up by the heads it would to-day have been doing duty in the hope of leading that party back to power. But it was repudiated as a fallacy so transparent, that even serious discussion could not be prolonged in a House of Commons, mainly composed of manufacturers. Mr. L. displays to our view a quantity of truisms, well, we all accept these at their true value, well knowing that truisms, like figures, may be made to prove anything. Brushing Fair Trade out of the way, there still remains the vital question, How are the trade in- terests of England to be advanced? This, I contend may be dealt with in a pactical fashion; mere theorising is not required. I have had occasion just recently to say a few words upon this question, and it seems to me, Mr. Editor, that the more space the press gives to the elucidation of this problem the sooner we may arrive at the truth. A correspondent in one of your contemporaries refers to the dead weights that British mangfacturers have to contend against, and I am of opinion that herein lies the whole se- cret. Men Who income is derived from trade have so many calls upon them that to meet these a high per centage has to be derived trove their invested capital. £5,000,000 is yearly absorbed by a 'National Church for which we receive not one tittle in return, millions more are wasted upon a Nonconformist ministry, no two individuals of which agree as to the truth of their teachiogs. Instead of these men wasting their time cracking theological nuts they were to turn their undoubted talents to mundane affairs we should then have an immense sum of money at the nation's disposal, and fewer drones to keep. Another dead weight is the land. From this, according to the most reliable authority, sufficient could be pfbduced to satisfy the wants of the people. Instead of this we have the land lying comparatively idle, and our gold goes to maintain foreign countries instead of supporting a rural population. And this is not all. This population flocks into the town, making the keenness of town life in a thou- sand different ways more difficult and sharp for those who hare to meet it. One of the dead weights that is hanging round the necks of all, employer and employed alike, is our present selfish railway system, and as upon this question I have also the Ship Canal in view, I hope you will ungrudg- ingly allow me to occupy a little more of your space. 'Manchester entered into the Ship Canal question with a steady determination to carry it through if possible. As the centre of the Lancashire staple trade her mer- chants felt that it was a question of life and death. Outlying towns have been guided in their actions by various motives, good, bad, and indifferent, at Warrington lying midway between the two great cities, Manchester and Liverpool, has almost stood idly by. Jealous lest the canal should be taken a few hundred yards away from Market Gate, she maintains a stolid indifference, leaving one, or at most two, of her

townsmen to look after her rights. Trade unions, with one exception—the Wire Drawers Society—have refused to make a grant out of their monies, excusing themselves by saying that "As the manufacturers weuld reap all the profits, they 1 should run all the risks." This is not so. Where the ono I receives a benefit the other must also be benefited, and the same with the reverse, At a ship canal meeting, held in Manchester, Mr. J. C. Fielden, speaking as one intimately connected with the cotton trade, said: "Cheapness in pro- duction was one of the essential features of commercial success. The canal was one means of doing this. The re- duction in wages now threatened in the cotton trade was the third within the last five years. The saving in the transit charges upon the cotton trade by the construction of the canal would be more than the entire reduction of wages now proposed." This statement put forward by a large and responsible em- ployer should not fail to make a great and powerful impres- sion on workingmen. It amounts to this: that employers not having sufficient strength to force a reduction in transit charges turn to the weakest point, the employe. The Radi- cals have for years been urging that the railways should be managed by and for the nation's good. To this it will come eventually. In the meantime let us make use of our water- way, and now that the necessary papers are deposited, let us have a town's meeting with the member in the chair, so that the fresh effort may be launched amidst cheering prospects. I understand that a wet blanket enshrouds the Wilderspool district, and-that while the people are with us in spirit they mast keep their bodies away from our meetings, or else their temporal welfare will suffer. Well, it is not so in Warrington. Here we are at liberty to speak out, knowing full well that a railway dividend does not mean altogether big wages. One more feature on the trade outlook, and then I have done. In the splendid past that England has enjoyed, our firma have made themselves a reputation world-wide, and depending upon this are failing in that per- sonal attendance se requisite with customers now-a-gays. Writing about the trade of Constantinople and Turkish commerce generally, Consul Wrench says that the products of the Continent are gradually edging those of England out ef the market. In cotton yarns, grey goods, and prints Manchester still retains the bulk of the trade, but Switzer- land and Italy now supply Turkey red yarns to the exclu- sion of England, while French and Austrian cotton print goods are gradually working their way into the market. Belgium and Germany push their woollens with success against Yorkshire fabric; and in the items of hardware. cutlery, and small wares, Germany, Austria, and Italy have pretty well superseded Birmingham and Sheffield. Two causes have brought about this result. One is that in this market cheapness is the first and quality the second desideratum. The other is that continental manu- facturers taka much more pains to learn the market than British manufacturers care to bestow. German, Belgian, and Austrian manufacturers have always travellers on foot study- ing the market, and they adapt their manufactures to its fashion and caprices. An English traveller is never seen at Constantinople now. The British manufacturer neither canvasses the market nor makes any effort to suit it. If the market will take what he has to offer and come to him for it, well and good, but he is not at pains to woo its custom, as the manufacturers of the Continent are. Consequently, little by little the import trade of Constantinople is being led away from England. Now, sir, this is not mere theoris- ing, but good practical work, that if attended to will entirely banish fair trade notions, and make the future of ourselves and children brighter than it otherwise would be. December 3rd, 1883. H. WHITHAM.
THE TRADE INTERESTS OF ENGLAND.

Sir,—Mr. S. Lawrenson is evidently inviting diseussion on the above subject. With this object in view he first launched his theories on the London evening press, where he seems to have been unsuccessful, and now has recourse to your own excellent medium, in which he vents his dis- appointment by telling us that "There appears a desire in certain directions to avoid the Free Trade question." What- ever truth there may be in that assertion with regard to the direction of London, I think he will have no cause to com- plain of his own locality. Already, I see Mr. Whitham has responded to his apparent invitation, in a certain direc- tion, and it is not by aay means with a view to presuming to assist that gentleman that I myself appear on the scene, for I doubt not he be able to give a good account of himself to Mr. Lawrenson ere the discussion closes. There- fore, I leave him to pursue his own course; but in Mr. Lawrenson's letter which appeared in the same issue with Mr. Whitham's, there is an amount of misconception and plausibility which is thoroughly delusive, and which, whilst giving Mr. Lawrenson the fullest credit for sincerity, I be- lieve will delude no one more than himself. He appears to fall into the error, common with men of his school, of sup- posing that in substituting a Free Trade for a Protective policy, we were only actuated by a desire to confer a favour on our commercial neighbours all the world over, and as they have Rot reciprocated, by following in the same steps, they are thereby placing us in an unfair commercial posi- tion; that in consequence of this our irnporel are vastly in excess of our exports, causing our trade to languish by paying for this excess out of our accumulated capital, and thereby driving thousands of our fellow-countrymen to emigrate, thousands more into crime, and thousands more into pauperism. Now, sir, if all this be true, I agZki with Mr. Lawrenson that our workingmen will, in the near future, demand an enquiry into this. policy, and if these truths are established pretty speemii 11c1 rightly, make an alteration in the laws affecting our foreign 1 coninieree, but not till then. Now, I propose to Make this enquiry myself, so far as available information (not in any sense meagre),and the limited compass of this letter will allow. Mr. Lawrenson is either totally ignorant of the his- tory of this country daring the present century, or he wil- fully ignores the facts. Otherwise it is well-known to him that the one great contention of the advocates of Free Trade, previous to its adoption by us, was, that it was essential to the preservation of the people, and our existence as a commercial community, and that it was the irrefutable reasoning in support of that contention, together with the famishing condition of the people, which led ultimately to the triumph of those principles. But Mr. Lawrenson would have us to believe it was all a mistake. To test this, I will take the condition of our trade, and the people before and after the adoption of Free Trade. From 1815 to 1845, there had been very little development in the trade of the United Kingdom. In 1816, the export trade stood at £51,000,000; in 1841 it stood at about the same amount. Taking the total value of trade for 1840, we have, in round numbers, 172,000,000, or £3 las per head of population; in 1860, £375,000,000, or £l3 per head of population; in 1870, £547,000,000, or £l7 103 per head of population: in 1882, £720,000,000, or £2O lie per head of population. Mr. Lawrenson says," whilst poverty lasts, crime will never cease." A statement having more truth in it then is good for his position. I have no means of ascertaining the number of paupers previous to 1849. But the condition of the people previous to the repeal of the corn laws was wretched in the extreme, as well it might be, when we remember that the prices of the 41b. loaf for ten consecutive years were as follows: Is id, is lid, Is 3p, 100, is 4P, is Id, is sid. is 6P, is 2d, is 2d, and in one year it rose to is 10p, the average price was is 2P. Hundreds of thousands of people were unable to ter.v wheaten bread, and were compelled to exist on potatoes. It is said that 21!009 "-isons In Leeds bnly earned on the apftigt)llld per week. In Paisley 'nearly the whole popula- tion was starving. In Glasgow 12,000 persons were on the relief fund, and such was the misery in Bolton, that it was compared to a city ire te state of seige. The prisons of the country were litetalily crammed. The number of persons committed were, in 1840, 54,892, to a population of 26,487,026; 1849, 74,162, to a population of 27,669,579; 1859, 26,011, to a population of 28,590,224; 1869, 26,979, to a population of 30,913,513; 1881, 22,541, to a population of 34,929,679. The above figures speak for themselves, and I will leave your readers to judge whether a return to protection is desirable or not. Mr. Lawrenson speaks as if pauperism is on the increase. In 1849 the total number of paupers in England and Wales amounted to 934 419, popula- tion 17,564,656. In 1882 the total number was 797,614, population 26,406,820, showing an increase in population of 8,842,164, and a decrease in pauperism of 136,805. I now come to imports and exports, the excess of one of which Mr. Lawrenson says we are paying for out of our accumulated capital, and in support of his assertion he is very fond of taking individual cases, I will follow his example. It has been explained again and again that the excess of imports over exports represents the amount of profit on goods sold, cost of freightage in Eng- lish bottoms, and interest on capital in foreign loans and investments. Time And space won't permit me to explain by the laws of political economy how this is, but I will give a short quotation from Mr. J. S. Mill, who says :—" All in- terchange is in substance and effect, barter: he who sells his productions for money, and with that money buys other goods, really buys those goods with his own produce. And so of nations, their trade is a mere exchange of ex- ports for imports." Suppose a man in Warrington manu- factures £lOO worth of goods here, and then, being his own carrier, takes them up to London to sell, he would pos- sibly get £llO for them there. But in order to make his carrying power on his return journey productive he bays £llO worth of London goods, and suppose he also has some investments there, and draws the interest on then, with which he buys other goods to the amount of £5O, leaving him £25 in cash, and with these goods and cash he returns to Warrington. His goods on arriving here would possibly be worth £176, which, in addition to his £25 in cash, would make £2Ol, so that he returns with over 100 per cent. more in value than he took out. Would that man be considered to have been engaged in a losing transaction? I trow not. And yet this is analogous to us as a trading nation. I will take the imports and exports in merchan- Size, and tirtiiren, and specie separately for the 'ye years, from 1875 to 1879 inclusive. which

I were - about as bad as any we have h3d. From 1875 to 1879 we imported merchandize to the valla of £1,875,276,579, and exported during the same time £1,285,003.167, showing of X 590,273,412. sow, excess of imports over exports w, according to Mr. Lawrenson's rea- soning, we ought AS a nation to show a considerable re- do auict i for oi n o t ourof wealth, inasmuch as that excess has been d accumulated capital. But what do we find ? Taking the gross annual value of property, Sze., assessed under all schedules of the income tax for those years, we find an increase in value of nearly £35,090,000. If we turn to the savings banks we find an increase of 1.81. mil- mions. If we turn to the quantity of various kinds of food and drink consumed, such as tea, coffee, sugar, eggs, butter. bacon, dzc., we should there find a considerable increase per head of population. These figures themselves ought to be sufficient to refute the assertion of Mr. Lawrenson. But if more is needed we will look at the returns for bullion and specie, and if what Mr. Lawreuson says is true we

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER, 8, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER, 8, 1883.

ought certainly to have sent out more money than we !ROBBIG PETER TO have received. If we find that is not so, then, I think, the N last prop of his argument is struck away, and the whole structure tumbles to the earth. During the five years PA.Y PA_UL. above alluded to we imported bullion and specie to the amount of £164,050,420, and exported to the value of £119,776,634, leaving a balance of imports over exports to the amount of £44,273,786. Perhaps Mr. Lawrenson will acknowledge the balance on the right side in this case. But whether he does so or not, I think I have now given suffi- cient proof so far as the reasonable limits of a letter will allow, that on the whole we are far from being in the sorry plight , which he would have us believe, that so far from losing ground we are still steadily 'gaining, per- haps not qaite so fast as in the past, nor is it good for the nation on the whole that we should; for I believe that the condition which Mr. Lawrenson so bitterly bewails, is due in a great measure to the inflation of ten years ago. Time will not permit me to take up the other points of his letter, but I will just say this : He harps mainly on the de- pression of a few manufactures. Well, no doubt some are depressed, but would he have Government to make the whole country suffer for the interests of a few ? If he would he is leading a forlorn hope. It is the functien of a Government to legislate for the benefit of the nation as a whole and not the interests of a few, and where a nation is importing food and raw material to the extent of 90 per cent. on the total imports, leaving only a bare 10 per cent. of manufactured goods, and exporting manufactured goods to the extent of 80 per cent. of the total, there is not much of a margin left for the protection of manufactures. He would, therefore, be wise in recognising the hopelessness of help coming from that direction, and look more to meeting this foreign competition by improvements and increased facilities of manufacture, rather than by calling helplessly on the Government for the succour it has not the power to give.—Yours, A. RATHBONE. 7, Arpley-street, Warrington, Dec., 1883.
BY JOHN SAUNDERS, Author of "HIRELL ; OR, LOVE BORN OF STRIFE," " ABEL DRAKE'S WIFE," "ISRAEL MORT, OVERMAN," &C., &C.

CHAPTER LL—Tien CORPORAL IN THE BALL-ROOM ANTS-CHAMBER. To seek the Major in the interior of the house, Stephen could not belt) thinking, was to incur the risk of meeting his own relatives, an event that he desired of all things to avoid. It had been arranged that Stephen in his communica- tions with the Major, if he had occasion to make any, should use the same door as that used by the soldiers on their return. Thither ha went, and after finding his own way into a long corridor, he saw a livery servant at the other end, and called to him. But the man was either too busy to attend to a common soldier, or too excited by the presence of the guests, the music, and the dance, by the flow of wines in which pos- sibly he man tged to share, or by the news, which began to get hnown, of the possibility of a Fenian attack, together making a veritable sensation. At all events he only stopped for a moment to see who it was called, and then hurried away. Guided by the hum of many voices, and thinking as he threaded the intricacies of the place in search, how easily a few Fenians, did they know, might follow his example, and then let in their whole body suddenly upon soldiers, hosts, and guests alike; Stephen at last came to a large servants' hall, where many of the soldiers were posted, sitting on chairs, on forms, or on the floor—but all having their arms in their hands, or by their side. There he found Sergeant Grabbe, told him briefly what had happened, and asked him to find the Major, and say where he was waiting orders; adding with some cmbarass- ment, as if conscious he was a little disingenuous, "I don't want to go any further, in ease of anything hap- pening to the men I left in charge that necessitates my im- mediate return!" " All right, Shand," said the Sergeant, whose speech was a little thick, as if he had not very strictly enforced in his own case the rule of temperance he had most carefully en- joined on his men. So he went to an 'ante-room adjoining the ball-room, where he found servants in waiting, and sent one of them to say Major Etheredge was wanted outside. The opening of the door for the servant's entrance caused a flood of dance music to stream through, and so was heard by Stephen faintly in the servants' hall. Again rose the desire to get a glimpse of Miss Vandeleur, if but a single one; and he regretted now that he had not himself demanded to see the Major, who was not unlikely to be annoyed at his not doing so, seeing how special had been the mission entrusted to him. The reality of that desire and of that regret were at once put to the test, for the Sergeant presently returned, the jolly face with which he had gone having changed in the inte- rim to a stormy one. "He says why don't you go to him yourself, and that he isn't at all understand what I told him. But that's your fault, not mine." "No doubt, Sergeant—and lam sorry I was not clearer in my report." "Anyhow, he waits you in the ante-room." "How shall I find my way ?" "Any fool can tell you that ;"and the Sergeant went to his meat, and to his unfinished glass of toddy. Stephen could not make general proclamation among his comrades, for the one individual fool who would do what he wanted, so he set off in the direction he had seen the Sergeant go, and then guided by the music, reached the place. Major Etheredge was on the watch, evidently impatient for his coming; and after giving him a slight reproof for not hastening directly thither, told Shand to tell him exactly what had happened. He listened with the deepest interest; and well he might do so. For he had already heard a rumour that there was a large body of armed Fenians collected at a pat ticular spot sheltered from general observation, who had been marching with great rapidity, had then unexpectedly paused, and were still pausing, as though waiting foe some special imforma- tion ; or, as some vague remarks that had been overheard in the darkness by a scout seemed to imply, as though their leader had not yet arrived, OT had left them some important purpose, and not yet rejoined. "Is it possible, Major, this is the man ? ". asked Stephen. "I do believe it is! If so, it is a-haul of the first. impor- tance. Wait till I call Lord Ilarlaxton." " He was going when interrupted by Stephen's sudden call— " Major, I beg you pardon." Here he paused in the search for fitting thoughts and words • and the Major could not but notice how his face had coloured. "You were so kind—l think—as to say to me on one occasion that —that—" "That I would gladly be of service to you if I could. I did so. Has the occasion come? " His penetrating glance in Stephen's face as he said this was so full of conscious- ness that he might be on the eve of some discovery about Stephen's family, that the latter course became only the more difficult, and he could but say, "If Major you would kindly excuse me—l--" *Tou know Lord iiariaiton "He knows me." " Ah, I understand. It's awkward, perhaps impossible to avoid a meeting. He is the magistrate who will have to examine these tnen—or rather the one man who alone seems to be importaat—and you are the one indispensable wit- ness." "Very well, Major. I cannot presume to ask that I should be an obstacle to justice, or to the performance of duty."
THE CONSERVATIVE MEETING: MR. ATKINS

"But let me see," thoughtfully remarked the Major. "The whole business is yet in the vague, and concerns the military rather than the civil authorities. I am not sure indeed whether it would not be better for me 'alone to deal with this man at present. Keep him under our charge till we return to camp, pump him, and see if he will respond, and finally hand him over with all the information we can collect to the proper authorities for his examination and trial, should the evidence ba sufficiently complete. You can greatly help in that matter." "Perhaps I ought to tell you, Major, that I have seen and conversed with that man before and that but for a partial recollection of his voice I am afraid I should have let him

" You did not tell me that before," said the Major, sharply. "No, Major, because I desired not to confuse my general report with anything not necessary at the moment. But I intended to ask your permission at the first oppor- tunity," "All right. But the opportunity must be now. Sit down." Stephen, still keeping his weapon, which looked strangely out of place, within the circle of his arms, sat down and narrated most faithfully the substance of the whole conver- sation in the train, not concealing his own sympathy with the man, while hostile to his cause, "lie must have been trying to deceive you in order to dis- cover if you were either friend or foe." "Pardon me, I think not, Major. I fancy there is a pas- sage in the Bible which gives the explanation roughly but naturally—the dog going tack to his vomit." "Exactly. You think he did intend to quit the Fenian cause—but the old Adam in him was the conqueror—and so he is here, our prisoner. Go for him and the others, and I will myt,elf examine them—somewhere where we can be private. Stay! Wait till I have spoken to Lord Harlaxton and I will go with you to find a place so that you can come there without fuss or inquiry, We must keep all as quiet ,as possible. Lord Harlaxton and I had a subdued laugh together a few minutes ago between the dances as we made mutual acknowledgments what hypocrites we were, seeing to have no other thought and wish than to bask in the smiles of the ladies, while really thinking and anxious about possible business of so opposite a character. "As to Lord Harlaxton, if I do not quiet him with regard to your story he will certainly be, seeking us both to hear more, for I said a few words to him oft receiving the Ser- geant's not very perspicuous report." And so saying he passed into the ballroom, leaving the door half open as it happened, so that Stephen could not only see a large part of the room but also many of those whc occupied it. Some were promenading, and passing on their way so near that Stephen could hear their voices, and distinguish their faces. Should he now sea Mies Vandeleur ? - Strange as it may sound, her's was the first voice that he next heard ; and while it thrilled it also jarred, for she was engaged in what seemed to his possibly exaggerating fancy, an animated conversation it ith a handsome young fellow, and laughing in answer to some of his remarks, which Stephen thought were made in an insidiously low and fervid tone. As he sat, with the light behind him, and therefore with his face in partial shade, he ventured to stare boldly right before him, but making no movement, • looking as a mere solelier might be expected to look when a scene so brilliant and so novel was passing before his eyes. In that position he was when she again passed, and in that position he sat im,novable, as she looked, saw the young soldier there and directed her companion's attention also to him, and the result was that she herself was to him in the moment when they looked at each other little more than a shadow seen in a dream, through the emotion he felt at the fear she might be recognising him, and then what would she say or do ? But the pair passed on, and he saw no more of them. For the Major came out and they went away together.
ing, which had been hastily supplemented by a pair of silver candlesticks and wax candles, placed upon a plain round deal table.

A fire had been lighted on account of the extreme coldness of the night, bat was burning badly and smoking, yet every now and then it puffed forth a jet of flame which cast a sudden radiance on the nearest forms and faces, and died out again as sudden.

The one small window revealed only the intense darkness of the night, but gave a new trial to the feelings of those inside, by the frequent sound of dull heavy raps on the glass, due to some branch which the wind shook, as if to accentu- ate something which particularly interested it, in weird fashion, and to urge more rapid progress. The Major was seated at the head of the table, and at the other end stood the driver and the two pig-jobbers, all looking chilly, careworn, and anxious, and carefully keep- ing aloof from the Three Days' Fenian. He, on his part, stood with folded arms, his tall, slender, sinewy figure, loftily surveying by turns now his late com- panions, now the Major and Stephen (who stood near his commanding officer), but as if the proceedings might con- cern anyone rather than him.

The driver was first examined, ind repeated the evidence he had given Stephen; but with the rather serious addition that the man whom they had taken up in the car had joined them scarcely a hundred yards away from the spot where Stephen had arrested their course; and, therefore, was doubtless the man who had been hovering for some un- known purpose about the sentries, and the man whom Stephen had followed. _ _
That fact was confirmed by the two pig-jobbers, who, anxious to clear themselves at the earliest possible moment. stated that they were both well known to the driver, and called on him to speak. , .

" And I, your honour," called out the driver, with sudden animation," am well known to one of the servants of this very mansion—Phil Joyce by name, a cousin of my wife's cousin—who can speak to my character for many a year, and that I've never had dealings of any kind with the I.'`enians—if that is what I am suspected of." Phil Joyce was sent for, and so thoroughly confirmed the driver's statement that the Major was satisfied the driver and the pig-jobbers were innocent, and therefore valuable witnesses against the man they had taken up into the car at his request, simply, as he said, to give him a lift, but more probably because seeing his danger from the un- known person who had so persistently followed him through the wood, he thought thus to battle his pursuers, and pass with them if there were soldiers about likely to stop passers by.

The three men then te3tifled to their entire ignorance about that man; and their names and addresses haviag been taken down, and warned they might be called on as wit- nesses, they were told they might go. "But my horse is killed, your honour! I'll be a ruined man if I don't get another at once."

"Ah, well, that mast be seen to. I daresay that will be set right for you by and bye." " Ah, but your honour how am I to take these gentlemen to their homes—they have ten miles to go. And then I have to get back fifteen miles."
_ "Oh,'7 said one of the pig jThbers, "your honour can easily settle that for him and us too." "Ah : How ?" "Just lend us one of your trooper's horses for the night." _
7fhe Major laughed right out before he could answer.
"There are two difficulties in the way, my friend. I have no spare cavalry, so cannot oblige you if I would; and I would not if I could, so you must manage as well as you can."
"I wish you all a good night and a pleasant walk home if that be possible."
_ The driver was about to remonstrate, but Stephen gently forced him out of the room, the pig-jobbers following in silence but full of discontent that the Major would not lend them one of his horses.
faces; and at length the former, grasping Stephen'shhand, ejaculated,

"I know what you must mean, and was thinking it must be so—while the Major was examining my companions, and I took careful measure of you." "Then I need say no more, but that it is likely I may be found in quite a different position within the next four or five years, so—"

"If I do seek the assistance of anyone it shall ba you." " I will leave an address with your counsel before I leave Ireland—if Ido leave it—that will be sufficient for your purpose. Farewell!" Again they grasped hands, and the Fenian seemed so unwilling to let go' that Stephen fancied something had been unsaid which the prisoner wanted to say. "Is there anything more that —" he asked, leaving the sentence_ unfinished.

" Well, I have been in many minds about it, but I think you should know. I could have shot you down from the car. I saw the precise moment—and was tempted." " But resisted, if I am any judge," said Stephen, with a smile. "I knew you, and could not do it. That's all, Good- bye."
With moisture in the eyes of both they Eeparated, to meet in all probability no more, (To be continued.)

When they were gone, the real business of the meeting began: the Three Days' Fenian and the Major alike pre- pared, as was shown by the looks they exchanged. "What is your name ?" "I decline to answer." "Where were you coming from and where bound to when arrested ?" "I decline to answer." "Upon what business were you engaged ?" "My own business." "Of what nature ?" "That concerns myself alone." "I am afraid I shall have to convince you it also con- cerns me. Observe now. You are found at midnight with two pig jobbers; you declare yourself one, yet you are quite unknown to the companions who have taken you up as a matter of kindness; a revolver fully loaded is found on you; nad when you perceive the Corporal here grow suspicious and likely to arrest you, you seize the driver's whip, you lash the horse cruelly, and would probably have escaped but that the horse was instantly shot. Under these remarkable circumstances you decline to tell your name, your business, or to give yourself any chance of escape from being treated as one engaged unlawfully, perhaps criminally. I invite you, therefore, to reconsider the matter, and satisfy me, for your own sake, if you can." There was in the tone of the Major's voice, as well as in his words,something that did produce a momentary hesitation and give time to reconsider. But it rapidly passed away as he said, recovering his defiant attitude, "I have nothing more to say." "And you have no witnessea that you can produce, now or at a later period, who can prove that you are a loyal subject of the Queen; and so allow me to take it for granted that the suspicious circumstances of the night are essen- tially of a private and individual nature, about which I need not further concern myself ? " Again the Three Days' Fenian paused a few seconds to reflect, perhaps thinking that such evidence might be obtained somehow; but if so the idea was ,Deedilv rejected, as tending only to bring friends into the danger in which he was. "No. In brief I decline to acknowledge that there has been anything in my behaviour to justify my arrest. And when I am set free, as I must be, I shall make it my busi- ness to seek redress for whatever injuria I may have suffered in my business or person." "That is enough. I shall not at present hand you over
to the civil power—. I must know more about you first, and the information you decline to give I must seek elsewhere. You will, therefore, be taken back with us

to the camp as a prisoner when we go; and mean- time no one will be permitted to see, speak, or comirunic tte with you in any way except through the Corporal who ar- rested you." The Three Days' Fenian looked at Stephen, and Stephen at him, neither able to say whether he was pleased or sorry at being thrown into a renewal of acquaintance under such painful circumstances. The prisoner was then removed under a strong guard to an underground but airy cellar, and sentinels placed over him, one inside the cellar door, and one outside the cellar window, while others were on guard near in case the ex- pected Fenian attack should be first directed in search of him, as the Major strongly suspected would be the case; for he was more and more inclined to think the bold fellow was the real leader of the proposed attack, and had in the un- certainty about the presence of the soldiers at Gaultmore determined to discover at his own risk the true state of the case, before leading his men into what might prove to be a trap for their destruction. "Ala," thought the kindly Major as he thus speculated on the motives of the man, "how sad it is such qualities cannot be used to bind up the wounds of this unhappy country, instead of as at present, for ever widening them, and making them rankle by dwelling on a past, which no true Englishman wishes to perpetuate." The Major went back less disposed than ever to the enjoy- ments of the song and the dance, but feeling it a duty to aid Lord Harlaxton in keeping up the confidence of his relatives and friends in their security • while maintaining the position first assumed for the benefit of the Fenian scouts or spies if any such were near, if that security was still to be menaced. Stephen and the sentries had once more resumed their duties outside; and so once more the former had moments of eager curiosity and anxioas suspense in passing the win- dow of the ballroom; yearning, while annoyed at his own behaviour, to see her again. The loyal scJuts, horse and foot, now began to bring in news that it was true there had been a great assemblage of armed men, but they had dissolved, had been seen dispersing, and followed to make sure the fact was so. And with it came (though on more doubtful evidence) the explanation that the Head Centre, their commander, who had been seen by the scouts on a white pony, was taken prisoner. And, to anticipate the end of this episode in Stephen's career, subsequent discoveries confirmed these reports. Little by little evidence was collected that proved beyond doubt the Three Days' Fenian was an honoured as he was un- doubtedly an able Fenian leader. He was after some weeks' delay accordingly put on his trial. Stephen was necessarily an important witness. But when questioned beforehand by the prosecutor as to his con- versation with the prisoner in the Holyhead train, he posi- tively refused to say one word on the subject. "It was mere gossip in mutual confidence," so he des- cribed it, and only mentioned to the Major to invoke sympathy if that were at all admissable for the prisoner, not to injure him. And in spite of threats and prospective rewards, it was found impossible to move him. The Major was then ap- pealed to, but declined to interfere. The trial proceeded. But it was soon seen the prisoner had no chance of escape. He was found guilty of treason, and sentenced to twenty years' penal servitude. His last act before disappearing into the awful obscurity of the life to which he was condemned was to send for Stephen to thank him for his reticence—and for all he had individually done apart from the arrest—which he acknow- ledged to be a duty—from Stephen's own point of sight. And Stephen was moved to reply, "If circumstances should leave the intervention of a friend possible as time passes, and the country settles down—" "It will never settle down while things-are as they are ! " passionately broke in the Fenian. God forbid that they should, or that I should wish it for ray own selfish sake." "Well, but if they do," persisted Stephen, with a gentle smile. "Strange things happen, and should this hanpen, , I and I be able to assist,"—there ho paused, co rsidering what ; next he should say, feeling he had gone too far and not to go farther. The Three Days' Fenian and he looked in each other's

div.head: AND THE ILBERT BILL
div.p: AND THE ILBERT BILL

Sir,—Will you kindly allow me to say a few words res- pecting the proceedings at the late Conservative meeting. I attended the meeting with the intention of asking the chair- man a question. I understand Sir Gilbert is the selected Conservative candidate who will be put forward at the next election in Warrington, and I wished to know whether he I was in favour, or not, of a committee of enquiry into the free trade policy of the country. When the Chairman an- nounced that Mr. Atkins was going to address the meeting and would also take a vote upon the Ilbert Bill, I was simply thunderstruck. Here was a man sent to this coun- try by his fellow workmen of India, for the purpose of explaining how the Bill, if passed, would injure European residents in India, appealing to political party feeling for a vote upon the question. It became clear at once to me that this was a dishonest course to take, and I determined to ask him two questions :—First, "Were his constituents in India aware that he, Mr. Atkins, was resting satisfied with a vote gained at a Conservative political party meeting ? " and next, "Did he not think that it would be better to lay his statement respecting the bill before a public meeting irrespective of political parties?" Now, sir, I was convinced that this was the only course Mr. Atkins could take, and I appealed to the chairman in a reasonable and respectful manner, when immediately an uproar commenced, and the Conserva- tive portion of the meeting were successful in destroying a time-honeured custom, viz., that of putting questions to the speakers at a political meeting. Mr. Atkins appealed to the prejudices of his audience, herslandered the subjects of the Empress of India, and he did not say half a dozen words respecting the Ilbert Bill. I ask you, sir, by printing these questions to enable me by this means to approach Mr. Atkins in a public and Liberal manner, in spite of the few Conservatives who bellowed at the meeting. Warrington, December, 1883. H. WHITHAM.

div.head: TREAT TO OLD PEOPLE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: TREAT TO OLD PEOPLE AT RUNCORN.

Sir,—l do not know whether anything is being done with regard to the treat to old people at Runcorn this year. I therefore beg to make a few suggestions on the subject. Instead of its being a treat for old people, irrespective of class or position, it should be definitely understood to be a treat for the aged poor only. Nothing should induce the committee, however high the fever of philanthropy may carry them, to commit the blunder of a free breakfast for children again. If two hundred old people can be provided with a good " square " meal next Christmas, followed by a little music, a noble act will be accomplished. Donors to the fund will be able to sit down to their goose or turkey with the comfortable feeling that they have helped their less favoured fellows to a little enjoyment at the festive season.—Yours, tkc DELTA. Runcorn, Dec. sth, 1883.

A fire occurred on Thursday evening at the Blackridings Mill, Oldham, and damage was done to the amount of about 00,000. THE SEIZURE OF A BRITISH VESSEL BY RUSSIAN Au- THORITIES.—A telegram has been received in London sta- ting that the owner alai crew of the British otter-hunting schooner Ottome, which was seized by a Russian vessel in August last at Behring Island, have been released from con- finement at Vladivostock. It is not known whether the vessel has been restored, but the question is at present the subject of discussion between the British and Russian ' Governments. Its devalopnaent is watched with much in- terest among Europeans in the East. ENGLAND AND SPAIN.—The report given by El Liberal with regard to the commercial convention between England and Spain is confirmeel. The Times correspondent at Madrid said that the disclosure was made "in bad faith " i c., with intent to injure the Spanish Cabinet. Telegraph- ing on Wednesday, he says:—" In Catalonia, Biscays, and other districts interested, numerous telegrams have been received from here repeating the statement that an arrange- ment between the two countries had positively been made, and the feeling against the present Government has con- oequently been further excited. The Foreign Office up to the present refuses to give any information, and as the semi-official press says nothing, the general deduction is that the Government cannot deny and is afraid to affirm ,he truth of the statements made.

The Major's first business was to make arrangements for the Winging in the prisoners so as to attract as little notice as possible. That settled he sought for and obtained what was not then a very easy matter, a private room for their examina- tion, the house beilg so crowded. Meantime Stephen hur- ried away to bring the men; and before many minutes had passed, all concerned were collected together in the house while a guard watched outside the door and windaw. The scene was curious, and interested Stephen greatly.

The room was simply a very large linen closet with bare floor,and entirely empty of furniture, except a fine old oak chair, richly carved, that bad been breught in for the Major. L was lighted by a tiny jet of gas from the cell-

BURTON WOOD. SERVICE OF SONG AT BURTONWOOD WESLEYAN CHAPEL. —A service of song, entitled " Heaven," was given in the Buttonwood Wesleyan Chapel on Saturday evening last. There was a large congregation, who manifested great in- terest in the service. The choruses, &c., were nicely and effectively rendered by the choir, under the able leadership of Mr. R. S. Sims. Mr. W. Sims presided at the harmonium, while Mr. J. Fairhurst gave the connective readings. The proceeds were in aid of the new school building fund. CADISHE A D. An old man ba4 just died in this village upwards of 90 years of age.

FARN WORTH. ENTERTAINMENT BY THE FARNWCRTII NEGRO TROUPE.- -The minstrels known by the name of the Farnworth Negro Troupe gave an entertainment in Widnes National schools on Saturday evening. The troupe was assisted by the Star of Temperance Brass Band, in whose aid the enter- tainment was given, and several singers. FRODSHAM. FRODSHAM LITERARY AND DEBATING SOCIETY.—A meeting of the above society was held in the girls' school. Frodsbam, on Tuesday evening, under the presidency of Mr. Charles Reynolds, J.P. The subject for debate was "Should not international differences now be settled by arbitration instead of by war? " and was introduced by Mr. E. Rhodes, who concluded his paper with a motion in the affirmative, which was seconded by Mr. Samuel Davies. The motion was, however, negatived by a majority of three votes, the leader of the opposition being Mr. Charles E. Linaker. The usual vote of thanks to the chairman and essayist concluded the meeting. CONCERT AT FRODSIIAM.—An amatear concert was given in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Monday evening, by Dr. Simpson and a few friends, the proceeds being devoted to the funds of the Frodsham Men's Institute. Unfortunately the weather proved very unpropitious, but in spite of thiS drawback there was a large and fashionable audience. The principal vocalists were Miss Wiuward, Miss A. M. Simpson, Mrs. Mayson, Mr. Spafford, Mr. Gilliat, and Dr. Simpson. Pianoforte, Miss Ellam and Miss A. Hutchings. The pro- gramme was a lengthy one and contained some choice pieces, which were carefully rendered and warmly appreciated. It would be invidious to closely criticise the efforts which were kindly put forth; suffice it to say that encores were frequent, and in each case received a graceful recognition. Miss Ellam afforded a rich treat by her skilful execution of two pianoforte solos, the first bein,E,, " Rigaudou (Ralf), and the;sccond a study in C minor ( Ch,,pin),and "Capriccio" (Scarlotti), each being given in finished style and with marked distinction and precision. At the close of the con- cert the vicar, Rev. H. B. Blogg, M.A., proposed a vote of thanks to Dr. Simpson, and in the course of his remarks ex- pressed the hope that Dr. Simpson would again favour than with a concert, by which time he trusted that they would have a more suitable room for the purpose, as it was an open secret that it was seriously contemplated to enlarge and improve the present room. The National Anthem brought the concert to a close.

The reading of the paper was followed by a very animated diS- cussion, in which the following gentlemen joined :—MessrS. R. Hughes, W. Chrimes, S. Barrow, J. H. Gannon, J. BaS- nett, H. div.head: IRLA M.
div.p: IRLA M.

A lecture was delivered i;---t-h—e—Wesleyan Chapel, Mani on Tuesday evening, by the Rev. R. Dillon, of the Cadis- head circuit, on one of Cornwdll's worthies, "Billy Bray, or the King's Son." It was consecutively arranged, aptly illustrated, and thoughtfully delivered. It gave prominence to the characteristics of Billy Bray's life, the integrity of his character, the quaintness and originality of his preaching and its popularity and usefulness; and fidelity to the church of his choice, having lived and died in the communion with the Bible Christians after a membership of 40 years. The practical character of the lecture was maintained, and the lessons taught were suggestive and forceful. It was tened to with deep interest by the audience. There was a collectim at the close for circuit objects. OVER.

YOUNG MEN'S LITERARY SOCIETY.—A soiree in connec- tion with the above Society was held in the Marshall me- morial schools on Wednesday evening. These soirees are becoming very popular, and the one. on Wednesday was ne exception to the rule. The programme consisted of songs, glees, recitations, readings, cornet and harmonium solos by friends and members of the sociesy. During the interval tea, coffee, fruits, and other refreshments were handed round. The Rev. J. Maxwell presided. MA fOR'S SuNDAY.--According to the custom of the last' few years, the Mayor of Over, Edmund Leigh, Esq., was accompanied to St. Chad's Church, Over, on Sunday last. The meeting of gentlemen, friends, rifle volunteers, fire brigade, and police, as well as a miscellaneous crowd took place at the Cross, and with the band playing marched to divine service. The church was crowded as usual on the occasion when fine. The service was performed by the Vicar, the Rev. G. Wyatt Ninis, who made allusions to the gathering, the duties of civic functionaries, /cc., in his ser- mon, and by the special prayer for such. The offertory was devoted to the usual purpose. The bells rang out merrily when the civic procession left the church, but before dismissing, the Mayor invited all to accompany him in the evening to the Congregational Chapel. In the evening the procession formed at the junction of Delamere and High street and proceeded to the chapel, where there was an ex- cellent attendance. The Rev. J. T. Maxwell preached. The offertory was devoted to the Town Mission. SOUrIIWORTII- WITH-CROFT.

ENTERTAINMENT AT THE CROFT BOARD ScnooL.--- Mr. A. Evans, of Haydock, gave the second of a series of dissolving view exhibitions in the above school on Bata' uvralug, but, LUcto viily a Slllall autneut:e. ne entertainment was entitled " Journey to Bethlehem," with selections from miscellaneous subjects. Mr. Evans des' cribed the different scenes in an excellent manner, and hiS remarks were very attentively listened to by the audience. Some of the views were very amusing, and created much laughter. The scholars sang selections of music during the evening, and the proceedings which were highly enjoyed throughout, concluded with the National Anthem.

THE PLOT AGAINST THE GERMAN

EMBASSY. At Bow-street Police Court, on Thursday, William Wolff,. and Edward Bondurand were charged on remand wit' having in their possession explosives for an unlawful put' pose. Colonel Majendie, chief inspector of explosives, der, cribed the nature of the machine found in the possesion Wolff, and said that, properly applied, the quantity of 01' powder it contained would have heen very destructive. 'l' pieces of iron would have been like so road pieces of shell, and would have been most clan' gerous to life. Jacob Kalbon, of 20, Panto 11, street, stated that he had known Bondurand to' about three months. Bondurand took him to Wolff's boat and he agreed to buy some powder for them. Then the)", spoke about the German t mbassy, which Wolff said theY were wishing to blow up. They had previously spoko! of the explosion in the tunnel, is connection with whieP the amount of reward was mentioned. Wolff and Bel; durancl both said what they were inventing would be mtlci more terrible, and that at least £2,000 would be effete!" Witness said they were undertaking something dangerotl", but they both told him not to trouble as filo had the police with them. Wolff said there were 11 persons concerned, namely, himself, Bondurand and 111 brother, a police-officer, and a Polish Jew. Witness es: plained how the explosion was to be effected, and state' that Wolff WAS to throw down at the scene of the explosil a letter written in red ink. Witness was commissioned t, take some paper and an inkstand with red ink to the hol of any German, it did not matter whom so long as he 0,1 a German, and when the explosion took place, and a reWerA was offered, Wolff and the policeman would.. there et 3; take the German into custody. Witness was promised £low The case was adjourned until Friday.

IRELAND.

THREA.TEIIING EA R L SPENE-I;l7—i:Dublin, On Thursday, a youth named Phorpe was sentenced to nine months' impri- sonment for sending threatening letters to Earl Spencer. On Sunday night a Cork steamer ran aground in the river Lee, and whilst the passengers were leaving, in boats, ano- ther steamer approached dangerously close. The occupants of one boat jumped into the water in their fright, and two —a man and child—were drowned.

_ AN IRISH JOURNALIST SENT TO PRISON.—At a special court at Ballinasloe on Monday, Mr. John Callanan, pro- prietor of the Ballinasroe Western News, a Land League organ, WAS sent to prison for a fortnight under the Crimes Act for publishing an article against a herd, named Crehan. A large number of Nationalists assembled at the station to witness Mr. Callanan's departure. AN INSANE MOTHER ATTEMPTING TO DROWN HER CHILD.—At Dublin Assizes, on Thursday, Bridget Keegan was tried for drowning her child in a pool. She jumped in heselt, but was rescued. She said she feared her soul would be lost, that the world was going to be consumed, and she wished to offer herself and child as a sacrifice to the Lord. The jury found her insane, and she was ordered to be con- fined during her Majesty's pleasure. A DREAM AND ITS FULFILMENT.—The County Limerick police are inquiring into the case of a lad named Linehan, whose dead body has been found in a bag under extraordi- nary circumstances. The deceased had been missing for some time, until one night last week his father, according to the latter's statement, dreamt that the lad's body was lying in a particular bog. On rising next morning he pro- cured bloodhounds, and in the identical place he had dreamt of the body was found. ALLEGED ABDUCTION FROM A CONTENT. The Dublin Freeman's Journal gives particulars of an alleged abduction of Catholic children in Dublin. A little boy was carried away in a cab by a clergyman and two ladies; and a little girl named Collins was mysteriously abducted from a con- vent by an unknown woman, who obtained an interview with her on the plea that she was her mother. She threw a shawl over the child, and ran at full speed from the con- vent to a cab, which drove off quickly, leaving the nuns in a state of consternation. No clue to either child has been found.

THE CONDEMNED FENIAN, POOLE: A FRESH TRIAL REFUSED.—In the Irish Queen's Bench, on Monday, before Judges Lawson and Johnson, Dr. Webb, Q.C., with whom were Messrs. Teeling and M'lnerney, renewed his applica- tion for a new trial of the Fenian centre, Pole, who is under sentence of death, on the ground that the notice of the trial by special jury required by the Crimes Act was spent on the occasion of the jury disagreeing, and that no new notice having been served for the second trial there had been a mistrial, and that some of the jurors on the special panel were in duplicate, and others had died. The Court unanimously refused the application as without a shadow of foundation.

MURDERED ON HIS WEDDING DAY.-At the Dublin Assizes, on Thursday, James Eghan, aged 50, was indicted for having wilfully murdered Constable Crowley. It ap- peared that on the 11th July last the deceased was married, and while walking on that day with his bride on the road was attacked by. the prisoner, and mortally stabbed by him. The accused had been evicted by the deceased some time before. The defence was that the prisoner was insane, brit Lord Chief Justice May, in summing up, observed that there was not a particle of evidence to support this plea. The jury, after consulting for 35 minutes returned a verdict to the effect that the accused was insane when he com- mitted the act. The Judge ordered the prisoner to be de- tained during Her Majesty's pleasure, and expressed his ap- proval of the verdict, The jury was a petty and not a special one under the Crimes Act.

THE NATIONAL LEAGUE IN DUBLIN.-At the fortnightly meeting of the National League in Dublin, on Wednesday, Mr. Healy, M.P., presiding., Mr. Harrington, M.P., an- nounced, among other contributions, £l,OOO from the Na- tional League of America. Mr. Biggar referred to Mr. O'Connor Power as the James Carey of Irish politics, and said no Irishman had a chance of getting a situation under the Government who had nof first become traitor to the in- terests of his country. Mr. T. D. Sullivan, speaking upon the proclamation of the Newry meetings, said it had not been the custom of the Nationalists to interfere with Orange celebrations, but it would not surprise him if henceforward, whenever any Orange demonstration was announcad, the Nationalists followed the example set in Newry, and held counter demonstrations at the same time and place. The Government, under the circumstances, would be bound to proclaim both meetings. He attributed the present unhappy state of affairs to the recent tour of Sir Stafford Northcote through the North of Ireland; and he also attributed the Wexford riots to the proceedings in the North since that tour.—Mr. Healy asserted that the reports of theWexford riots were gross exagrra:ions, and expressed a hope that the Nationalists, who were a great majority in the country, and who occipied an impregnable and un- answerable position of legality, would not be betrayed into the iniquitous folly of holding counter demonstrations merely for opposition sake. He considered Lord Rossmore had reason to complain of the action of the Commissioners in depriving him of his commission of the peace. Either he ought to be retained on the commission, or the other men who had acted precisely as Lord Rossmore had done should also be stripped of their commissions. Referring to the proclamation of meetings, he said Lord Spencer believed he was playing the Whig electoral game, and issued proclama- tions in order further to infuriate and embitter the National party in Ulster against the Tories.

div.head: WILL OF THE LATE LORD EGERTON.
div.p: THE WILL OF THE LATE LORD EGERTON.

The will of the late Lord Egerton of Tatton has been proved, the personalty being sworn at £316,531. It is dated the 28th September, 1878. Its chief provisions are as fol- low :—The testator desires to be buried at the parish church of Rostherne in the family vault with his departed wife Lady Egerton of Tatton, and that his funeral be conducted as privately and unostentatiously as possible, and that no achievement or hatchment be erected on any house of his. He gives to his son Wilbraham all his furniture, gold, silver, and gilt plate, including 4t such plate as is marked with his coronet, articles of vertu, books, glass and china of every description, wines, print., pictures, horses and carriages and harness; and all his farming, live and dead stock, and timber which shall be cut down at his decease at Tatton Park, or in the several counties of Chester, Lancas- ter, and Derby, over which he has absolute power of disposal. He gives specific legacies of plate, ckc., to his daughter Eliza Anna Maria Barbara ; his daughter Emily Marion, now the wife of Mr. Percy Mitford ; to her husbarid ; to his daughter Beatrice Catherine Lucia, now the wife of Mr. Lionel Tolle- mantle; to his daughter-in-law Lady Mary Sarah Egerton, the wife of his son Wilbraham; to his daughter-in-law Anna Louisa, the wife of his son Alan de Tatton. To his son Alan de Tatton he gives all the plate formerly belonging to the Countess of Bridgewater, and also the silver inkstand presented to him by tke troop of yeomanry cavalry which he formeily commanded in Cheshire. He also gives the following pecuniary legacies, namely :—To his son Wilbraham the sum of £10,000; to his son Alan de Tatton the legacy of £40,000; to his daughter Elizabeth Anna Maria Barbara the sum of £35,000; to each of his daughters Emily Marion Mitford and Beatrice Catherine Lucia Tollemache, the sum of £30,000. He gives all his estates situate at Fullthorpe or ;elsewhere in the county of Durham, and Mobberley, 011erton, and Knutsford, to his son, Alan de Tatton. His freehold mansion-house in St. James's-square he gives to his son, Wilbraham Egerton. All the residue of his personal estate he gives to his sons, Wil- braham Egerton and Alan de Tatton Egerton, upon trust for his daughters. Legacies or annuities are given to a number of servants.

Two of the largest shipbuilding firms on the Clyde, Messrs. Denny Brothers, and Messrs. A. M'Millan and Son, Dumbarton, posted notices on Thursday, of a 10 per cent re- duction in ironworkers' wages. SHOCKING SUICIDE.—A young man named John Maynard, who had been under medical treatment for somo time, threw himself, on Thursday, under a train on the Launceston and Tavittock line, and was cut in two. DEATII OF MR. T. KNOWLES, M.P. After a protracted illness, Mr. Thomas Knowles, the senior member for the borough of Wigan, died on Monday afternoon at his residence, Darnhall Hall, near Winsford. Mr. Knowles was first returned for Wigan, in the Conserva- tive interest, along with Lord Linclsay, in 1874, the success- • ul candidates taking the places of the two retiring Liberals, fMr. Henry Woods and Mr. John Lancaster; and at the last general election both of them were again returned by a small majority over Mr. Lancaster and Col. MlCorquodale. Mr. Knowles was born at Inca, near Wigan, in May, 1824, and when nine years old he began working in the mine. ' By attending night school—although frequently after 15 hours' confinement in the coal pit—he raised himself above his fellow-workers. He filled most of the offices at the colliery, and where 24 years old was appointed mana- ger by the late me. Thomas Pearson, at his Inca collieries. 141 x years later, owing to his business abilities, he was taken into partnership by Mr. Pearsoa. Ten years ago the works connected with the Dallam Ironworks, Warrington, Were amalgimated with the Wigan collieries, and the con- cern has since been worked by the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iran Co., Limited, Mr. Knowles being chairman. In addition Mr. Knowles carried on cotton spinning at the Sovereign Mills, Wigan. lie was a member of the Wigan Town Council for twenty years, and twice filled the office of Mayor. He'was a director of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and of the Manchester and Liverpool District Banking Company, a justice et the peace for the ceunty, and amongst other public offices occupied the post of president of the Mining Association of Great Britain, for two years. He took on active part in the de- bates on the Employers' Liability Bill, but was overcome with his exertions, and a voyage to America with the Duke of Sutherland and others failed to completely restore him. He was able afterwards to attend to his parliamentary duties for a time, but his health again failed him, and a few weeks ago he was seized with a paralytic stroke, and never rallied, He was twice married, and leaves a family of one Son and three daughters. Mr. Knowles was a strong church- man, and shortly before his last illness promised a sub- scription of £3,000 tow.irds the erection of a new church in his native township of Ince. The funeral of the deceased took place on Thursday in Inca Cemetery, his remains being interred in the family vault, where rest already the bodies of his two wives.

BOILER ACCIDENT: NINE PERSONS KILLED.—The Royal Mail Steam Company have received information by tele- graph of a boiler accident on their steamer Severn at Colon on November 18, when starting on the homeward voyage to Southampton. Nine persons were killed, viz., one engineer, one boiler master, four firemen, one coal trimmer, and a store-keeper. No others were injured. It is announced by the Directors of the London and San Francisco Bank that the loss by the frauds of the late secre- tary will not, exceed £50,000, the amount originally stated. There is reason to believe that a portion of the stolen securi- ties will be recovered. Of the loss £44,000 will be charged to the reserved fund and the balance will be carried to the revelue account of the current year. A WIGAN MAN'S LODGINGS IN Sr. HELENS. Arthur Reed, who said he belonged to Wigan, was, on Monday, charged at the St. Helens Police Court, with haying been , drunk and with having assaulted P.C. Pope. At a quarter- past two o'clock on Monday morning P.C. Pope found the prisoner lying helpless in Liverpool-street. He raised him up and was bringing him to the police office when he resisted , violently and committed the assault.—Fines amounting to 115 s and costs were imposed. ANFIELD (LIVERPOOL).—The first teams of these clubs met as the gt ound of the former, at Wargtave, on Saturday, to fulfil their engagement in the second round of the Liverpool and District Association Challenge Cup competition. The weather was of a very favourable character, and in conse- quence a moderately large assemblage of spectators put in an ' appearance. The ball was set rolling a few minutes alter three by Rich for Earlestown, and was qu'ckly brought down to the Anfield gnat, wio re a corner kick fell to Earlestown, but no good came of it. Play now began to be very fast and exciting, and was being pretty even on both sides. About 15 minutes before half-time Earlestown began to play with care, and about a minute before the change of ends Duxbury secured the first goal for Earlestown amidst great enthusiasm. At half-time the score stood—Earlestown one goal. Anfield none. On the re- commencement of the game k'arlestown strove hard to increase their scare, and after some good play their efforts were attended with success, Champion scoring the second goal. Enlivened by this they began to press Anfield severely, and two more goals were quickly registered by Mather and Duxbury, each receiv- ing hearty cheers from the spectators. The play was now very exciting both to players and onlookers, and about five minutes before "time" Green, from the right wing, shot the sphere under the crossbar for the filth time for Earlestown. Time " was Low celled, and Earlestown thus won a good gime by five goals to nil, a result which evoked the hearty cheers of the spectators as the winr ers left the field. The umpires were Messrs. P. Hastie (Earlestown) and Robson (Anfteld) ; while Mr. J. Hill, of the Birkenhead P.C., ably efficiated as referee. FATAL FIRE.:-A fire occurred on Thursday morning in a house at Glasgow, the roof having been burned off. After the flames were extinguished the firemen discovered the charred remains of an old married woman na ned Eliza Barnes lying on the middle of the floor. SWALLOWING VITRIOL —A young man, named William Hewlett, died on Tuesday night, in St. Thomas's Hospital, London, from the effects of swallowing vitroil. It is thought that he committed suicide because of being jeered at by companions on his joining the Salvation Army. THE LANCASHIRE WEAVERS' STRIKE.—There were large meetings held on Thursday evening at Preston, Burnley, and Clayton-le-Moors. The speakers for the most part— especially the officials—deprecated a strike. At Preston it was agreed to accept the reduction, "working only from dawn to dark," and at Burnley a resolution was passed in favour of remaining at work on the understanding that the reduction was on the Burnley list. At Clayton-le-Moors the feeling was in favour of a strike. ALLEGED ROASTING OF A MAN BY A PUBLICAN.—Thomas Robb (31), publican, of the Freeholders' Arms, Schofield- street, Birmingham, was charged on Thursday with a des- perate outrage upon John Broughton, general dealer, Com- mercial-street, by thrusting him upon a blazing fire, and with kicking and otherwise assaulting him. The prosecu- tor (who was led into the witness box, his eyes being ban- daged owing to the serious injuries he had sustained) stated that on Friday he, the prisoner, and another man took a drive to Cash' Bromwich. They had something to drink, and upon returning they were refused more at a public-house. Shortly afterwards the third man fell out of the trap and "nearly broke his face to pieces." The men then went to prisoner's public-house, and after having something to drink the prosecutor went home. Soon afterwards the prosecutor missed all his money, and, getting on horseback, drove to the prisoner's house, and said, " Give me a little silver, Tom." Prisoner replied, "No, I shall give it the man (the third man) back again." Prosecutor afterwards charged prisoner with robbing him, whereupon the latter, according to the former, exclaimed, "I will burn you to death," and immediately flung him upon the fire, and held him there until he had struggled from his grasp. Prisoner then kicked and struck him several times about the body, rendering bim insensible.—Prosecutor admitted that he had suffered seven years' penal servitude for obtaining money by false pre- tences. Medical evidence showed that the prosecutor was severely burned about the body, besides having his nose broken and sustaining other injuries which will render recovery a work of several weeks.—The prisoner was com- mitted for trial,

div.p: WARRINGrON LIBERAL ASSOCIA- TION, LECTURE ON "THE LAND QUESTION: DEAR FOOD AND SCARCE LABOUR." The second of the series of lectures under the auspices the Warrington Libeial Association took pia, ze at the Wycliffe Hall on Tnursday evening last, when, the Rev. J. D. Alford, of We National Rsform Union _d..4livered an ad- dress on "The Land Question: Pear Food and scarce labour." There was a good attendance . Councillor Monks presided, and there were also an the platform the Rev. R. Filcher, Mr. F. A. Roberts, Mr. Tb .omas Hall, and the lec- turer. The CHAIRUAN (wil() 7ap, cordially received) said he was very glad to be present t ..ere in their own ward and to take his snare in the inter ening coarse of lectures they were holding- gl letter from Mr. Councillor Broadbent saying how sorry ,ae was that he could not attend that even- Ing,.he hadAbee'l in town the best part of the day on public bleineas and 'clad to leave for home, but they had his hearty sympathy and good wishes. (Applause.) He should not mu:ch in introducing to their notice the Rev. J. D. Alfo".d, who would address tuem on a question upon which kg was well (pistil:led to speak. He knew of no question in this country likely to come to the front as the importance Of the land question. Tne land was not like cotton and iron; ,it could not be made into any quantity, as it was limited so far as England was concerned to a certain acreage and it could nut be very mucn increased. Therefore, it was a sort of monopoly, and he thought in the interests of the whole nation they would have to see how that land could be made to serve the best interests of the nation at large and nut the interests of a few individuals. (Hear, hear.) When they considered that landlords and farmers looked to live like gentlemen out of the proluce of the soil and lived mainly out of the lab3ur of the agriculturist he was not surprised that they were beginning to find that they were having very hard times, and that the land was not so productive and profitable as it used to be. The competition with ocean going steamers and railways bringing produce from America. Australia, and New Zealand for a very small amount of car- riage was a question landlords w4uld have t) face, and the l land of this country must not be allowed to go out of cultiva- tion simply because the landlord chose to teed cattle or let it for deer-stalking or game. The land had a much higher purpose thaa for mere sport. Out of the land they had to live. Cotton, iron, silk, and woollen industries were net to be compared at all with the aggregate value of the agri- cultural produce of this country, and to allow such an en- ormous industry as their agricultural interest to go to ruin, to do that they would be the greatest fools the world had ever seen. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that the question of landlords and land together would come prominently before the country with a view to its settlement on a right and honest basis. (Applause) He would not detain them longer, but introduce to them at once their friend the lecturer to speak on that very important subject—" The laid . question: dear food and scarce labour." .(Ap- plause.)

If any person had a claim it was aeferred to the Registrar at once, and the whole thing was settlea without lawyers fees. tie thought it would be well to go back to that old ctiecom of dispesing of land. (Hear, hear.) 'I hose were two privileges which they had not at the present day. By and bye there came William of Normendy at the head of his army and conquered the country, and when he did so he claimed to be the only land-owner .in the country, and the right of distributing estates amongst his followers. He made them tenants, and gave them the use of the estates. but it was done in this way. Supposing the chairman was king, and had given to him an estate of 60.000 acres; well, he could not cultivate that quantity, so he would cut up the estate into eight or ten parts, and he gave one part to this man and ano- ther to that. He thereby became lord of a lot of tenants, a•nd they were under the same conditions as he was with the king. Then the men to perh 'pi he had granted 10,000 acres could not cultivate so much, and he cut them up in like manner, giving one 25 acres, another 50, and another 80, and so on, so he in the same way became lord of the large number of tenants, and these estates were held under a law of primo-geniture. Mr. Alford then pro- ceeded to speak of the system of collusive alienation which was adopted by the landholders, by the means of which the king was deprived of all his rents. When Edward I. came into office he tried to recover the king's rights ; but then scientific farming went to the monasteries. Having referred in an interesting manner to the " dodges " between land- lords and Churchmen to obtain possession of the land, he said that they came te the year 1660, when there took place in this country a revolution, in which landholders made themselves landowners and effectually put the whole of the rents into their own pockets. When that revolution was accomplished, and when they succeeded in being themselves owners and getting rid of all feudarclaims over their estates, the land was still encumbered by all those different estates. Complicated systems of title deeds were then drawn up— drawn up as awkwardly and as complex as they could be devised —in order to conceal the right possessor of the land, and that had come down to them to- day.
