This was a younger brother of the lad who some time ago stole some money from his parents, and had a feast in the Market, an account of which went the round of the papers. Another brother had served three months imprisonment for breaking into a shop and stealing a number of articles, while the parents were a very re- spectable and industrious pair.—The Bench thought it would be best to send the lad to a reformatory school, but the father begged that his son might have another chance.— The Chief Constable : We have several lads in Warrington who have done their four er five years in reformatory schools, and who when they came out could searcely write their own names.—Mr. George Riley, school attendance officer, said, in answer to questions, that some time ago the School Attendance Committee were troubled with the boy's irregular attendance at school, but now he was attending re- markably well.—The prisoner was ordered to receive six strokes with the birchrod.
A SEQUEL TO HANDOCK COURSING MEETING. A VICTIM TO TEMPTATION.

Yesterday, at Warrington Police Court, a respectably- dressed man giving his name as Wm. Pilkington, a clerk, of Leyland, was charged with stealing a gentleman's travelling bag, containing a quantity of docummts, the property of James Barnby.—lt seems that the prosecutor, who is em- ployed by tke Royal Liver Friendly Society as a travelling inspector, and whose residence is at Bradford, has for some weeks been staying at the Temperance Hotel, Sankey-street, kept by Mr. Herbert Richards. On Tuesday morning he went away, leaving his bag in charge of Mr. Richards. The prisoner lodged at the Temperance Hotel on Tuesday night, and on Wednesday morning Mr. Richards noticed the pri- soner leaving his house with the bag in his possession. He followed him, brought him back, and gave him into the custody of the police. When charged at the police station , with the theft, he said "I could not resist the temptation when I saw it." He first gave the name of William Savin, of Stockport-road, Manchester, but this statement was found to be incorrect, and be afterwards gave his name as Williern Pilkington, of Leyland, and said that he was formerly in business in Manchester, but latterly had been a clerk, and was now out of work.—The prisoner made a long statement to the Bench, which was to the effect that he had been living with two daughters at Leyland, and being out of work he came on Tuesday to Havdock coursing meeting, where he lost a bit of money. He, however, had a little money left, and finding that Warrington was not far away, he thought he would come here "to spend a quiet evening," after which he intended to raise a little money by pawning his overcoat, and then to return to Haydock and try to regain the money he had lost.—Captain Reynolds: What, by betting again 7—The prisoner: I thought so. Con- tinuing, he said he came to Warrington and lodged at the Temperance Hotel. While waiting for breakfast on Wednes- day morning he saw the bag, "and there like as if some- thing tempted him to pick it up, and go walking away out." —Captain Reynolds said he was sorry that a man in prisoner's position should so far forget himself as net to know his own property. He would have to go to gaol for a month with hard labour.

CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY.—A meet- ing of the Prescot branch of this society was held on Mon- day last in the Houghton-etreet Schoolroom. Interesting addresses bearing on the subject of temperance were given by the Revs. H. A. Macnaughten and J. Johnston, and a pro- gramme, which consisted of songs, readings, and recitations was gone through to the evident pleasure of the audience. A SMOKING CONCERT AT PRESCOT. —The first smoking concert, under the auspices of the Anfield Bicycle Club, was held at the Royal Hotel, Prescot, on Saturday last. In spite of the unfavourable weather several of the local clubs ,rure represented. A well selected programme was very c,editably rendered by the members and friends. These c .ocerts will be continued during the winter months, as they largely contribute to keep cyclists together.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF A CHILD AT WARRINGTON. THE MOTHER CENSURED.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF A CHILD AT WARRINGTON. THE MOTHER CENSURED.

Mr. T. W. Barker, coroner, held an inquest at the Wheat Sheaf Inn, Orford-lane, on Thursday afternoon, touching the death of Bridget Glyn, eight weeks old, daughter of John, Glyn, bricksetter's labourer, of 13, Silver-square.—Mrs. Don- nell, a neighbour of Glyn's, said that on Wednesday at noon she was called in to see the child, and she found it dead. The child was one of twins. She had known Mrs. Glyn five years, and she had never seen her drunk.—Bridget Glyn ' said she was mother of the deceased. The deceased and the other twin had been healthy' since their birth. She was in the habit of giving them the breast. At six o'clock on Wednesday morning she gave the deceased the breast and then went to her work, leaving it and the other babe in bed. Her mother took charge of the children when witness was at work. She returned home to breakfast at 10 o'clock on Wednesday morning. The babes were still in bed apparently asleep, and she asked her mother if they bad been good. Her mother replied that they had. She then went out to work again, not having looked at the babes because she did not want to disturb them as they were ap- parently asleep. Her mother was quite able to look after the children, and she usually gave them " pobs."—The Coroner : You put a drop of g,n is them sometimes P—Wit- ness : No, sir. Continuing, she said that she returned home to dinner at 12 o'clock and found the twin babes still in bed. On looking at them, however, she found that the girl was dead—the other was a boy. It had never had fits, and she did not think it had been smothered, nor that it died for want of food. It was well looked after for food.—The Coroner said he did not know about the latter. She had left the child six hours, and she did not know whether it had had any food during that time or not. —Witness said she did not know whether deceased had any food during the six hours. She did not know why the girl had died and the boy had not died. The girl was all right and the boy was ill.—Julia Hyland said she was mother to the last witness, and therefore grand- mother to the children. She was left in charge of the two children on Wednesday. Her daughter told her that she gave the twins the breast when she went to work at six, and they did not receive any breast after that. The deceased never stirred all the morning, but the boy cried, and she gave it some aniseed and gin. She did not know whether the deceased was living when she was attending to the other babe. She did not disturb the deceased to give it food, be- cause it was in the habit of sleeping all the morning, and she was not surprised at its not moving.— The Coroner: Supposing the child had wakened and wanted food, what would you have given it P—Witness : Bread and water, sir, which I have been giving them always.—By a Juryman : She did not give the deceased any aniseed and gin on Wednesday.— fhe Coroner: Did you give it any cinder tea ?—Witness: No, sir. Continuing, she said the hands of the deceased were clenched, and the body was discoloured.—The Coroner, addressing the jury, said he thought when he received the police notice and saw that the child had apparently been left six hours without food that there was some gross neg- lect on the part of someone. The case, however, was now changed, as it appeared the child had been left in the charge of its grandmother. The reason, a very natural , one, why its mnther did not feed the child when she went home at 10 o'clock was that it was sleeping. if the child ' had been left with no one in charge then it would have been a case of gross neglect. From the appearance of the body he should be inclined to think that the deceased died from donvalsions.—A juryman thought that there was neglect somewhere.—Another juryman said he did not think any blame should be attached to the mother, as it appeared she had five children and she had to turn out to work.— Another juryman said he had known the father and mother if the deceased for a long time, and he considered them res- nectable for their class. He did not think the mother had neglected the child intentionally.—The coroner and several )f the jury: Oh, no.—The juryman: But as far as I know of the children about here, they are being systematically

STOCK AND SHARE MARKET.

Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 1:4, Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (Dec. sth):-- Under the influence of what was supposed to be indication of more reaceful manifestations touchin the F, anco-Chinese affair, and a better look-out for the coal trade owing to strike of miners being averted, the leading markes have shown a deal of buoyancy during the greater part of the week, but to- day and yesterday uneasiness has been manifested, at d some decline from top points has occurred almost all r, und, though prices still show many advances compared with last week's figures. Foreign funds show a few alterations, but the balance of movement is favourable. Egyptian Unifieds are practically unchanged, only sellers quotations beimg altered, and that a fall of merely t wbi'st the preference are b and the Daira Sanieh If to it higher. Italians are 1, Argentine hard dollar f, and Spanish if to f bet- ter,but Russians are if to Mexican 3 per cents. and Peruvians to 3-8 low r. Mexican rails have been steadier and freer from violent fluctuations than of late, and on the week alters goodly number of dealings exhibit a rise of nearly 2 per cent. Their traffic return this weekwas a decrease, but of only R 1,402, but Vie total takings are not such as to warrant present values. The aggregate of business done in the miscellaneous series of Vivestments is very small. Contrary to recent experience coal, Iron, &c., and mining shares have produced the most transac- tions, but it is not owing to any general demand for those shares, but is more attributable to the paucity of the number of dealings in the other classes.

NEW POOMMATE FOR KNOWSLEY AND ECCLESTON (RIIRAL).—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Mr. Dunn, assistant overseer, applied for the sanction of the Bench to the levyinv of a poor-rate of is. 6d. in the pound for the township of Knowsley, and 2s. in the pound for Eccleston (Rural). EARLF,STOWN GOSPEL TEMPERANCE MISSION.—ThiS mission is still progressing in a satisfactory manner. On Sunday last the Co-operative Hall was crowded, when Mr. Morris Jones, of Liverpool, preached two excellent sermons. The weekly meeting and entertainment was held last evening.

ALLEGED THEFT OF A BROTHER'S TROUSERS. - At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, a youth named John Dolan was charged with having stolen a pair of trousers, the property of his brother, Peter Dolan. The prisoner, it seemed, lodged with his brother ia Crab-street. On the 25th ult. both the trousers and the prisoner were missing, and on Sunday last the complainant saw his brother wear• ing the missing trousers, and consequently gave him into custody.—The case was dismissed.

PRESCOT YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION.—The first of a series of entertainments in connection with the above was given in the EbenEzer Schoolroom on Saturday evening last. There was a pretty good audience, and the chair was occupied by the Rev. James Johnston, pastor of the Congregational Church. The programme, which was of a miscellaneous character, was gone through very credit- ably by Messrs. Anderton, Barlow, and Myres. Miss Lyon contributed two solos, which were well rendered.

THE MAINTENANCE OF CHILDREN.—WM. Waterwortb, a labouring man, was summoned before the St. Helens magistrates, on Friday last, to show cause why he should not be committed to gaol for non-paymmt " of is 6d per week towards the support of a child in a reformatory school. The defendant, it was stated, owed £1 8s to the reformatory school. He was at present earning 3s 8d per d 43, wages, and had four children to keep.—He was ordered to pay the full amount before the Monday followiag, or go to gaol for one month. Ma Com= X—.—Cammack.—Advt.

TEMPERANCE ENTERTAINMENT AT EARLISTOWN.—An entertainment of an enjoyable character was held in the Good Templars Hall, Bridge-street, on Saturday evening. when there was a full attendance. Bro. Edward Newman presided. Bro. James Barnard, of Newton, gave an in- teresting account of his experience at Gibraltar, Malta, Aden, Bombay, Calcutta, and throughout the Indian mutiny. Mr. William Walker, Mrs. Walker, Miss S. J. Walker, Mr. George Warburton, and Mr. John Gee took part in the subsequent proceedings.

SIIRVICII OF SONG AT EARLESTOWN.—The choir of the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Legh-street, Earlestown. as- sisted by a number of the school children, gave in that place of worship on Tuesday evening last, a service of song en- titled, "Poor Mike, or the story of a waif." There was a good audience, and the musical selections, which were capi- tally given, were very much appreciated. The connective readings seemed to create considerable interest, and they were given by the resident minister, the Rev. F. N. Shim- min. Mr. W. Banton conducted the singing, and Mr. W. Austin presided at the harmonium. ASSAULT ON A LANDLADY.—Patrick Duggan, of Earles- town, was charged at the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday with assaulting Elizabeth Lytbgoe, landlady of the Oddfellows' Arms, Ear.lestown. On the 24th ult. the defendant went to the Oddfellows' Arms, and asked to be served with beer. Mrs. Lythgos, seeing that he was drunk, refused to serve him, and requested him to leave the house. He thereupon hit her on the left side of the head and felled her to the ground, and while she was down he kicked her. The defendant called a witness named Margaret Knight,who said that Mrs. Lythgoe in pushing the defendant out fell, and that both Mrs. Lythgoe and her husband were the worse for drink. She added that Mr. Lythgoe said if he could have five minutes with the defendant he would not summon him, but would nuke an example of him.—The defendant was fined 20s and costs.

CONCERT AT NEWTON TOWN HALL.—The large MORI Of the Newton Town Hall was nicely filled last evening (Thursday), when the annual concert under the auspices of the Newton Cricket and Bowling Club was held. The vocalists were of known ability, and the audience did not fail to appreciate and applaud the praise-deserving efforts of the singers. A commencement was delayed owing to the late arrival of Dr. Mapei, of Golborne, who ought to have taken part in the opening song, "The open air." This was omitted, owing to Dr. Mapei's absence. Mr. W. Haskell, of Newton, gang "A gallant heart" (Barn), and in response to a recall, repeated the last verse. Miss Parry, ef St. Helens, who possesses a deep contralto voice, nicely gave "To the wood" (Warner), but appeared to over-exert herself in her efforts to bring out the most difficult parts " Sweethearts " (Sullivan) was sung by Dr. Mapei; and was succeeded by Miss Kay, of Wigan, who was well received. Her pure voice was heard to advantage in Hutchinson's popular piece " lihren on the Rhine ;" which, if anything, was given rather too speedily. Next came a capitt inter- pretation of the duet "The sailor sighs," by Miss Parry and Dr. Mapei. Dr. Coombs, of Wigan, who gave a humourous sketch from a Christy Minstrel's entertainment, created un- bounded amusement and enthusiasm. On being recalled, he sang "In a casual way" with marked ability. Mr. W. A. McClure, of Wigan, proved to have lost none of his popu- larity with the Newtonians, and he received a warm welcome. He gave an impressive and effective rendering of Barn's "Saved from the storm." Undoubtedly Miss Hart, of Wigan, was not far from securing the greatest success of the evening. This was her first appearance in Newton, though it is doubtful if it will be the last. She possesses a remarkably distinct utterance, and has an excellent command over her sweet-toned voice. Her ren- dering of the song "Cowslips" (Roeckel) brought forth rapturous applause, and on an encore being demanded she gave the amusing piece, "Terry O'Shay." The first part of the programme was concluded with the part-song, "Swing Song" (Pinsuti), by Miss Kay, Miss Ferry, Dr. Mapei, and Mr. McClure; and, after a short interval, the same quartette gave "The Lass of Richmond Hill." Miss Kay pest sang "Children's Home" (Cowen), and Dr. Coombsacl,aiu amused the audience with a humourous parody on " Just before the battle, mother." He received a vociferous encore. Dr. Mapei and Mr. McClure .afterwards capitally rendered "The Moon bath raised her lamp above." "The Broken Pitcher" (Roeckel) was finely sung by Miss Hart, who even acquitted herself to greater advantage than in her first effort.. She was again rewarded with a recall. Dr. Mapel received an encore for his renderiug of the well-known "Tom Bowling"; and Miss Parry nicely gave the Scotch piece, "Auld Robin Gray." Mr. McClure splendidly sang "Tell her, I love her so (De Faye) and on being re-called he simply bowed his acknowledgements. To meet the convenience of the singers the part song "Good night, beloved "was given by Miss Kay, Miss Parry, Dr. Mapei, and Mr. McClure; after which Dr. Coombs again convulsed the audience with laughter by his humourous sketches " Manders' Menagerie" and "Jolly old sow " ; the latter being given on his being re-called. The programme, which had taken two and a half hours to he carried out was coucludLd with the National Anthem, The accom' oanists on the pianoforte were Mr. P. Fairclough and Mrs Mapei.

LATEST NEWS. THE PLOT AGAINST THE GERUAN EMBASSY. Wolff and Edward Boudurmat were again charged at Bow- street, yesterday, with illegal possession of explosives, in- tended to blow up the German Enihasy.—Leon Darrell was further cross-examined as to his previous history and con- viction in France, and on behalf of Boudurant it was attempted to show that he was thecompanion of and worked for immoral persons.—lnspector Marshall deposed to Wolff giving him information as to the alleged plot at the same time Louis Boudurant was informing to Inspector Green- ' ham, Scotland-yard. He did not report the circumstance to his superiors until November 22. Wolff and Boudurant had previously given information concerning burglaries.— Adjourned for the night. THE WIGAN ELECTION. The Conservatives of Wigan have invited Mr. N. Eckersley, who formerly represented the borough, to con- test the present vacancy. Mr. McCorquodale was waited upon by the Liberal deputation yesterday afternoon, but has , deferred his decision for a day or two. BRADLAUGH V. GOSSET. The case of Bradlaugh v. Gosset came for hearing yes- terday, before the Lord Chief Justice and Justices Stephen and Matthew. The plaintiffs seeks to restrain the Sergeant- at-Arms from carrying out the orders of the House of Commons, directing Mr. Bradlaugh's exclusion from its precincts. Mr. Bradlaugh conducted his own case in per- son, the Attorney-General and other counsel representing the Sergeant-at-Arms. The Attorney-General took pre- liminary objection to the plaintiffs' right of action on the ground that the court could not questian the power of the House of Commons to pass orders for its own regulation. On Mr. Bradlaugh's application, however, the statement of claim was so amended that the whole question might be raised before the court, and he then pre- ceeded to address their lordships in support of his case, contending the court had ample power to adjudicate, and instancing various cases in which orders of the House of Commons had been declared illegal. He further contended that the resolution of July 9th was not a Standing Order, and that the House had no power to prevent him doing that which the statute law made it incumbent on him to do. The Attorney-General, in reply, argued that the court had no jurisdiction. The I ord Chief Justice said the court would take time to consider their judgment. ----- THE PARNELL NA.TIONAL BANQUIT.—At this bar quet in Dublin, on Tuesday, the gallery will be occupied by five hundred ladies, and every county in Ireland will be repre- sented. THE MORMONS AND THE PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE.—The principal Mormon organ, published at Salt Lake City, attacks the paragraph in the President's Message directed against Utah, and declares that polygamy is a portion of the Mormon "faith," and will never be abandoned. Ipswica ELECTION: SINGULAR INCIDENT.—It is stated at Ipswich that Mr. Felix Cobbold, brother of the late Con- servative member, has written to Mr. West, the Liberal candidate, stating his intention of supporting him, and thanking him for his consideration in avoiding any appear- ance as a candidate during his brother's illness. WRECKED IN A SNOWSTORM.—The Ramsgate lifeboat yesterday morning landed Captain Smith and the crew of 24 of the shields steamer Boadicea bound to Cavour with coals. She went ashore on ,Thursday afternoon in a snow- storm on the Shingles. The crew abandoned her, boarding the Tongue Lightship, whence they were brought ashore ' by the lifeboat. A meeting was held at Monaghan yesterday to protest against the suspension of Lord Rossmore. A large contin- gent of Orangemen, with flags and drums, proceeded to the raiiway station and enthusiastically cheered Lord and Lady Rossmore on their arrival from Dublin. The horses were taken from the carriages in waiting, and his lordship and other visitors were drawn by enthusiastic Orangemen to the place of meeting. O'DoNNELL's "COMPANION" IN LIVERPOOL.—The young woman who was O'Donnell's companion on the voyage to the Cape, when Carey was murdered, arrived in Liverpool on Wednesday night, and sailed on Thursday for New York in the White Star steamer Germanic. The woman is evi- dently of Irish nationality, and rather prepossessing. She is accompanied by a man:whom the police describe as havit the appearance of a well-dressed Bowery denizen. The pair took cabin passages. MORI RIOTS AT CANTON.—A New York Herald Hong Kong telegram, dated Thursday, says another mob at Can- ton on Wednesday destroyed the chapel which was built at the expense of the native Christians. The soldiers dis- persed the mob. Two hundred remained to guard the ruins. The mob seemed to think that General Pang had arrived to drive out the foreigners, and wanted to assist him. The mob did not attack the Shameen foreigners there, who are perfectly under cover of the Juamla and three other Euro- pean gunboats, besides the Viceroy's boat. Tan GREELEY EXPEDITION.—CcIpt4tI William Adams, of Dundee, an experienced arctic navigator, has published a statement regarding the Greeley Expedition to the North Pole. He expresses the belief that some of the party have survived, among whom is, perhaps, Dr. Parry. Captain Adams thinks that the party will be either in the vicinity of Cape York, or between there and Etah. He suggests that a relief expedition should leave England about next June, and indicates his willingness to take the command and re- urn in three months.
